He took Taormina on 1 August 902, completing the Muslim conquest of Sicily, then crossed into Calabria. He died of dysentery on 23 October 902 before Cosenza. His destruction of the Arab nobility left the Aghlabid army weak, and the Kutama Berbers led by Abu Abdullah al-Shi'i conquered Ifriqiya by 909, founding the Fatimid dynasty.
ibrahim-ii-of-karaman: The Karamanids, centred on the present-day provinces of Karaman and Konya, had been the strongest of the Anatolian beyliks that arose after the Seljuk era, until the Ottomans came to dominate most of Anatolia late in the 14th century. Ibrahim, born in 1400, was the son of Mehmet Bey. He fought his uncle Ali Bey for the throne and took it in 1424 with Ottoman support. In 1425 he married Ilaldi Sultan Hatun, a daughter of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed I; the marriage was unhappy.

Ottoman help did not buy his loyalty. He secretly allied with the Kingdom of Hungary and took Beyşehir while the Ottomans were at war in Europe. When Sultan Murat II returned to Anatolia in 1433, Ibrahim sued for peace in 1435, then besieged Amasya; Murat backed the Dulkadirids in taking Kayseri and Ibrahim's brother İsa in taking Akşehir, and Ibrahim lifted the siege in 1437. In 1444, as a crusader army marched on the Ottoman capital, he plundered Ankara and Kütahya. Murat signed the Treaty of Szeged with the crusaders, turned on Karaman and forced Ibrahim into an unfavourable treaty.

Relations with the Mamluks of Egypt were usually good, though they had backed İsa against him early on. Rivalry over Çukurova, ancient Cilicia, ended the friendship. In 1448 Ibrahim took the castle of Corycus, modern Kızkalesi, from the Kingdom of Cyprus, which opened the way to the rest of Çukurova, but in 1456 the Mamluks and their vassal, the Turkmen beylik of Ramazan, attacked him, and he gave up hope of conquering the region. After Murat's death he allied with Venice, but did not fight the Ottomans.

In his last years his sons fought for the throne. His chosen heir was Ishak, governor of Silifke, but the younger Pir Ahmed proclaimed himself sultan in Konya. Ibrahim and Ishak fled to Gevale Castle near Konya, and Ibrahim died as they reached it. One account, given by Şikârî and supported by Kıvâmî, holds that Mehmed II, promising him the rule of the Karamanid lands, induced Ibrahim's own vizier Ahmed Pasha to poison him with a cluster of grapes, and that Ibrahim died 26 days later; another says he died of natural causes.
ibrahim-khalil-khan: Ibrahim Khalil Khan Javanshir was the son and successor of Panah Ali Khan and the second khan of Karabakh from the Javanshir family. He was among the deportees taken with his father to Astarabad and returned when Adil Shah recognised Panah Ali as khan. His father used his marriages to build alliances: in 1749 he was married to Shahnisa, sister of Nazarali Khan Shahsevan of Ardabil, and to Tuti, daughter of Shahverdi Khan of Ganja, and he also married Hurizad, daughter of the Armenian melik Shahnazar II of Varanda. In 1759 he was handed as a hostage to Fath-Ali Khan Afshar and released by Karim Khan Zand.

With help from Umma Khan of the Avar Khanate he defeated his younger brother Mehr Ali Beg for the khanate. By the 1780s he was one of the most powerful rulers of the eastern Caucasus, allied with King Heraclius II of Kartli-Kakheti against Fatali Khan of Quba, until Heraclius accepted Russian protection in the Treaty of Georgievsk in 1783. From 1775 he also campaigned against the Armenian meliks of Karabakh: Melik Yesai of Dizak was captured after a long siege and strangled in 1781, and when the meliks secretly wrote to Catherine II in 1783 he seized several of them and the Catholicos Hovhannes, who died in prison.

In 1795 he refused to submit to Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, as the khans of Ganja, Nakhjavan and Erivan did, and held Shusha through a 31-day siege, later acknowledging Qajar supremacy in a verbal truce. In 1797 the shah returned and took Shusha, but was assassinated there three days later; Ibrahim, who had fled to the Avar Khanate, came back, gave him an honourable burial, and gave a daughter in marriage to his successor, Fath Ali Shah Qajar.

During the Russo-Persian War, General Tsitsianov promised to recognise him as khan, and after their agreement Russian troops garrisoned Shusha. After Tsitsianov's death in 1806 Ibrahim renounced his allegiance and asked the shah for help, camping outside the fortress as a Persian army approached. On 12 June 1806 Russian troops under Dmitry Lisanevich attacked the camp and killed him with one of his wives, a daughter and his youngest son. The Russians made his son Mehdi Qoli Khan Javanshir khan of Karabakh.
ibrahim-lodi: Ibrahim Lodi, the eldest son of Sikandar Lodi, ascended the throne without opposition after his father's death in late 1517. Early in his reign he tried a power-sharing arrangement by installing his brother Jalal Lodi as autonomous governor of Jaunpur. When Jalal began to assert independence, Ibrahim reversed the decision on the counsel of senior courtiers. He summoned Jalal to Delhi and, when Jalal refused, secretly told provincial governors and nobles to withhold recognition, forcing Jalal back to Kalpi.

Jalal won the backing of the noble Azam Humayun Sarwani and seized Awadh, but Azam went over to the Sultan when Ibrahim advanced with a large force. A truce let Jalal keep Kalpi, but it was short-lived. Ibrahim pursued him to Gwalior, Malwa and the Gonds, who betrayed him; he was captured on his way to Hansi and quietly executed on Ibrahim's orders. Ibrahim then sent an expedition of 30,000 cavalry and 300 elephants, led by Azam Humayun, against Gwalior, which fell in 1518 with the surrender of Vikramaditya Tomar. A further army sent against Rana Sanga of Mewar was defeated, a blow to his military reputation.

Jalal's revolt deepened Ibrahim's mistrust of his Afghan and Turkish nobles. He tightened court protocol and arrested prominent figures, among them Azam Humayun Sarwani and Mian Bhuwah. Azam's son Islam Sarwani raised about 40,000 men with the support of Lodi chiefs to demand his father's release; Ibrahim refused and crushed the rebellion in an engagement that killed around 10,000. He had Mian Bhuwah executed, Azam Humayun died in captivity, and Mian Husain Farmuli was murdered at Chanderi by Ibrahim's agents. Nobles in the eastern provinces began fortifying their positions, and Bahar Lodi proclaimed independence on the death of his father Darya Lohani.

Daulat Lodi, governor of Punjab, sent his son to Kabul to enlist Babur's support, and Ibrahim's uncle Alam also sought Babur's aid. In 1524 Babur seized Lahore and took control of the Punjab. By early 1526 he launched a full invasion, and at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526 Ibrahim's larger army was defeated by Babur's tactics and superior cavalry. Ibrahim died on the field, ending Lodi rule in Delhi and the independent Delhi Sultanate and opening the way for the Mughal Empire.

His tomb is often mistaken for the Shisha Gumbad in Lodi Gardens, Delhi; it stands near the tehsil office in Panipat, and in 1866 the British moved and renovated it during the building of the Grand Trunk Road.
ibrahim-nasir: Ibrahim Nasir was born on 2 September 1926 on Fuvahmulah, the son of Ahmad Didi of Malé and Aishath Didi of Fuvahmulah. He was descended from the royal houses of Huraa on his father's side and Dhiyamigili on his mother's. His family moved to Malé, where he studied at Madharusathul Salahiyya, later Majeediyya School, and he then studied for a time in Sri Lanka before beginning a rapid political climb.

Nasir became prime minister under Muhammad Fareed Didi on 12 December 1957 and was also Minister of Finance until November 1968. In 1959 the three southernmost atolls, Huvadu, Addu and Fuvahmulah, which benefited from the British presence on Gan, cut ties with the government when Nasir meant to cancel the Gan agreement. They formed the United Suvadive Republic under Abdullah Afeef. The British had backed it but changed their stance after Nasir sent gunboats from Malé, and Afeef went into exile.

The government then forcibly evacuated the whole population of Havaru Thinadhoo and destroyed its homes. Critics call this a violation of human rights and a crime against humanity, while others praised Nasir for ending the separatist movement. In 1960 he renegotiated the Gan agreement with the British.

The Maldives became independent on 26 July 1965. Nasir secured admission to the United Nations on 21 September 1965, when the population was under 80,000. He was sworn in as president on 11 November 1968. His government opened the first tourist resort, Kurumba, in 1972, though a United Nations mission had advised against tourism, and in 1976 the Maldives joined the Non-Aligned Movement.

Nasir resigned and went into self-exile in Singapore on 7 December 1978, and Maumoon Abdul Gayoom succeeded him. In 1981 he was sentenced in absentia on charges of corruption and plotting a coup, none of which were proven, and he was pardoned in July 1990. Nasir died in Singapore on 22 November 2008, aged 82, and was buried beside the Friday Mosque in Malé.
ibrahim-njoya: Njoya was the son of King Nsangu, a ruler known in the region as a warrior, and was born while Bamum was at war with the Fulani and divided within the royal family. He traced his line to Mfon Ncharé, who founded Bamum in 1394. After Nsangu was killed fighting the Nso, Njoya's mother Njapdunke ruled as regent until he came of age. His formal accession was delayed further because the Nso held his father's head, which is of ceremonial importance to the Bamum, and the Germans helped him to recover it.

Njoya ruled from the walled city of Foumban and kept generally good relations with the Germans, whom he received with great celebrations. On the birthday of Emperor Wilhelm II he gave him a throne, which was exhibited in Berlin by Felix von Luschan; in return Wilhelm sent him a cuirassier uniform of the Imperial Guard. The historian Stephanie Michel argues that Njoya was no mere subordinate in these dealings. By 1912 the Bamum had turned from the Germans towards the Fulbe, and in 1916 Njoya and much of his court converted to Islam and he accepted the authority of the Sokoto Caliph.

In 1916 the French took control of German Cameroon, and the kingdom lost its partial autonomy. Although France formally abolished his rule, Njoya kept the role of king in practice while he lived in Foumban. In 1931 he was sent to Yaoundé, where he died two years later, aged 66, and was succeeded by his son Seidou Njimoluh Njoya.

Njoya turned older picto-phonographic glyphs into a script in five stages over about fifteen years: from Lerewa, a logographic system of 510 signs, through Mbima, Nyi Nyi Fa Fu, Ri Nyi Fa Fu and Ri Nyi Fu Fen, to Akauku, completed in February 1910, with 70 syllabic characters, ten digits and three diacritics. In 1903 he built schools to teach it, and it was used for maps, birth certificates, court acts and archives. After the old palace of Foumban burned in 1913 he designed the present one, which he said was the result of his own ingenuity.
ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt: Ibrahim was the first-born son of Muhammad Ali and Amina Hanim, the widow of an Ottoman official. He was born in the village of Nusratli, near Drama in the Ottoman province of Rumelia, and was of Albanian origin through his father. In 1805, at sixteen, he was sent as a hostage to the Ottoman Kapudan Pasha during his father's struggle to establish himself in Egypt, and he returned once his father was recognised as Wāli. From 1811 to 1816 he was Prince of Upper Egypt, with his seat at Girga, and in 1816 he succeeded his brother Tusun Pasha in command of the Egyptian forces in Arabia.

His campaign in Arabia lasted two years and ended in the destruction of the House of Saud as a political power. He followed the Saudis into the desert of Nejd, and by the end of September 1818 he had forced their leader Abdullah bin Saud to surrender and had taken and sacked Diriyah. He entered Cairo in triumph on 11 December 1819. In 1824 he sailed for the Morea with 17,000 men to help Sultan Mahmud II against the Greek Revolution, landing at Modon on 26 February 1825.

He brought the siege of Missolonghi to an end on 24 April 1826, but was defeated three times in Mani. In reprisal against Greek guerrillas he devastated the country and sent thousands of inhabitants into slavery in Egypt, which aroused indignation in Europe. After the Battle of Navarino on 20 October 1827 he evacuated the Morea under the capitulation of 1 October 1828.

In 1831 he was sent to conquer Ottoman Syria. He took Acre on 27 May 1832, defeated Ottoman armies at Homs and Beilan, and routed the Grand Vizier Reşid Mehmed Pasha at Konya on 21 December. He stayed on as governor, but intensified taxation, conscription, disarmament and forced labour provoked revolts from 1834. In that year he besieged Al-Karak for 17 days and destroyed the town. After his last victory at Nezib on 24 June 1839, the United Kingdom and Austria intervened, and he was compelled to evacuate Syria in February 1841.

Ibrahim spent his last years in peace, but his health was ruined. He visited Western Europe in 1846, and when his father became senile he was appointed regent, holding the office from July until his death on 10 November 1848. In 1872 the Khedive Ismail commissioned a large statue of him by Charles Cordier, but the Ottomans objected to two reliefs showing their defeats, so it was first erected without them. On the centenary of his death in 1948 the reliefs were rebuilt, and the complete statue stands in a square in Cairo.
ibycus: Ibycus was an ancient Greek lyric poet, a citizen of Rhegium in Magna Graecia, active in the second half of the 6th century BCE and probably at Samos during the reign of the tyrant Polycrates. Few biographical facts are known and the testimonia are difficult to interpret.

The Byzantine encyclopaedia Suda gives his father as Phytius, Polyzelus or Cerdas, and says he went from Rhegium to Samos in the 54th Olympiad; its chronology has been dismissed as muddled, and Eusebius's date for the poet's first fame, between 542 and 537 BCE, fits Polycrates' reign better. A proverb tells that he refused the chance to become tyrant of Rhegium to pursue poetry. Some scholars think he spent time at Sicyon, and possibly in Sparta, before Samos.

Hellenistic scholars at Alexandria counted him among the nine canonical lyric poets. He was remembered mainly for love poetry, but he also composed narratives on mythological themes in the manner of Stesichorus, and structured his verses in triads. The scholars compiled only seven books of his work, numbered, not titled. His surviving verse is a blend of the public choral style of Stesichorus and the private style of the Lesbian poets, in a literary language largely Epic with Doric touches.

Until the 1920s only two fairly large fragments and about fifty lines from commentaries were known; papyrus finds since then added forty-eight lines addressed to Polycrates. Athenaeus quotes a fragment in which love, like the Thracian north wind ablaze with lightning, shakes the poet from the roots, in contrast with the calm of spring.

The Suda says he was captured by bandits in a deserted place and declared that cranes flying overhead would avenge him; later one of the bandits saw cranes in the city and cried out, and the crime was confessed. This gave the proverb the cranes of Ibycus.

The story is also found in Plutarch and Antipater of Sidon and inspired Friedrich Schiller's ballad Die Kraniche des Ibykus of 1797, though it may derive from a play on his name and the Greek word for a bird. An anonymous poem in the Palatine Anthology names Rhegium as his resting place. Ancient scholars said that Ibycus first told that Achilles would marry Medea in the Elysian Fields.
ichijodani: Ichijōdani is the valley of a branch of the Asuwa River, about 500 metres wide from east to west and about three kilometres long, in the Kidonouchi section of the city of Fukui. Mountains enclose it on the east, west and south and the river on the north, so that it formed a natural fortification.

In 1471 the Asakura displaced the Shiba clan as shugo, or military commanders, of Echizen Province, and that year Asakura Toshikage (1428–1481) fortified the valley with hilltop forts on the mountains around it and walls and gates at its northern and southern ends. Within them stood his fortified mansion, the homes of his relatives and retainers, and later the houses of merchants and artisans and Buddhist temples. People of culture and skill fleeing the Ōnin War found refuge there, and by the time of Asakura Takakage (1493–1548) the town had over 10,000 inhabitants.

The Asakura kept good relations with the Ashikaga shogunate, which brought them into conflict with Oda Nobunaga. After Nobunaga took Kyoto, Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiaki asked Asakura Yoshikage, head of the clan since 1548, to help drive him out. Nobunaga invaded Echizen, won at the Siege of Kanegasaki and the Battle of Anegawa in 1570, and razed Ichijōdani in the Siege of Ichijōdani Castle in 1573, ending 103 years of Asakura rule.

Excavation began in 1967 and has uncovered the whole town: the lord's house, samurai residences, temples, the houses of merchants and craft workers, and the streets. Samurai and merchant houses have been restored along a street 200 metres long, and four gardens have been partly restored. Of about 1,700,000 relics found, 2,343 are Important Cultural Properties, many shown at the Ichijodani Asakura Family Site Museum. The whole site of 278 hectares was designated a Special Historic Site in 1971.
idalion-tablet: The tablet was kept in antiquity in the official depository of the temple of Athena on the western acropolis of Idalion, where a farmer from the village of Dali found it in 1850. Honoré Théodoric d'Albert de Luynes bought it and gave it in 1862 to the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and it is now in the BnF Museum in Paris. Its script could not be read until after the discovery of the Idalion bilingual in 1870.

Both sides of the bronze are engraved with a long inscription in the Cypriot syllabary, read from right to left, in the Arcadocypriot dialect of Greek. It records a contract made by the king and the city, which rewarded a family of physicians for treating free of charge those wounded when the city was besieged by the Persians and the Kitians, in the years 478–470 BCE. A passage of about two lines orders the physician and his brothers to heal the men wounded in the battle without fee; in the syllabary each word is spelled out sign by sign, so that anthropos, man, is written a-to-ro-po-se.

The tablet is of exceptional importance for the history of the Cypriot kingdoms, since it tells historians about the political system and the social and economic conditions of the city during the war. That the decision was taken jointly by the king and the citizens has been read as showing a democratic character in the city's government, close to Greek models. The inscription has also been described as recording the earliest known system of social welfare, and it is often treated as the earliest example of an insurance contract, since it shares some of the main features of modern ones.
idar-oberstein: Idar-Oberstein lies on the southern edge of the Hunsrück on both sides of the river Nahe, in the Birkenfeld district, and is the largest town in the Hunsrück. The present town is the product of two rounds of administrative reform, in 1933 and 1969, which joined many municipalities into one. Nine villages, among them Enzweiler, Göttschied, Weierbach and Nahbollenbach, were added in 1969 and 1970. The districts have kept their own identities, and Idar and Oberstein are the more urban ones, the others recalling their past as rural villages.

Before the French period the area was split among many lordly domains. Oberstein grew out of the Imperially immediate Lordship of Oberstein, whose Herren vom Stein, the Lords of the Stone, are first mentioned in 1075. They sat at Castle Bosselstein, above the cliff where the Felsenkirche, or Rock Church, was later built, and after 1323 called themselves von Daun-Oberstein. Oberstein took on the character of a town without ever gaining the legal status of a market town, and its old town wall was built about 1410. The lordship passed to the Counts of Leiningen-Heidesheim in 1682, to the Counts of Limburg-Styrum in 1766 and to the Margraves of Baden in 1776.

The French reorganised the territory from 1794, and until 1814 it lay in the arrondissement of Birkenfeld. The Code civil and the abolition of noble and clerical privilege made French rule popular, though taxes and conscription weighed heavily. After the Congress of Vienna the Nahe became a border, and the centres on its north bank joined the Principality of Birkenfeld, an exclave of the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg. At the end of the First World War Grand Duke Friedrich August abdicated, and the French occupied the area on 4 December 1918 and stayed until 30 June 1930. Since 1938 the town has been a garrison town and later the site of the Bundeswehr artillery school.

Idar-Oberstein is known as a gemstone town. Until the 18th century the area was a source of agate and jasper, and cheap labour and the free water power of the Nahe, which drove the mills with cutting and polishing machines, helped the industry flourish. The Felsenkirche, built in 1482 by Wirich IV of Daun-Oberstein on the foundations of an older refuge castle in a great cave, is the town's defining landmark. The German Gemstone Museum stands in Idar, and a gemstone mine, the Steinkaulenberg, is open to visitors.
ide-anak-agung-gde-agung: Ide Anak Agung Gde Agung was born in Gianyar, Bali, on 21 July 1921, the son of Raja Anak Gunung Ngurah Agung, the Raja of Gianyar. Interested in history from childhood, he went to the Hollandsche-Inlandsche School, then to MULO and the Algemeene Middelbare School, studied law at the Rechtshogeschool in Batavia and later took a doctorate in history at the University of Utrecht. On 23 August 1943, during the Japanese occupation and after his father had been detained on suspicion of treason, he became Raja of Gianyar at the age of 22.

His political career began in the State of East Indonesia, where he was prime minister from December 1947 to December 1949 under Tjokorda Gde Raka Soekawati. In 1948 he founded and led the Federal Consultative Assembly, the association of federal states and territories formed to strengthen their hand in the negotiations between the Dutch and Indonesia, and he played a decisive part in the Round Table Conference that led to Dutch recognition of Indonesian independence. After the transfer of sovereignty on 27 December 1949 he was minister of the interior in the short-lived Republic of the United States of Indonesia.

His federalist sympathies set him against Sukarno, who wanted a unitary republic. After the federal system was abolished in 1950 he served as ambassador to Belgium, Luxembourg, Portugal, France and Austria, and as foreign minister he took part in the West New Guinea dispute. He was imprisoned from 1962 to 1966 without trial, until the foreign minister of the New Order, Adam Malik, released him and restored him to a senior post; he was again ambassador to Austria.

Abroad he wrote Twenty Years Indonesian foreign policy 1945–1965, a 660-page history arguing that Indonesian foreign policy rested on independence and action, free of foreign powers, and that Sukarno abandoned it by aligning with China and confronting Malaysia. He died in Gianyar on 22 April 1999. Besides the title of National Hero, he received the Bintang Mahaputra Adipradana, and a street in the Mega Kuningan district of Jakarta bears his name.
idi-amin: Idi Amin was born to a Kakwa father and a Lugbara mother. Virtually all retellings of his early life are contradictory, since he wrote no autobiography and never authorised an account of his life, and no records were kept for native Ugandans at the time. In 1940 he was rejected when he tried to register for primary school, reportedly because of his paternal Nubian heritage. He joined the King's African Rifles in 1946 as an assistant cook and received military training until 1947. He served in Kenya, was sent against Somali rebels in 1949 and against the Mau Mau rebels in 1952, and was promoted to sergeant in 1953.

After Uganda's independence in 1962 Amin was promoted to captain and then to major in 1963, and in 1964 he became Deputy Commander of the Army. A rift with President Milton Obote grew from Amin's support within the army, recruited from his home region of West Nile, and in October 1970 Obote took control of the armed forces. Having learned that Obote planned to arrest him for misappropriating army funds, Amin seized power on 25 January 1971 while Obote was at the Commonwealth summit in Singapore, and he declared himself president on 2 February.

Amin ruled by decree, placed military tribunals above the civil law and replaced the General Service Unit with the State Research Bureau, whose headquarters in Nakasero became a scene of torture and capital punishment. Lango and Acholi soldiers were massacred in the barracks at Jinja and Mbarara in July 1971, and bodies were often dumped in the River Nile. The killings continued throughout his eight years in power, and the exact number of dead is unknown, with estimates differing widely.

He expelled Asians, mostly Indian-Ugandans, in 1972, and India broke off diplomatic relations. In 1977 the United Kingdom broke off relations and he added CBE, for Conqueror of the British Empire, to his titles. His attempt to annex Tanzania's Kagera Region in 1978 led President Julius Nyerere to order an invasion, and Tanzanian and rebel forces took Kampala in 1979. Amin fled to Libya, then to Iraq, and finally to Saudi Arabia. He died in Jeddah on 16 August 2003.
idia: Idia entered the royal household after Oba Ozolua saw her dance and wished to make her his wife; historians are not sure of the date, but they married before 1504. According to an oral tale, an oracle advised that cuts above her eyes, filled with medicine, would keep Ozolua from choosing her, but the king saw what had been done and neutralised the medicine. The two incisions above her eyes appear on her later portraits.

Esigie was third in line for the throne. The eldest son, Ogidogbo, was crippled while playing with his brothers and could no longer reign, and many in Benin believed Idia had planned this through magical powers. Esigie's half-brother Arhuaran, next in line, saw him as a threat, but tradition holds that he held back because he believed Idia commanded magical arts. After Esigie's accession she fought beside him, and when the Igala crossed the River Niger to seize Benin's northern territories, his victory was credited largely to her counsel, magic and medicinal knowledge.

Custom required the king's mother to be killed after his crowning, but Esigie hid her in a room that only the authorised could enter until he had abolished the law. She then returned freely to the palace and, before her death, trained her son's wife in her ways.

After her death Esigie had brass heads of her cast by the lost-wax method for her memorial palace. The four known are in the British Museum, the World Museum in Liverpool, the Nigerian National Museum in Lagos and the Ethnological Museum of Berlin; like other Benin Bronzes, the images of her taken in 1897 are the subject of calls for their repatriation.

The London head shows her in a high ukpe-okhue crown of red coral beads and the parrot's beak hairstyle that only the Iyoba and the major war chief might wear. Two ivory masks of her, in the British Museum and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, were worn by Esigie at ceremonies; their crowns show Portuguese soldiers and mudfish.
idomeneus: In Greek mythology Idomeneus was a Cretan king and commander who led the Cretan armies to the Trojan War in eighty black ships. He was also one of the suitors of Helen and a comrade of the Telamonian Ajax, and Meriones was his charioteer and brother-in-arms. He was the son of Deucalion and Cleopatra and the grandson of King Minos of Crete and Queen Pasiphaë, so his line ran back to the sun god Helios. His wife Meda bore him Orsilochus, Cleisithyra, Iphiclus and Lycus. The chronicler Malalas described him as above average height, dark-skinned, with a thick beard and curly hair, and a berserker when fighting.

In Homer's Iliad Idomeneus stands in the first rank of the Greek generals, leads his troops against the enemy head-on and escapes serious injury. He is one of Agamemnon's trusted advisors and one of the main defenders when most of the other Achaean heroes are wounded, and he fights Hector briefly and repulses his attack. He is alive at the close of the story and is among those who enter the Trojan Horse. He is said to have killed twenty men and at least three Amazon women, including Bremusa.

A later tradition, kept by the grammarian Servius in his commentary on Virgil's Aeneid, tells of his return. A terrible storm struck his ship, and he promised Poseidon to sacrifice the first living thing he saw at home if the god saved ship and crew. It was his son, whom he sacrificed. The angry gods sent a plague to Crete, and the Cretans exiled him to Calabria and then to Colophon in Asia Minor, where he died. Apollodorus tells it differently: his foster son Leucus drove him out after seducing and killing Meda and seizing the throne, and Porphyry says Idomeneus sacked Lyctus and other cities Leucus had taken.

Varro held that the Salentini descended from Idomeneus, who sailed from Crete to Illyria and then with Illyrians and Locrians to Salento. The story was also told by the French writer François Fénelon in the seventeenth century. Mozart's opera seria Idomeneo of 1781 is based on the tale of his return to Crete, but in it Poseidon, called Neptune, spares Idomeneo's son Idamante on condition that Idomeneo hands his throne to the new generation.
idrieus: Idrieus was the second son of Hecatomnus and was married to his sister Ada. With her he succeeded their sister Artemisia II of Caria in 351 BCE. Like the earlier Hecatomnids he held the standing of a king or dynast, by virtue of the powerful position he inherited, while ruling as satrap under the Achaemenid Empire.

Soon after his accession the Persian king Artaxerxes III Ochus asked him for arms and troops to capture Cyprus. Idrieus fitted out a fleet of 40 triremes and an army of 8000 mercenaries, sent against the island under Evagoras and the Athenian general Phocion. This is the only recorded event of his reign. A passage of Isocrates suggests that by 346 BCE relations with the king had turned to open hostility, yet it also counts Idrieus among the wealthiest and most powerful princes of Asia, and Demosthenes says he added Chios, Cos and Rhodes to his hereditary lands.

He was an active builder. He may have completed the Mausoleum, the tomb of his brother Mausolus at Halicarnassus, which Artemisia had left unfinished at her death. At Labraunda he continued the building of Hecatomnus and Mausolus: inscriptions show that he dedicated the temple of Zeus and its southern and eastern gateways and built the so-called Doric house. Unlike Mausolus he called himself Mylasan in his dedications, stressing his local roots, and some of them may predate his rule.

Idrieus died of a disease in 344 BCE after a reign of seven years, and Ada, who had shared his rule as the junior partner, succeeded him. The two appear together in dynastic portraits at Mylasa and at Tegea in the Peloponnese and in statues at Delphi dedicated by the people of Miletos, and an inscription in the Carian language from Sinuri records an edict issued in both their names.
idrija: Idrija lies in the Idrija Basin, surrounded by the Idrija Hills, in the traditional region of Inner Carniola, though its inhabitants now mostly consider it part of the Slovene Littoral. The Idrijca River runs through the town. Under Austrian rule the town was known as Idria.

In the Middle Ages Idrija was managed by the Patriarchate of Aquileia and the Counts of Gorizia. Mercury was discovered in the late 15th century, with various sources citing 1490, 1492 and 1497. According to legend, a bucket maker working at a local spring saw a small amount of liquid mercury in 1490. Idrija is one of the few places where mercury occurs both in its native state and as cinnabar ore. The Republic of Venice occupied the town for one year, in 1508, but it was otherwise governed by the House of Habsburg. The mine owners built Gewerkenegg Castle between 1522 and 1533, and the government took over the mining in 1580.

Idrija was a cornerstone of the global supply of mercury, and it supplied the silver mines of the Spanish Empire when other mines faltered in their deliveries. The mineral idrialite, found there in 1832, is named after the town. In the later 19th century lace-making became a source of international trade, and by 1905 lace was exported to Europe, America and Egypt. Idrija passed to Italy in 1920 under the Treaty of Rapallo and in September 1943 came under Nazi Germany. After the war it formed part of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia within Yugoslavia, and in June 1991 it became a town in independent Slovenia.

The mercury mine, with its stores and infrastructure, the miners' living quarters and a miners' theatre, forms a World Heritage Site together with the Spanish mine at Almadén, inscribed in 2012. Visitors can tour the upper levels through Anthony's Shaft, while the lower levels, which reach almost 400 metres below the surface, are no longer worked. Idrija lace is a bobbin tape lace with protected geographical indication.
idrimi: According to his inscription, Idrimi was a younger son of Ilim-Ilimma I of Halab, and his mother's family were connected with the lords of Emar on the Euphrates. After what the text calls a crime in his father's house, the family fled from Aleppo to Emar, where Idrimi said that whoever lived among its people was a slave. Leaving his brothers, he took his horse, chariot and squire into the desert and joined the Habiru at Ammiya in the land of Canaan, where refugees from Halab, Mukish, Nihi and Nuhašše gathered around him.

In the seventh year, the inscription says, the storm-god Teshub turned towards him. He built ships and brought troops by sea to Mukish, and Ni'i, Mukish and Alalakh came over to him in a single day. His brothers then joined him, and they swore a mutual alliance.

Idrimi sent the envoy Anwanda to Barattarna, king of Mitanni, who had been hostile to him for seven years, recalling the old treaties between the kings of Halab and the Hurrian kings. Barattarna accepted his tribute, and Idrimi swore an oath as a loyal vassal. The historian Paul Collins notes that Mitanni left him limited freedom of action as long as he did not cross its policy.

The inscription says he attacked Hittite territory, destroyed seven cities and built a palace from the booty. A treaty with Pilliya of Kizzuwatna, another vassal of Barattarna, provided for the exchange of fugitives and set rewards of five hundred copper shekels for a returned man and one thousand for a woman. His seal was later used by his son and successor Niqmepa.

Leonard Woolley found the statue in a pit of a later temple at Tell Atchana. Its 104 lines are written in a provincial dialect of Akkadian, and Jacob Lauinger dates the inscription to around 1400 to 1350 BCE, after Idrimi's lifetime. Many scholars read it as pseudo-history or a moralising tale, and Tremper Longman finds in it the threefold structure of Akkadian fictional autobiography. Adolf Oppenheim compared its pattern of sevens with the story of King David, and Edward Greenstein with those of Jacob, Joseph and Moses.
idris-alooma: Idris, also called Idris Amsami, was a son of mai Ali II Zainami and of Amsa Aliram, who was probably a daughter of a Bilala ruler. Ali died after a brief reign without adult male heirs and was followed by his nephew Dunama VI Muhammad and Dunama's son Abdullah IV. The magira, or queen mother, Aissa Koli then held the throne until Idris could take it, and abdicated in his favour. Accounts differ on how the two were related; some say she raised him in secret in a brick palace at Gambaru, near the Yobe River, away from the capital Ngazargamu.

His reign is the best documented of any Sayfawa ruler, because his chief imam, Ahmad ibn Fartuwa, recorded its first twelve years. Idris established qadi courts that separated the judiciary from the executive, built mosques of fired red mud bricks and made at least two pilgrimages to Mecca, where he arranged a hostel for pilgrims from his empire. Ibn Fartuwa noted that most Bornu notables converted to Islam, though the historian Mervyn Hiskett finds no convincing evidence that Islamic law became Bornu's state law.

Besides musketeers trained by Turkish advisers, his army relied on fortified posts called ribats and on camel cavalry, and large boats crossed Lake Chad quickly. His campaigns reached from Fezzan to Kano. A first attack on Amsaka, a fortified non-Muslim town east of Mandara, was repelled; on a second, his men filled its ditch under cover of musketeers on high platforms, cut down its stockade and sacked it, and he ordered all its inhabitants slaughtered. More than five expeditions against the Bilala ended with the annexation of Kanem.

When the Ottomans seized the Fezzan oases in 1577–8, Idris sent envoys to Istanbul; Sultan Murad III refused to give up the territory but ordered good relations with Bornu. Idris then sought help from Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco, seemingly pledging allegiance to him, and soon afterwards the Ottoman garrison in Fezzan was slaughtered, which the historian Remi Dewière thinks Idris may have planned. Idris was killed near present-day Maiduguri by an archer hidden in a tree and buried in the middle of Lake Alau, from which came the name Alooma.
idris-i-of-morocco: Idris ibn Abd Allah, also called Idris the Elder, was a Hasanid, a great-grandchild of Hasan, the son of Fatima and Ali and grandson of Muhammad. He was born and raised in Arabia. His paternal half-brothers Muhammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya and Ibrahim had been killed by the Abbasids during an abortive rebellion, and his brother Yahya, who rose in revolt in Daylam, was forced to surrender and was afterwards persecuted and repeatedly imprisoned by Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

Idris himself took part, with Yahya, in the Alid uprising of 786 under al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Abid. After the revolt's defeat at the Battle of Fakhkh he escaped and hid, then moved to Egypt, where Wadih, the local head of the caliphal postal system, helped him reach the Maghreb.

In 789 Idris arrived in Tangier and went on to Walīlī, the site of the Roman Volubilis. Recent excavations by the Moroccan Institute of Archaeology and University College London have found his headquarters just outside the walls of the Roman town, which the Berber tribe of the Awraba, under Ishaq ibn Muhammad, then occupied. He married Kenza of the Awraba and fathered a son, Idris II. This is regarded as the consolidation and birth of the Idrisid dynasty, the fourth Muslim state in Morocco after Nekor, Barghawata and Midrar. Idris conquered large parts of northern Morocco, founded the city of Fez, and captured Tlemcen from the Sufrite Ifranid Abu Qurra.

These successes prompted Harun al-Rashid to send emissaries to kill him. Idris died in 791 at Walīlī, allegedly poisoned by the caliph's agents. His son Idris II was born a few months later and brought up by the Awraba under the regency of Rashid, his father's freedman and adviser; he left Walīlī for Fez in 808 and consolidated the Idrisid state. Idris I was buried on a hill not far from Walīlī, and the site grew into the village of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun, where a zawiya centred on his mausoleum developed over the centuries and remains an important religious site in Morocco. He is regarded as the founding father of Morocco.
idris-ii: Idris II was born in Walili in August 791, two months after the death of his father, Idris I, in June of that year. His mother was Kenza, his father's wife and the daughter of Ishaq ibn Mohammed al-Awarbi, chieftain of the Awraba tribe, and he was raised among the Berber Awraba of Walili. In 803 he was proclaimed Imam in the mosque of Walila, succeeding his father. Among the Idrisid rulers he was one of the best educated.

Idris II oversaw the arrival of two waves of Arab refugees, from al-Andalus in 818 and from Ifriqiya in 824-826, who settled mainly in the capital, Fez. The Arabization of Morocco began in his reign, and Fez became predominantly Arabic-speaking. He was guarded by an Arab bodyguard and had an Arab minister, Umair bin Mus'ab. Ibn al-Abbar quotes a correspondence between Idris II and his contemporary the Aghlabid emir Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab, in which Idris invited him to renounce his claims to his territories.

He led numerous successful expeditions and attacks against the Kharijites. By the end of his reign the Idrisid realm included the area between the Shalif river in modern Algeria and the Sous in southern Morocco.

Idris II died in Fez in 828. The Idrisid emirate was then divided into nine principalities ruled by his sons, with the eldest, Muhammad ibn Idris, ruling as the emir from Fez. His grave lies in the Zawiyya Moulay Idris in Fez. It was rediscovered under the Marinid sultan Abd al-Haqq II in 1437 and became an important place of pilgrimage in the 15th century. It is considered the holiest place of Fez.
idris-of-libya: Idris was born at Al-Jaghbub, the headquarters of the Senussi movement, the son of Sayyid Muhammad al-Mahdi al-Senussi and his third wife. His grandfather, Sayyid Muhammad ibn Ali as-Senussi, founded the Senussi Sufi order, a revivalist Sunni movement based largely in Cyrenaica. By the end of the 19th century the order had set up a government in Cyrenaica that united its tribes, controlled its pilgrimage and trade routes and collected taxes. In 1916 Idris became head of the order when his cousin Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi abdicated.

Ahmed Sharif had attacked British forces in Egypt under Ottoman pressure. Idris stopped the attacks and made a tacit alliance with the British Empire that lasted half a century. Through British intermediaries he negotiated with the Italians, who had invaded Cyrenaica in 1913, and agreements at al-Zuwaytina and Akrama left most of inland Cyrenaica under the Senussi. In 1920 the Accord of al-Rajma made him Emir of Cyrenaica with autonomy over several oases. In 1922 Tripolitanian leaders asked him to extend the emirate into Tripolitania, and he agreed in November. Fearing Italian retaliation under Mussolini, he went into exile in Egypt in December 1922.

The Italian reconquest followed. Cyrenaica's livestock was decimated, much of its population was interned in camps, and an estimated 12,000 Cyrenaicans were executed in 1930 and 1931. In the Second World War Idris supported the United Kingdom, and a Libyan Arab Force of volunteers served in support and gendarmerie roles. After the war British and French forces governed Libya. The United Nations General Assembly resolved in November 1949 that Libya should become a single independent state under Idris as king by January 1952.

Idris proclaimed the United Kingdom of Libya from Benghazi on 24 December 1951. The country had about one million people and was one of the poorest in the world, with an illiteracy rate of 94 percent. It was federal, with Benghazi and Tripoli as joint capitals. Idris banned political parties, and from 1952 all candidates were government nominees. In 1963 he abolished the federal system and the country became the Kingdom of Libya. He allowed British and American air bases in return for aid. Large oil reserves found in 1959 raised per capita income from $25 to $35 in 1951 to $2,000 by 1969, and Libya joined OPEC in 1962.

Idris was deposed on 1 September 1969, while in Turkey for medical treatment, by army officers under Muammar Gaddafi; the coup came a day before his intended abdication. He went into exile in Egypt and was sentenced to death in absentia in November 1971. He died in Cairo in 1983 and was buried at Medina. He had married five times, and none of his children survived childhood.
idwal-foel: Idwal was a member of the House of Aberffraw and is also known as Idwal ab Anarawd, Idwal son of Anarawd. His father was Anarawd ap Rhodri, King of Gwynedd, and his paternal grandparents were Rhodri Mawr, King of Gwynedd, and Angharad ferch Meurig of Ceredigion. He inherited the throne of Gwynedd on his father's death in 916, and the chronicler William of Malmesbury called him King of the Britons, as his father had been called.

Idwal allied himself with King Æthelstan of England after Æthelstan's accession in 924. The English king was eager to establish his authority across Britain, and Idwal honoured him by visiting his court in 927, 928 and 937. On the first of these visits Idwal signed charters agreeing to campaign with Æthelstan against the Scots. That year he marched with Hywel Dda of Deheubarth and Morgan ab Owain of Gwent against Owain ap Dyfnwal, King of Strathclyde, who was forced to submit to the English king and appear at his court by Christmas.

Æthelstan died in 939 and was succeeded by his half-brother Edmund. In 942 Idwal, apparently fearing that the Saxons would support Hywel in taking his throne, attacked the Saxons in Wales together with his brother Elisedd. The Annales Cambriæ record the outcome: "Idwal and his brother Elisedd are killed in battle against the Saxons". The throne should then have passed to his sons Iago and Ieuaf, but Hywel Dda invaded Gwynedd and drove them out.

Idwal had several sons, among them Meurig, Iefan, Iago, Cynan, Rhodri and Ieuaf, also called Idwal Fychan, little Idwal. Iago and Ieuaf returned to reclaim their patrimony after Hywel's death in 950, and the line continued through Meurig's grandson, Iago ab Idwal ap Meurig.
iestyn-ap-gwrgant: Iestyn ap Gwrgant, whose name means Iestyn son of Gwrgant, also appears as Jestyn ap Gwrgant. He was the last ruler of the royal house of Morgannwg, a kingdom that took in the later counties of Glamorgan and Monmouthshire and whose line reached back more than five centuries to Tewdrig. The house was linked by marriage to the other royal houses of Wales and descended from Rhodri Mawr. Iestyn's seat is believed to have been at Dinas Powys, south-west of Cardiff.

Iestyn probably ruled Morgannwg for a little less than a decade, from about 1081 to 1090, and is believed to have built castles in the districts of Cardiff and Kenfig. In the popular version of events he quarrelled with his rival Einion ap Collwyn and invited Robert Fitzhamon and his twelve knights into the region to settle the matter, but once there they refused to leave.

About 1090 Fitzhamon, lord of Gloucester, deposed him, set up a lordship based on Cardiff and went on to conquer the lowlands of Glamorgan, the Vale of Glamorgan, which he divided among his followers, while the mountainous parts were left in Welsh hands. Iestyn's eldest son, Caradog ap Iestyn, was the only Welsh lord to keep lands in the lowlands, between the River Neath and the River Afan; he and his descendants were known as the lords of Afan.

Families said to descend from Caradog include the Williams family of Aberpergwm and the Powell Wilkins family of Carreg Cennen in Carmarthenshire. Iestyn's arms form the Flag of Glamorgan, which in turn is a charge on the flag of Cardiff, and they appear in the crest of Pontypridd Rugby Football Club. The writer Richard Williams Morgan later claimed that the family records of Iestyn ab Gwrgant mentioned Saint Cyllin, a son of Caratacus, and cited this as evidence of an early arrival of Christianity in Britain.
ifa: Yoruba tradition holds that Ifá began at Ilé-Ifẹ̀, where Orunmila initiated himself and then his students, Akoda and Aseda. Samuel Johnson and Obadiah Johnson wrote in 1921 that Arugba, mother of Onibogi, the 8th Alaafin of Oyo, brought Ifá to Oyo in the late 1400s. The linguist Wande Abimbola argued that it probably grew out of a simpler system, dilogun. From Yorubaland it spread across lower Nigeria and west into Benin, Togo and Ghana; the Fon adopted it while Dahomey was a vassal of the Oyo Empire, and it was well established at the royal palace under Gezò.

Sixteen major Odù combine into 256 signs, which believers hold to cover every situation in life through countless ese, poetic teachings that are passed down orally from one babalawo to another and never written. Eshu-Elegba is held to carry Ifá's will to humanity and to the other spirit-deities. Among the Fon, where the system is called Fá and the word evokes coolness and calm, the female spirit Gbădu, Fá's wife, is regarded as the source of its power. A divining chain may be made of eight nut halves tied together, and its fall gives one of the 256 signs.

Traditionally only men became babalawos, though women have been initiated, and by the early 21st century female practitioners called iyanifá were becoming institutionalised in some communities in the United States. In Benin a priestly initiation takes place in Fá's sacred forest, where the initiate's sign is divined and fixes the taboos he must keep. In Cuba Ifá became the most complex and prestigious divination of Santería; an estimated 200 babalawos there in 1959 had grown to tens of thousands by the 1990s, by their own claims.

Cuban migrants carried Ifá to the United States, where the Nigerian babalawo Ifayẹmi Elébùìbọn led ceremonies in Miami in 1978, and Nigerian teachers ran an Ifá course in Brazil from 1977, though Candomblé uses dilogun instead. A church founded in Lagos in 1934, the Ijọ Ọ̀rúnmila Adulawọ, treated Ifá's teachings as the Yoruba Bible. UNESCO proclaimed Ifá a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005.
ifat-sultanate: The Sultanate of Ifat, called Wafāt or Awfāt in Arabic texts and also the Kingdom of Zeila, was a Sunni Muslim state of the eastern Horn of Africa. It formed around eastern Shewa in present-day Ethiopia and stretched from Zequalla to the port of Zeila, which gave it a trade outlet and an entry point for Islam into Ethiopian lands. According to al-Maqrizi, the Walashma ruling class claimed Arab descent from the Hejaz and from Aqil ibn Abi Talib, but scholars hold this claim was probably fictitious and that the dynasty was of local origin.

Ifat arose when Umar ibn Dunya-huz, later called Sultan Umar Walasma, carved out a kingdom and conquered the Sultanate of Shewa. In 1288 Sultan Wali Asma imposed his rule on Hubat, Zeila and other Muslim states. Taddesse Tamrat compares this effort to unite Muslim lands with the one Emperor Yekuno Amlak was making among the Christian highlands.

In 1320 a conflict began between the Christian monarchy and Ifat. Emperor Amda Seyon I had warned the Mamluk sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad to stop persecuting Copts, and Sultan Haqq ad-Din I responded by invading Amhara, burning churches and forcing conversions. He also seized the emperor's envoy and killed him when he would not convert. Amda Seyon raided Shewa and Ifat in return. In early 1332 Sabr ad-Din rebelled, aiming, according to the emperor's chronicle, to become king of all Ethiopia. Amda Seyon destroyed Ifat's capital, took Sabr ad-Din prisoner and appointed his brother Jamal ad-Din I in his place.

Fighting continued under the emperor's successors. Haqq ad-Din II moved the capital towards the Harar plateau and Zeila, and is regarded by some as the true founder of the Adal Sultanate. According to al-Maqrizi, he fought the emperor in over twenty battles and died in 1376. His successor Sa'ad ad-Din II raided Ethiopian lands. In the early fifteenth century an Ethiopian emperor invaded Ifat and its troops were defeated in 1403 on the Harar plateau. Sa'ad ad-Din fled to Zeila, where he died. The sources disagree on which emperor led the campaign, and on whether he died in 1403 or 1410.

The Muslims were harassed for over twenty years after the defeat, according to al-Maqrizi, who wrote around 1435. Adal, with its capital at Harar, emerged as the leading Muslim principality in the later fifteenth century, and small territories were ruled by Walasma groups until the eighteenth century. Harari tradition holds that the Argobba fled Ifat for the Harar area during the fifteenth-century conflict. Ifat's infantry consisted of Argobba, and its people included Somalis, Afars, Warjih, Silte and Hararis, speaking Cushitic and Ethio-Semitic languages with Arabic as the common tongue. The name survives in the Ethiopian district of Yifat in North Shewa.
ife: Ife lies in Osun State in south-western Nigeria, about 218 kilometres north-east of Lagos, in a mixed rural and urban landscape within the tropical savanna climate zone. Roads link it to Ibadan, to the west, and to Osogbo, 40 kilometres away. The city is said to have been founded sometime between 1000 BCE and 500 BCE, and by 900 CE it had become an important West African emporium producing sophisticated art. By the 1100s it had entered a classical period and become the capital of a significant regional empire. The name Ife means "expansion".

In Yoruba tradition the supreme god Olodumare ordered Obatala to create the earth, but Obatala became drunk on palm wine on the way. Oduduwa took the items of creation, descended on a chain and cast earth on the primordial ocean, so that it rose as a mound called Oke Ora; a five-toed cockerel scattered the earth. Oduduwa planted a palm nut that grew into a tree with sixteen branches, which stands for the sixteen clans of the early Ife confederation. The rivalry of Oduduwa and Obatala is still re-enacted at the Itapa festival.

The sons, daughters and grandchildren of Oduduwa are held to have founded other kingdoms, among them Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ilesha and Oyo. Oranmiyan served in Benin and left behind a son, Eweka, who became the first Oba of the second Edo dynasty; Oranmiyan later founded Oyo.

Ife is known for its naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculpture, which reached its peak between 1200 and 1400. Around 1300 artists developed a refined naturalistic tradition, many works apparently made under the patronage of King Obalufon II, who is said to have invented bronze casting. Production declined as political and economic power shifted to Benin. Excavations at the grove of Igbo Olokun show glass bead making from between the 11th and 15th centuries, one of the earliest known glass workshops in West Africa, and the beads have been found as far away as Mali, Mauritania and Ghana.

Ife is called the city of 401 deities, and festivals of the orisha are held through the year, among them Olojo and Itapa. Its sacred sites include the shrine and grove of Oduduwa, the Agbonniregun Temple, grove of Orunmila, and Igbo Olokun.
ifni-war: Morocco ceded the city of Sidi Ifni to the Spanish Empire at the end of the Hispano-Moroccan War in 1860, under the Treaty of Wad Ras, but Spain did not occupy it until 1934. When Morocco regained independence from France and Spain in 1956, it claimed that Spain's remaining possessions were historically and geographically Moroccan territory. Sultan Mohammed V encouraged efforts to recapture the land and personally funded anti-Spanish guerrillas. Violent demonstrations against Spanish rule broke out in Ifni on 10 April 1957, and in June Francisco Franco sent two battalions of the Spanish Legion to El Aaiún.

On 23 November 1957 a force of 2,000 Moroccans stormed Spanish garrisons and armouries in and around Ifni, after lines of communication had been cut. The Spanish held Sidi Ifni itself but abandoned two outposts, and many others were besieged. At Tiliuín, 60 locally recruited Tiradores de Ifni held off several hundred Moroccans until paratroopers were dropped on 25 November and the Legion's 6th Battalion broke the siege on 3 December. A platoon sent to relieve Telata was ambushed and lost its commander, Captain Ortiz de Zárate, with two dead and fourteen wounded in all.

Within a fortnight the Moroccans and their tribal allies controlled most of Ifni. They tried to besiege Sidi Ifni, but the town, supplied by the Spanish Navy and protected by trenches and forward outposts, had 7,500 defenders by 9 December. The siege lasted into June 1958. In January 1958 Morocco reorganised its army units in Spanish territory as the Saharan Liberation Army, which attacked El Aaiún on 12 January and ambushed Legion companies at Edchera the next day. In February a Franco-Spanish offensive, with about 9,000 Spanish and 5,000 French troops and 150 aircraft, broke up the Liberation Army.

On 2 April 1958 Spain and Morocco signed the Treaty of Angra de Cintra. Morocco obtained Tarfaya, or Cape Juby, and the Ifni territory, excluding Spanish Sahara, though legally it gained full control of Ifni only in 1969. Spain kept Sidi Ifni until 1969, when it returned it under international pressure, including United Nations resolution 2072 of 1965. It held Spanish Sahara until 1975, when the Green March led it to sign the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania.
ifriqiya: Ifriqiya, Arabic for Africa, was an Arabic derivation from the Latin Africa. Some Arabic sources gave it mythical origins, deriving it from a king of Yemen named Ifriqis or Ifriqish who conquered the Maghreb in ancient times, or from a son of Abraham named Ifriq. The region lay between the sea and the edges of the Sahara and included all of the former Byzantine province of Africa Proconsularis and more, though not the Mauretanias.

Its boundaries changed between authors and periods. The Mediterranean and the Saharan border areas were normally the northern and southern limits, and the east usually lay between Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, which was attached administratively to Egypt in the early Islamic period. The western boundary varied most. Al-Bakri thought Ifriqiya nearly equivalent to the whole Maghreb up to Morocco, but most writers placed it in northeastern Algeria and divided the Maghreb into three parts: the Far West, the Middle West and Ifriqiya. For most of its early history the capital was Qayrawan (Kairouan). It moved to Mahdiya in some periods and later remained at Tunis.

The Umayyads created the province in 703 when they seized North Africa from the Byzantine Empire. Religious tension and conflict between the invading Arabs and the native Berbers continued, most sharply between coastal cities and villages. After the Umayyads collapsed, the Aghlabids governed as agents of the Abbasids in Baghdad. The Fatimids overthrew them in 909, taking their capital of Raqqada. As the Fatimid regents, the Zirids, became more autonomous, they separated fully in the mid-11th century.

Religious divisions helped the Almohads take western Ifriqiya in 1147 and all of it by 1160. Their empire lasted into the early 13th century, when the Hafsids, a clan that supplied many of its governors, replaced it. In 1229 they declared independence under Abu Zakariya, who built the Hafsid state around its new capital, Tunis. The Black Death reached the Maghreb through Europe in the 14th century. Maghreb and Ifriqiya were largely under Ottoman rule between the 16th and 18th centuries.
iftikhar-ali-khan-pataudi: Iftikhar Ali Khan was born on 16 March 1910 at Pataudi House, the elder son of Nawab Muhammad Ibrahim Ali Khan and of Shahar Bano Begum, daughter of the Nawab of Loharu. Pataudi was a small princely state near Delhi whose ruling family descended from Faiz Talab Khan, a Pashtun of the Barech tribe from Kandahar, who became its first Nawab in 1804. Iftikhar succeeded his father in 1917 and was formally appointed ruler in December 1931. He was educated at Chiefs' College in Lahore and Balliol College, Oxford, and in 1939 married Begum Sajida Sultan, daughter of Hamidullah Khan, Nawab of Bhopal.

At Oxford he won a blue and in 1931 scored 1,307 runs for the university at an average of 93. After Alan Ratcliffe set a record of 201 for Cambridge in that year's University Match, Pataudi declared he would beat it and scored 238 not out the next day, a record that stood until 2005. An innings of 165 for the Gentlemen at Lord's in July 1932 won him a place on the Ashes tour that winter, and he was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1932.

In the first Test at Sydney he scored 102 on debut, but he objected to Douglas Jardine's bodyline tactics and refused to take his place in a leg-side field, and he was dropped after the second Test. His last Test for England came in June 1934 at Trent Bridge, and ill health limited his later cricket. He captained India on its 1946 tour of England, averaging 46.71 on the tour but scoring only 55 runs in five Test innings, and his captaincy was criticised.

After his state was absorbed into independent India he kept a privy purse and the use of the title Nawab of Pataudi, and he worked in the Indian Foreign Office. He died of a heart attack while playing polo in Delhi on 5 January 1952, his son Mansoor's eleventh birthday, and Mansoor succeeded him as Nawab. In 2007 the Marylebone Cricket Club commissioned a trophy in his name for Test series between India and England.
iga-province: Iga lay in what is today the western part of Mie Prefecture. It bordered Ise to the east and south, Ōmi to the north, Yamato to the west and south, and Yamashiro Province to the northwest. It roughly coincides with the modern municipalities of Iga and Nabari in Mie and Yagyu in Nara Prefecture. Surrounded by mountains, it was historically rather inaccessible because of extremely poor roads. Under the Engishiki classification it ranked as an inferior country and a near country, and it was counted among the provinces of the Tōkaidō. It was divided into four districts and 197 villages, with an assessed value of 110,843 koku.

Iga was separated from Ise Province around 680 CE, in the Asuka period. The provincial capital stood in what is now part of the city of Iga, where the ruins of the Iga Kokubun-ji remain, and the province's Ichinomiya is the Aekuni Shrine. Little is known of the Heian and Kamakura periods. By the middle of the Muromachi period Iga had become effectively independent of its nominal feudal rulers and formed a confederacy, the Iga Sokoku Ikki. It was then known as a centre of ninja activity, and with Kōka in what is now Shiga Prefecture it claims to be one of the birthplaces of the ninja clans and ninjutsu.

In 1581, two years after a failed invasion led by his son, Oda Nobunaga attacked Iga from six directions with 40,000 to 60,000 men, which effectively destroyed the political power of the ninja (the Tenshō Iga War). After the Tokugawa shogunate was established, Iga was briefly under the Iga-Ueno Domain of 200,000 koku, ruled from 1600 to 1608 by Tsutsui Sadatsugu, a former retainer of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The Tsutsui were dispossessed in 1608, and the territory went to Tōdō Takatora, daimyō of Tsu Domain, to which it belonged until the Meiji Restoration. Iga Ueno Castle remained a secondary administrative centre of the domain.

After the abolition of the han in July 1871 Tsu Domain became Tsu Prefecture, which later became part of Mie Prefecture. In 1896 the four districts were merged into two, Ayama and Naga. The province was the home of the samurai Hattori Hanzō and the haiku poet Matsuo Bashō. The area is now relatively easy to reach from Nara, Kyoto, Osaka and Nagoya.
iga-ueno-castle: The castle stands on a hill at the north-western corner of a plateau formed by the Kizu and Tsuge rivers, in the centre of Iga. The city lies in a mountain basin on an important route linking the old capitals of Nara and Kyoto with the Ise Grand Shrine and eastern Japan. Iga Province, ringed by mountains, was governed from around the 1460s by its warrior families, later known as ninja, as the Iga ikki, with a headquarters on the site of the present castle, until Oda Nobunaga conquered it in 1581.

Construction began in 1585 on the orders of Takigawa Katsutoshi. Under Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Tsutsui Sadatsugu was moved from Kōriyama Castle to rule Iga; he divided the hill into an upper eastern and a lower western half, with the innermost bailey, or honmaru, on the upper part and a three-storey keep on its eastern edge.

After the Battle of Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu expelled Tsutsui for siding with the Toyotomi and gave Iga and northern Ise to his trusted general Tōdō Takatora, already the builder of Uwajima and Imabari castles. Tōdō moved the inner bailey to the western half of the hill and added terraces over 100 metres long to east and west, giving the castle an overall extent of 800 by 400 metres. His new five-storey keep was still being built when the storm destroyed it, and once the Toyotomi were destroyed at the Siege of Osaka in 1615 the castle lost its importance, so the keep and the planned moats and walls were never finished.

All the remaining buildings were destroyed after the Meiji restoration. The wooden keep of 1935 houses a museum of the area's history, while the rest of the castle lies in ruins within Ueno Park, its high honmaru walls still standing. It has been a National Historic Site since 1967, and the Iga-ryū Ninja Museum stands beside it.
igbo-people: The Igbo homeland straddles the lower Niger River, east and south of the Edoid and Idomoid groups and west of the Ibibioid cluster. The Igbo language belongs to the Niger-Congo family. Evidence of early iron smelting has been excavated in the Nsukka region, dated to 750 BCE at Opi and 2,000 BCE at Lejja. Igbo-Ukwu, in what is now Anambra State, has yielded more than 600 prestige objects, including cast copper-alloy sculptures and over 165,000 glass and carnelian beads, dated to the 9th and 10th centuries. They may be associated with the Kingdom of Nri and its priest-king, the Eze Nri, whose traditions trace the people back to a figure named Eri.

Traditional Igbo government was in most places a consultative one. Communities were governed by councils of elders and assemblies of the common people, and many towns were also partly governed by the Ozo society, whose titles could be earned or inherited. A few places had kings, such as Onitsha with its Obi, or priest-kings, such as Nri and Arochukwu, and the spiritual though not political authority of the king of Nri was recognised across Igboland. Igbo unity as one identity is comparatively recent, and the novelist Chinua Achebe placed it somewhere between a tribe and a nation.

Many of the people taken across the Atlantic from the Bight of Biafra were probably Igbo, usually sold to Europeans by the Aro Confederacy. Enslaved Igbo were known to planters as outspoken and rebellious, and were dispersed to colonies including Jamaica, Cuba, Saint-Domingue and Trinidad. British colonial rule, which depended on appointed warrant chiefs, did not suit Igbo decentralised government, and the period was marked by conflicts. The Igbo embraced Christianity and Western-style education.

After ethnic clashes in 1966 and 1967, General Emeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu proclaimed the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967, beginning the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970. Millions of Biafran civilians died of starvation under a blockade by the Nigerian military, and Biafra was defeated and reintegrated.

The traditional Igbo religion is Odinani, whose supreme deity is Chukwu, the "great spirit", who created the world. Christianity and Odinani are now the major religions, with Islamic minorities. Yam is the staple crop, cultivated mostly by men. Traditional compounds group several houses around a central courtyard, built of mud, clay, wood and thatch. Instruments include the udu, a clay jug, the ekwe, a hollowed log, and the ogene, an iron bell.
igbo-ukwu: Igbo-Ukwu, whose name means Great Igbo, lies in the south-central part of Nigeria. The town is made up of three quarters, Obiuno, Ngo and Ihite, with several villages in each and thirty-six administrative wards, and it borders Ora-eri, Ichida, Azigbo, Ezinifite, Amichi, Isuofia and Ikenga. Its climate is warm all year round, with average temperatures between 18 °C and 29 °C, and a muggy dry season and an overcast wet one.

Originally known simply as Igbo, the town was the capital of the Kingdom of Nri from the 8th or 9th century CE. It was the centre of an extensive trade system linking it with Gao on the Niger bend and, through Gao, with Egypt and North Africa, and a prominent centre of lost-wax casting in bronze, one of the earliest in Africa.

The first of its three archaeological sites came to light in 1938, when a villager, Isaiah Anozie, found bronze works while digging beside his home. Five pieces from it are now in the British Museum: a small staff, the head of a ram, a large manilla, a crescent-shaped vessel and a small pendant in the shape of a local chief's head with ichi scarification marks. The archaeologist Thurstan Shaw, excavating at the request of the Nigerian government, found the other two sites.

The three are known as Igbo Isaiah, a shrine, Igbo Richard, a burial chamber, and Igbo Jonah, a cache. Besides the bronzes they held jewellery, ceramics, a corpse adorned in what appears to be regalia, and copper and iron objects, some of materials that came through long-distance trade. Radiocarbon dating placed the sites at around 850, and the finds show that by the 9th century the people had a complex religious system and an economy based on agriculture and trade reaching as far as the Nile valley.
igboland: Igboland is a cultural and linguistic region, divided by the lower Niger into a larger eastern and a smaller western part. West of the river it reaches Aniocha, Ndokwa, Ukwuani and Ika in present-day Delta State; in the east it ends at the Cross River, and in the north it enters savannah country around Nsukka. It lies mainly in the lowland forest of Nigeria, bordered by the Igala, Tiv, Yako, Idoma and Ibibio. The Niger has long joined the Igbo on both banks, and routes through Asaba, Onitsha and Aboh carried trade and migrants.

Late Stone Age people were present at least 10,000 years ago, and in 1978 a team led by Thurstan Shaw excavated a rock quarry that had served as a mine for tool and pottery making for a settlement at Ibagwa. The Nsukka-Okigwe axis is proposed as the heartland from which most Igbo-speaking groups spread. Bronze and copper works found at Igbo Ukwu from 1939, made from local copper by the 9th century, show an industry of local origin, and glass beads that originated in India were found in a burial there.

The Kingdom of Nri, said in Umunri tradition to stem from the divine figure Eri, rose around the 10th century. In the 1560s Eze Chima, exiled by the Oba of Benin, founded the western communities known as Umuezechima. The Aro Confederacy, centred on Arochukwu, rose in the Cross River region in the 17th century and built much of its economy on the slave trade to Europeans through coastal middlemen.

Missionaries arrived from the 1850s, and palm oil became the chief export. Igboland was conquered by the British after decades of resistance, among it the Ekumeku Movement, the Anglo-Aro War and the Aba Women's Riots, and British rule set warrant chiefs where no monarchies had existed. After independence in 1960 most of Igboland lay in the Eastern Region, which seceded as the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967 under Emeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu. The Nigerian Civil War lasted from 6 July 1967 to 15 January 1970.

More than 30 million people live in Igboland, at densities of 140 to 390 inhabitants per square kilometre, over an area of some 40,900 to 41,400 km2. Its cultural subgroups include the Ngwa, the Mbaise, the Ezza, the Etche and the Anioma-Enuani, and Nri is the oldest existing monarchy in present-day Nigeria.
ignacy-krasicki: Ignacy Krasicki was born on 3 February 1735 in Dubiecko, on the San River in southern Poland, into a noble family that bore the title of Imperial Count. He attended a Jesuit school in Lwów, studied at a Catholic seminary in Warsaw and took holy orders in 1759.

On returning to Poland he became secretary to the Primate and formed a friendship with the future King Stanisław August Poniatowski. When Poniatowski was elected king in 1764, Krasicki became his chaplain and helped found the Monitor, the leading periodical of the Polish Enlightenment, which the king sponsored.

In 1766 Krasicki, after serving that year as coadjutor, became Prince-Bishop of Warmia, with a seat in the Senate of the Commonwealth. The cathedral chapter received him coolly, and Prussia was applying growing pressure in preparation for taking Warmia in the First Partition. Krasicki protested publicly against outside intervention. In 1772 the partition made him a Prussian subject, though he did not pay homage to his new ruler, Frederick II.

He nevertheless cultivated an acquaintance with Frederick and visited Berlin, Potsdam and Sanssouci often. He officiated at the opening of St Hedwig's Cathedral in Berlin in 1773 and was called to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in 1786. In 1795 he became Archbishop of Gniezno and Primate of Poland.

Krasicki began as a poet late, nearing forty, with the hymn Święta miłości kochanej ojczyzny, published in 1774, which later served for many years as a national anthem. His novel Mikołaja Doświadczyńskiego przypadki of 1776 is the first modern Polish novel and combines the satirical, adventure, utopian and didactic strands of the Enlightenment novel. Tradition holds that his mock-heroic poem Monachomachia, published in 1778, grew from a conversation with Frederick II at Sanssouci. Its publication caused a public scandal.

His most lasting works are the Fables and Parables and the Satires, both of 1779. The fables usually place their moral in the last line, so that even a reader who could not read well could take it in. He also wrote the epic Wojna chocimska and a two-volume encyclopedia of 1781–83. He died in Berlin in 1801, and in 1829 his remains were moved from St Hedwig's Cathedral to Gniezno Cathedral.
ignalina-nuclear-power-plant: The Soviet Union intended the Ignalina plant as a symbol of its technological progress. Preparations began in 1974 and fieldwork three years later. The plant had two RBMK-1500 reactors, water-cooled and graphite-moderated, each with two turbines built by the Kharkiv turbine plant. After the Chernobyl disaster of April 1986 the reactors were de-rated to 1,360 MW. Unit 1 came online in December 1983 and Unit 2 in August 1987, a year later than planned because of Chernobyl.

The town of Visaginas was built for the workers, about 5,000 of whom staffed the plant. It produced 70 percent of the electricity of the Lithuanian S.S.R. and exported power elsewhere in the Soviet Union. Cooling water came from Lake Drūkšiai, the largest lake in Lithuania.

When Unit 1 came online in December 1983 a design flaw of the RBMK was noticed for the first time: graphite-displacer tips on the control rods caused a power excursion when they were inserted. The problem was not addressed until a similar surge partly caused the Chernobyl disaster, and the modifications that followed were tested at Ignalina in 1987 and 1988.

In 1999 Lithuania agreed to close the units as a condition of joining the European Union, citing the lack of a containment building as a high risk. The European Union agreed to pay 820 million euros towards decommissioning and compensation. Closure met fierce opposition because the plant gave income to most local residents. A 2008 referendum on keeping Unit 2 open until a replacement was built won 1,155,192 votes but failed to reach the required 50 percent turnout, and President Valdas Adamkus opposed it on the grounds of Lithuania's international commitments. Unit 1 closed on 31 December 2004 and Unit 2 on 31 December 2009.

The plant had accounted for 25 percent of Lithuania's generating capacity and supplied about 70 percent of its electrical demand. Decommissioning was funded about 95 percent by the international community, through the European Union and a fund set up in 2001 under the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and 5 percent by Lithuania. The first phase ran from 2004 to 2013, and a second was scheduled for 2014 to 2029, so that the site could be reused by 2030.

A new plant at the site was discussed. Parliament passed a law in 2007 and the power companies of Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Poland agreed in 2008 to form a company for it, but the project stopped after a 2012 referendum gave no mandate to continue. Ignalina also served as a filming location for the 2019 television series Chernobyl.
ignatius-of-loyola: Ignatius was born Íñigo López de Oñaz y Loyola, probably on 23 October 1491, in the castle of Loyola in Azpeitia, Gipuzkoa. He was the youngest of thirteen children of parents from the minor nobility, and his mother died soon after his birth. He became a page in the household of Juan Velázquez de Cuéllar, treasurer of the kingdom of Castile, and in 1509 entered the service of Antonio Manrique de Lara, Duke of Nájera. On 20 May 1521, at the Battle of Pamplona, a cannonball ricocheting off a wall broke his right leg. Several operations left it shorter than the other, and he limped for the rest of his life.

While recovering he asked for romances of chivalry, but the castle had none, and his sister-in-law Magdalena de Araoz brought him lives of Christ and the saints. Ludolph of Saxony's De Vita Christi struck him most, and its method of imagining oneself at a Gospel scene shaped his later meditation. In March 1522 he visited Montserrat and hung his sword and dagger at the Virgin's altar. He then lived for about a year at Manresa, begging and praying in a cave, where he formulated the basis of his Spiritual Exercises. In September 1523 he reached the Holy Land, but the Franciscans sent him back.

He studied at Alcalá in 1526-1527, where the Inquisition questioned him because he preached without a degree in theology, and then at the University of Paris, adopting the name Ignatius. There six fellow students joined him, among them Francis Xavier, Diego Laynez and Peter Faber. With them he founded the Society of Jesus and became its first Superior General. He aimed it at missionary work and teaching and added a fourth vow of obedience to the Pope to the usual vows of chastity, obedience and poverty.

Ignatius died on 31 July 1556. His method of spiritual formation, recorded in the Spiritual Exercises of 1548, became known as Ignatian spirituality. The Jesuits were instrumental in leading the Counter-Reformation. He was beatified in 1609 and canonised on 12 March 1622, and his feast day is 31 July. He is patron saint of the Basque provinces of Gipuzkoa and Biscay and of the Society of Jesus, and in 1922 Pope Pius XI declared him patron of all spiritual retreats.
ignaz-seipel: Ignaz Seipel was born on 19 July 1876, the son of a Viennese carriage driver. He studied Catholic theology at the University of Vienna and was ordained a priest on 23 July 1899. He received his doctorate in 1903 and published a work on economic ethics in 1907. From 1909 to 1917 he was professor of moral theology at the University of Salzburg, where he wrote Nation and State (1916), which prepared his later role in the Christian Social Party. In 1917 he returned to a chair at the University of Vienna. On 27 October 1918 Emperor Karl I appointed him a minister in the last imperial government, under Heinrich Lammasch.
