Rebellions in southern Pannonia and northern Dalmatia from 14 to 10 BCE, known as the Pannonian war, are poorly recorded, mostly in brief accounts by Cassius Dio.

The Batonian War of 6–9 CE began when native auxiliaries gathered for a campaign against the Marcomanni rebelled under Bato the Daesitiate. Bato the Breucian led the Breuci of southern Pannonia, and the two leaders joined forces on Mount Alma. Tiberius took command of the Roman army and met their guerrilla tactics with counterinsurgency operations. Paul, writing to the Romans in the winter of 57–58 CE, names Illyricum as the westernmost point of his missionary travels so far.
ilocos: The region was originally inhabited by Negritos as early as 30,000 BCE, who were displaced over time by successive waves of Austronesian migrants arriving along the narrow coast in traditional boats. The first wave, some 10,000 to 7,000 years ago, brought the ancestors of the indigenous groups of the Cordillera Central, and later migrations introduced agriculture. Before colonial rule, the Ilocanos, then known as Samtoy, traded with local and foreign merchants at coastal hubs such as Vigan, Candon and Lingayen, which were visited by Austronesian, Arab, Indian, Chinese and Japanese ships. Gold from the Cordillera, porcelain, silk, cotton, beeswax and stoneware jars were among the goods exchanged. In the south the polity of Caboloan lay in the Agno River basin.

A year after Miguel López de Legazpi declared Manila the capital on 24 June 1571, Spanish colonization expanded to northern Luzon. Martín de Goiti began the conquest of Pangasinan and founded settlements between 1571 and 1573, and in 1572 Juan de Salcedo landed at the mouth of the Agno River with eight armed boats and 80 men. In 1574 the Chinese pirate Limahong fled to Pangasinan after being driven from Manila, but an army led by Salcedo chased him out after a seven-month siege.

American forces landed in the region on 18 November 1899 in pursuit of Emilio Aguinaldo, and guerrillas under Gen. Manuel Tinio kept fighting in the countryside. At the Battle of Tirad Pass on 2 December 1899, Gen. Gregorio del Pilar and about 60 soldiers faced over 300 American troops and lost their position. Japanese forces landed at Vigan on 10 December 1941 and took it the next day.

The Ilocos Region, designated Region I, lies in north-western Luzon between the Cordillera and the West Philippine Sea. It has four provinces, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union and Pangasinan, and the city of San Fernando in La Union is its regional centre. Pangasinan was transferred to it from Central Luzon by a decree of 1973, and Abra, Mountain Province and Benguet were moved to the Cordillera Administrative Region in 1987. The 2020 census counted 5,292,297 people, mostly Ilocanos, with Pangasinans the second largest group.

Ilocano is the main language, and the epic Biag ni Lam-ang belongs to its literary tradition. Two UNESCO World Heritage sites stand here: the Baroque churches of Paoay and Santa Maria, and the colonial city of Vigan. Pangasinan is known for milkfish farming and salt production, and the region's crafts include inabel weaving and damili, red clay pottery.
iloilo-city: Iloilo City lies on the southern shore of Panay, facing the Iloilo Strait and the island of Guimaras, which together form a natural harbour and a safe anchorage for ships. The Iloilo and Batiano rivers flow through its districts into the strait. The name derives from the older Irong-irong, meaning nose-like, which referred to the promontory between the two rivers where Fort San Pedro and the 17th-century Spanish port stood. The city is a conglomeration of former towns, now seven districts: the City Proper, Jaro, Molo, Mandurriao, La Paz, Arevalo and Lapuz. In 1930 the architect Juan Arellano drew a plan for it based on Ebenezer Howard's Garden City concept.

The earliest written reference to Iloilo appears in Yuan dynasty records of the 1300s, which identify Oton, west of the city, as a bustling trade outpost in the Visayas. In 1565 Miguel López de Legazpi sent his grandson Felipe de Salcedo and Augustinian missionaries, among them Martín de Rada, to explore the Visayas for resources, and they set up a temporary settlement at Araut on Panay to secure food supplies. In 1566 the Spanish settled in the area, which became the second Spanish colonial centre in the Philippines after Cebu. Mexican soldiers from Latin America reinforced the garrison in 1603, 1636, 1670 and 1672.

Queen Regent Maria Christina of Austria gave the city the title La Muy Leal y Noble Ciudad, Most Loyal and Noble City, in recognition of its loyalty to the Spanish crown during the Philippine Revolution. Iloilo served as the last capital of the Spanish Empire in Asia and the Pacific before the Philippines was ceded to the United States in 1898. By 1900 it was widely known as the Queen City of the South, and it was considered the second most important city in the Philippines after Manila. Japanese forces invaded Panay in 1942. A fire in 1966 destroyed nearly three quarters of the downtown area.

Iloilo City is the regional centre of Western Visayas and the capital of Iloilo Province, though it is administered independently of the province. It had 473,728 inhabitants in the 2024 census, and Hiligaynon is the predominant language. The Calle Real Heritage Zone preserves buildings of the Spanish and American periods. The city is the centre of devotion to Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria de Jaro, and holds the Dinagyang Festival every January. UNESCO recognises it as a Creative City of Gastronomy, known for dishes such as La Paz batchoy and pancit Molo.
ilona-zrinyi: Ilona Zrínyi was born in 1643 at Ozalj, in present-day Croatia, the eldest child of Petar Zrinski, Ban of Croatia, and his wife Katarina Zrinska, née Frankopan, a Croatian poet. She and her siblings Judita Petronila, Aurora Veronika and Ivan Antun were the last generation of the once-powerful Zrinski family. Little is known of her schooling, but she was known for her beauty and learning, gained from her parents, both writers, and from her uncle Nikola VII Zrinski.

On 1 March 1666 she married Francis Rákóczi. Their children were György, who died in infancy, Julianna, born in 1672, and Ferenc, known as Francis Rákóczi II, born in 1676. Her husband died on 8 June 1676, and against the advice of Emperor Leopold I's counsellors and her husband's own will she gained guardianship of the children and with it control of the Rákóczi estates, among them the castles of Regéc, Sárospatak, Makovica and Munkács.

After her marriage to Imre Thököly she took an active part in his Kuruc uprising against the Habsburgs. When the Ottoman forces and their Kuruc allies were defeated at the Battle of Vienna in 1683, Thököly lost one Rákóczi castle after another, and by the end of 1685 the imperial army had surrounded the last, Munkács Castle, also called Palanok, in present-day Ukraine. She defended it in person against the forces of General Antonio Caraffa, and was pregnant during the siege.

After the recapture of Buda her position became untenable, and on 17 January 1688 she surrendered, on the understanding that the defenders would be amnestied and the Rákóczi estates kept in her children's names. In Vienna, against the agreement, the children were taken from her. She lived in the Ursuline convent until 1691, while her son was sent to the Jesuit school at Neuhaus.

When Thököly captured the Habsburg general Heissler, a prisoner exchange freed her, and she joined her husband in Transylvania. After the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699 both went into exile in the Ottoman Empire. She lived in Galata, a district of Constantinople, and later in Izmit, where she died on 18 February 1703; she was buried in the church of Saint Benoit in Galata.

She is honoured in Croatia and Hungary as a national heroine who opposed the absolutist aims of the Habsburgs, a struggle her son Francis II Rákóczi carried on from 1703 to 1711. In October 1906 her remains were reinterred with his in St Elisabeth Cathedral in Košice, now in Slovakia.
ilorin: Ilorin lies where Nigeria's northern savanna meets the southwestern forest belt, in the transitional Middle Belt, about 300 kilometres north-northeast of Lagos. The Asa is the longest of the rivers that drain the area. Its people speak mainly Yoruba, in a local dialect known as Ilorin Yoruba, while the ruling dynasty is of Fulani origin and its titles, festivals and Islamic scholarship tie it closely to the Hausa–Fulani north. Scholars therefore describe it as a meeting point of north and south.

Oral tradition holds that the area was settled for many centuries by successive groups. Tradition credits Ojo Isekuse, a hunter and blacksmith, as one of the early founders, and traces the city's name to okuta ilọ irin, the stone for sharpening iron. By the 18th century Ilorin was a border settlement of the Oyo Empire with a mainly Yoruba population and growing numbers of Hausa and Fulani immigrants.

In the early 19th century Afonja, the Oyo field marshal (Aare Ona Kakanfo) stationed at Ilorin, rebelled against the Alaafin with the support of the Fulani scholar Shehu Alimi. Their alliance collapsed in a struggle for power and Afonja was killed. Alimi's eldest son Abd al-Salam became the first Emir of Ilorin, receiving a flag from Sokoto and bringing Ilorin into the Sokoto Caliphate as an emirate, traditionally dated between 1823 and 1831.

Ilorin repelled an Oyo-led coalition at the Battle of Ilorin, around 1835, an event that hastened the collapse of Old Oyo. The army of Ibadan halted its southward expansion at Osogbo in 1840. Through the century it was a major trading node between the Hausa–Fulani north and the Yoruba south and a centre of Islamic learning.

Ilorin resisted British rule but was occupied by the Royal Niger Company in 1897 and incorporated into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate in 1900. In 1967 it became the capital of the newly created Kwara State.

Ilorin is the capital of Kwara State and the seat of the Ilorin Emirate, ruled by eleven emirs, all from the house of Shehu Alimi. Islam is the majority religion, though Christianity is widely practised. The Ilorin Central Mosque, begun in 1977 and opened in 1981, has 99 domes and four minarets. Its Durbar, a procession of decorated horses and riders led by the Emir, is held a day or two after Eid al-Adha. The city has some of the largest traditional pottery workshops in Nigeria and produces hand-woven aso-oke textiles.
ilterish-qaghan: Ilterish, whose personal name was Ashina Qutlug, was a grandson of Illig Qaghan, the last ruler of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate. According to the Old Book of Tang his father was a chief under the Tang administration of the Chanyu Protectorate, but the Chinese text of the Kul Tigin stele gives the father the title Qutlug Irkin, which suggests that Qutlug may have been an inherited title rather than a name. The Tonyukuk inscriptions call Ilterish a shad, a title of military commanders, before he became qaghan.

After the failed rebellion of Ashina Funian in 681, Ilterish rose against the Tang with more than 5,000 men, many of them survivors of that revolt. The Tonyukuk inscriptions say that Tonyukuk and Boyla Bagha Tarkan enthroned him, and he made his younger brothers Mochuo and Duoxifu shad and yabghu. From 12 July 682 his forces raided the Tang frontier prefectures, killing several officials and capturing the military governor Cui Zhibian.

In 684 he turned to the steppe. Advised by Tonyukuk, he struck first at the Toquz Oghuz, who held Ötüken, the old heartland of the Turks, and by 685 the conquest of Ötüken was complete. The inscriptions claim that his armies went on to reach Shandong and the sea and besieged 23 Tang cities, although Tang generals such as Heukchi Sangji defeated the Turks at the Battle of Liangjing in 686 and again in 687.

A coalition of the Tang, the On Oq and the Kyrgyz then formed against him. The Turks crossed the Sayan and Tannu-Ola mountains and destroyed the Kyrgyz army in a night attack. When his khatun, Ilbilga Khatun, died, Ilterish returned to Ötüken, and Tonyukuk led the army that defeated the Türgesh on the Yarïsh Plain.

Little is known of his last years. The Kul Tigin and Bilge Qaghan inscriptions, which give the ages of his sons when he died, suggest that he died in 691, and his brother Mochuo succeeded him as Qapaghan Qaghan. The historian Mihaly Dobrovits believes Ilterish replaced lateral succession with primogeniture. Kutlu, Kutluk, İlter and İlteriş remain common Turkish given names in his memory, and on 23 August 2022 his memorial complex, with an inscription in Turkic and Sogdian, was found in the Khangai Mountains of Mongolia.
iltutmish: Iltutmish was born into a well-off family; his father Ilam Khan led the Ilbari Turkic tribe. According to Minhaj's Tabaqat-i Nasiri, his jealous brothers sold him to a slave dealer at a horse show, a story that seems modelled on the Quranic account of Yusuf. He spent his early life in Bukhara and Ghazni under several masters. In about 1197 the Ghurid slave-commander Qutb al-Din Aibak bought him in Delhi for 100,000 jitals, making him the slave of a slave.

He became head of Aibak's bodyguard and was later given the important iqta of Badaun. His campaigns against the Khokhar rebels in 1205–1206 won the notice of Muhammad of Ghor, who freed him before Aibak himself was freed.

After Aibak died in 1210, the nobles at Lahore appointed Aram Shah as his successor. Nobles elsewhere, led by the military justiciar Ali-yi Ismail, proposed Iltutmish instead, since Aibak had called him a son. He marched to Delhi, defeated Aram Shah's forces and set up his capital there. Some nobles rebelled, and he had many of them beheaded. He then brought Badaun, Awadh, Banaras and Siwalik back under Delhi's control and faced rival former Ghurid slaves, among them Taj al-Din Yildiz and Nasir ad-Din Qabacha.

In 1228–1229 he invaded Qabacha's territory, which the Mongols and the Khwarazmians had weakened, and annexed large parts of Punjab and Sindh. On 18 February 1229 an embassy from the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir reached Delhi with a deed of investiture and the titles Yamin Khalifat Allah and Nasir Amir al-Mu'minin. In 1230 he defeated Malik Balkha Khalji in Bengal, and in 1231 he besieged Gwalior, which fell on 12 December 1232. He died in Delhi on 30 April 1236.

Iltutmish freed the sultanate from a subordinate position to Ghazni. He introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital, the basic coins of the later sultanate, and the iqta system, which assigned the revenues of a region to officers in return for military service. He is probably the first ruler of the sultanate to organise a centrally recruited and paid army.

Delhi became a centre of Islamic power and culture under him; he patronised the historian Minhaj-i-Siraj and the Sufi Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki. He completed the Qutb Minar, built the Hauz-i-Shamsi reservoir and in 1231 raised the Sultan Ghari tomb for his eldest son, the first Islamic mausoleum in Delhi.
ilya-muromets: Ilya Muromets, also called Ilya of Murom, is a bogatyr, or hero, of the Russian byliny, a type of oral epic poem set in the time of Kievan Rus' and collected as folklore in the 18th and 19th centuries. He often appears with the bogatyrs Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich, the three being known in Russian culture as the three bogatyrs. Attempts have been made to find a historical nucleus for him. The main candidate is Ilya Pechersky, a 12th-century monk of the Kiev Pechersk Lavra who was canonized in 1643 and whose relics are kept in the monastery. His character probably does not represent a single historical person but a fusion of several real or fictional heroes of different epochs.

In the byliny Ilya is the son of a peasant, born in the village of Karacharovo near Murom. A serious illness left him unable to walk until the age of 33, lying on a Russian stove until two pilgrims miraculously healed him. A dying knight, Svyatogor, gave him superhuman strength, and he set out to free Kiev from Idolishche and to serve Vladimir I of Kiev. On the way he defended Chernigov from a nomadic invasion, possibly by the Polovtsi, and declined the local ruler's offer of knighthood. In the forests of Bryansk he killed the monster Nightingale the Robber, who murdered travellers with his whistle.

In Kiev Vladimir made him chief bogatyr, and he defended the land from attacks from the Pontic–Caspian steppe, traditionally personified as Kalin-tsar of the Tatars. Generous and simple-minded but also temperamental, he once destroyed all the church steeples of Kiev after Vladimir failed to invite him to a celebration, and was soon appeased. The cycle of tales has its own type, SUS -650C*, in the East Slavic Folktale Classification, with variants from Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian sources.

Ilya Pechersky is said by hagiography to have been a warrior known for his strength before taking monastic vows, nicknamed Chobotok, small boot. In 1988 Soviet archaeologists exhumed his remains and reported a tall man whose bones showed signs of spinal disease at an early age and the marks of many wounds, one fatal. The hero has inspired Catterino Cavos's opera of 1807, Viktor Vasnetsov's painting Bogatyrs of 1898, Reinhold Glière's Symphony No. 3 of 1911 and Aleksandr Ptushko's film Ilya Muromets of 1956.
ilyas-shahi-dynasty: The ancestors of Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah came from Sistan; according to Syed A M R Haque they arrived in the subcontinent as Muslim missionaries and received jagirs in Bengal in 1227, when it was ruled by the Delhi Sultanate. Ilyas Shah took service under Izz al-Din Yahya, governor of Satgaon, and after Yahya's death in 1338 seized Satgaon and declared himself a sultan independent of Delhi. He went on to defeat Alauddin Ali Shah of Lakhnauti and Ikhtiyaruddin Ghazi Shah of Sonargaon, making Bengal a single political entity.

His son Sikandar Shah ruled for some 30 years and built the Adina Masjid at Pandua in 1368 and the Kotwali Darwaza at Gauḍa. Sikandar's son Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah established friendly relations with Ming China and encouraged trade, and in his reign the Chinese traveller Ma Huan visited Bengal.

Political confusion and weakness then let the family of the slave Shihabuddin Bayazid Shah overthrow Saifuddin Hamza Shah, and the House of Ganesha soon followed. Ganesha's son Jadu converted to Islam and reigned as Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Shah, and was succeeded by his son Shamsuddin Ahmad Shah, whom his nobles killed in an attempt to restore the old line. Two short-lived rulers, Qutbuddin Azam Shah and Ghiyasuddin Nusrat Shah, struck coins in eastern Bengal in AH 837 (1434 CE), and a third, Siraj-al Din Sikandar Shah, is known only from undated coins; whether any was related to Ahmad is unknown.

The dynasty was restored by Mahmud Shah, a descendant of Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, who took the throne as Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah. Its last ruler, Jalal ad-Din Fatih Shah, was killed in 1487 by Shahzada Barbak, the Habshi commander of the palace guards, who became sultan as Barbak Shah. The dynasty laid the foundations of the late medieval Sunni Muslim Sultanate of Bengal.
imad-al-dawla: Ali was the eldest son of Abu Shuja Buya, a fisherman of modest origin from Daylam in northern Iran, probably a recent convert to Islam, which explains his sons' Arabic names. He served first in the entourage of the Samanid ruler Nasr II and around 928 joined Makan ibn Kaki, the Samanid governor of Gorgan and Ray, who gave army commissions to his younger brothers Hasan and Ahmad. When the Ziyarid prince Mardavij defeated Makan, the brothers went over to Mardavij, who gave Ali the town of Karaj. Warned that Mardavij meant to kill him, Ali hurried to Karaj and grew rich on campaigns against the Khurramites in the nearby mountains.

Ali then marched on Isfahan, held for the Abbasids by the governor Yaqut, but Mardavij's approach forced him away, and he took Arrajan between Fars and Khuzistan instead. In the spring of 933 he invaded Fars with the help of Zayd ibn Ali al-Naubandagani, a wealthy landowner hostile to the Abbasids, defeated Yaqut and entered Shiraz in May or June 934. The caliph confirmed him as viceroy that autumn, though Ali delayed the tribute. A Ziyarid advance into Khuzistan briefly forced him to recognise Mardavij, but Mardavij was assassinated in January 935.

Strengthened by many of Mardavij's Turkish mercenaries, Ali sent Hasan to take Isfahan and Ahmad to Kirman and then Khuzistan, from where Ahmad entered Baghdad in 945. The brothers then received their honorific titles from the caliph: Ahmad became Mu'izz al-Dawla, Hasan Rukn al-Dawla and Ali Imad al-Dawla. Rukn al-Dawla, who had built his realm in central Iran on his own, was largely independent, but Mu'izz al-Dawla remained subordinate, and his brother's name came before his own on the coins he struck. Imad al-Dawla never officially held the title of senior amir but was recognised as holding the position.

Imad al-Dawla had no heir, and a few months before his death he chose Rukn al-Dawla's eldest son Fana-Khusraw as his successor. He died in December 949 and was buried in Istakhr. His brothers installed Fana-Khusraw, who took the title 'Adud al-Dawla, in Shiraz, and Rukn al-Dawla, the most powerful of the Buyids, claimed the title of senior amir with the recognition of both Mu'izz al-Dawla and 'Adud al-Dawla.
imad-al-din-zengi: Zengi's father, Aq Sunqur al-Hajib, was the Turkic governor of Aleppo under the Seljuk ruler Malik-Shah I and was beheaded for treason in 1094, when Zengi was about ten. Zengi was raised by Kerbogha, the governor of Mosul, and served the governors of Mosul, then entered the service of the Seljuk ruler Mahmud in 1118. In 1122 he received his first major command, an expedition against the Banu Mazyad leader Dubays ibn Sadaqa, and was granted the governorship of Wasit. He added Basra in 1124 and Baghdad in April 1126, which put him in control of Seljuk Iraq.

Zengi became governor of Mosul in 1127, after the assassination of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, and atabeg of Aleppo in 1128, uniting the two cities under his personal rule. In 1130 he allied with Taj al-Mulk Buri of Damascus against the Crusaders, only to seize Hama from Buri's son. Damascus remained his goal, and he besieged it several times without success, while the Damascenes under Mu'in al-Din Unur allied with the Kingdom of Jerusalem. In 1137 he defeated King Fulk of Jerusalem at the Battle of Ba'rin, and in 1138 his forces turned back the Byzantine emperor John II Comnenus and the Crusader princes at Shaizar.

In 1139 he took Baalbek by promising its defenders safe passage and then broke his word, having the governor flayed and the rest hanged, according to Ibn al-'Adim. He granted the town to his lieutenant Najm al-Din Ayyub, father of Saladin. In 1144 he captured Edessa on 24 December after a siege of four months.

The County of Edessa was the first of the Crusader states to be created and the first to fall. Its loss led to the Second Crusade, and later Muslim chroniclers noted it as the start of the jihad against the Crusader states. Zengi was killed in September 1146. Islamic sources say a Frankish slave named Yarankash assassinated him, while western sources blame his own court officials. He founded the Zengid dynasty. His eldest son Sayf al-Din Ghazi I succeeded him in Mosul and his second son Nur al-Din in Aleppo, and Qutb al-Din Mawdud followed Sayf in Mosul in 1149.
imagawa-ujichika: Imagawa Ujichika was born in 1473, the son of Imagawa Yoshitada, head of the Imagawa clan of Suruga Province, and Lady Kitagawa. In 1476 Yoshitada invaded Tōtōmi Province and defeated the Katsumada and Yokota clans, but on his way back to Suruga he was waylaid at Shiokaizaka and killed by the remnants of the two families. A succession dispute followed between the supporters of the infant Ujichika and those of Yoshitada's cousin Oshika Norimitsu, in which Uesugi Sadamasa and Ashikaga Masatomo became involved.

Hōjō Sōun proposed that Norimitsu act as regent in Ujichika's name until the boy's coming of age, which averted war within the clan for a time. When Ujichika turned 17, however, Norimitsu would not hand over control, and fighting resumed. Sōun attacked Norimitsu's mansion on Ujichika's behalf, and after Norimitsu's defeat Ujichika took his place as the tenth head of the clan.

In 1491 Ujichika gave asylum to Ashikaga Yoshizumi, who had fled Kyoto, and afterwards escorted him back. He spent much of his rule campaigning in Tōtōmi and Mikawa, strengthening the Imagawa on the Tokai coast, though his general Fukushima Hyōgo was defeated by Takeda Nobutora at the Battle of Iidagawara in 1521. In 1525 he built Nagoya Castle in Owari, an unusual step, since the Imagawa had only the most tenuous hold over Owari Province. He also sent three of his six sons to temples to become monks.

His house code of 1526, the Imagawa Kana Mokuroku, set rules for his retainers. It punished unlawful entry into another's residence, imposed capital punishment in violent quarrels between retainers, held parents accountable for their children's fights, regulated the private sale and leasing of land and the repayment of debts, and forbade Imagawa retainers to arrange marriages with houses outside the Imagawa domain.

Ujichika died of illness on 1 August 1526 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Imagawa Ujiteru, born of his wife Jukei-ni, who outlived him until 1568. Jukei-ni was also the mother of Imagawa Yoshimoto. Ujichika's daughters married into other houses, among them Zuikei-in, who married Hojo Ujiyasu, and Tokuzo-in, who married Kira Yoshitaka.
imagawa-ujizane: Ujizane was born in Sunpu, the eldest son of Imagawa Yoshimoto and his wife Jōkei-in, and bore the childhood name Tatsuomaru. In 1554 he married Lady Hayakawa, a daughter of Hōjō Ujiyasu, as part of the Kai-Sagami-Suruga Alliance. He became the tenth head of the Imagawa clan while his father turned his attention to the Imagawa advance into Tōtōmi and Mikawa Provinces.

After Yoshimoto's death at Okehazama in 1560, Tōtōmi and Mikawa fell into chaos and many vassals turned against Ujizane. His grandmother Jukei-ni, who had wielded great political power, died in 1568, and her death encouraged Takeda Shingen and Tokugawa Ieyasu to attack the Imagawa lands. Ujizane answered the landlocked Takeda with an embargo on salt, but it had little effect, because Uesugi Kenshin took the chance to sell salt to the Takeda, and it hastened the downfall of his own clan.

When Shingen invaded Suruga in 1568 the Imagawa army was routed and Sunpu Castle was quickly occupied, and Ujizane fled to Kakegawa Castle in Tōtōmi Province. After his defeat in the Siege of Kakegawa in 1569 he allied himself with Ieyasu, in return for help in recovering his lands in Suruga.

The Shincho Koki, the account of Oda Nobunaga, records that in 1575 Ujizane met Nobunaga and Ieyasu at the temple of Sokoku-ji, and he joined the army at the Battle of Nagashino against the Takeda. Ieyasu later summoned the Imagawa family and made them Tokugawa retainers with the rank of kōke. Ujizane enjoyed kemari and writing poetry. He died at the family estate in Shinagawa on 27 January 1615. His sons included Imagawa Norimochi and Shinagawa Takahisa.
imagawa-yoshimoto: Imagawa Yoshimoto was born in 1519, the third son of Imagawa Ujichika of the Imagawa clan, which claimed descent from Emperor Seiwa. As a younger son he was sent to a temple, where he was named Baigaku Shōhō. In 1536 his elder brother Ujiteru died suddenly and a succession dispute followed. His half-brother Genkō Etan sought the lordship, and the clan split. Yoshimoto's faction argued that his mother, Jukei-ni, had been Ujichika's consort. With help from Hōjō Ujitsuna of Sagami and the support of Takeda Nobutora of Kai, the other faction was eliminated in the Hanagura Disturbance, and Yoshimoto took his name and the headship.

Yoshimoto married a sister of Takeda Shingen, which sealed an alliance with the Takeda, and in 1540 he helped Shingen imprison Nobutora. He defeated an invasion of Suruga by the Later Hōjō clan. His advance into Mikawa met a defeat at the 1542 Battle of Azukizaka, but in 1548 he beat Oda Nobuhide in the Second Battle of Azukizaka and gained Suruga, Tōtōmi and Mikawa. Marriages tied him to the Takeda and the Hōjō, and a peace with the Hōjō followed in 1554. He was known as the number one archer in the Tōkaidō. Later he left the clan's political affairs to his son Imagawa Ujizane to concentrate on the advance westward into Mikawa and Owari.

In the summer of 1560 Yoshimoto marched towards the capital with Matsudaira Motoyasu, later known as Tokugawa Ieyasu, in the vanguard. He had a force of 25,000 but announced 40,000, and some sources support the larger figure. After taking several Oda castles his army feasted with song and sake. Following a downpour, Oda Nobunaga attacked by surprise with 3,000 men. Two Oda samurai, Mōri Shinsuke and Hattori Koheita, killed Yoshimoto at Dengakuhazama on 12 June. Ujizane succeeded him, but the Imagawa fell from power. Yoshimoto's body is buried at the Daisei-ji temple in Toyokawa, in modern Aichi Prefecture.
imam-shamil: Shamil was born on 26 June 1797 into an Avar Muslim family in the small village of Gimry, in present-day Dagestan. He was first named Ali, but after an illness his name was changed to Shamuyil, which is pronounced Shamil in the Caucasus. His father, Dengau, was a landlord, and this let Shamil and his friend Ghazi Muhammad study Arabic and logic. He grew up while the Russian Empire expanded into Ottoman and Qajar lands, and many Caucasian peoples united in resistance in what became known as the Caucasian War, which lasted from 1817 to 1864. Shamil became the disciple and counsellor of Ghazi Mollah, the earlier leader of the resistance.

Ghazi Mollah died at the battle of Gimry in 1832, and Shamil was one of only two murids to escape, badly wounded by a bayonet. He rejoined the murids under the second Imam, Hamzat Bek, and when Hamzat Bek was killed in 1834 he became the leader of the resistance. In 1839 he and about 4,000 followers, men, women and children, were besieged by General Pavel Grabbe in the stronghold of Akhoulgo. He refused Grabbe's demand to surrender and accept exile. The Russians stormed the stronghold; Shamil escaped on the first night, and many Dagestani and Chechen chieftains declared loyalty to the Tsar. He then fled to Chechnya and extended his influence over the clans there.

He united quarrelsome peoples through charisma, piety and fairness in applying sharia law, and used guerrilla tactics against the larger Russian army. In 1845 his forces surrounded and destroyed a column of 8,000 to 10,000 men under Count Mikhail Vorontsov in the forests of Chechnya. Shamil hoped for help from Britain, France or the Ottoman Empire, which never came. After the Crimean War Russia redoubled its efforts, and in September 1859 Shamil surrendered.

Shamil was sent to meet Tsar Alexander II and was then exiled to Kaluga. In December 1868 he was allowed to move to Kyiv, where he was given a mansion. In 1869 he received permission to make the Hajj. Sultan Abdulaziz received him at Istanbul, and at Mecca he met Emir Abdelkader. He died in Medina in 1871 and was buried in the Jannatul Baqi.

Peoples of the Northern Caucasus regard him as a hero. Russians came to respect him despite the bloody conquest of Chechnya and Dagestan, and Alexander II is said to have admired his resistance. His grandson Said Shamil was one of the founders of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, set up in 1917 and conquered by Soviet Russia in 1920.
imamate: The Arabic word imamah comes from a root meaning to lead or to go before, and refers to leadership, the office of an imam, or religious and communal authority. The concept emerged in the early ages of Islam out of the disputes over who should succeed Muhammad. One question was whether leadership came by selection, consultation, lineage or divine designation, and the disagreements grew into the separate Sunni and Shia views of authority.

In Sunni Islam the imamate usually means the caliphate, the leadership of the Muslim community, which theology and law hold to be needed to protect the religion, keep order and enforce the law. Appointing an imam or caliph is an obligation on the community, met by election, nomination or military power rather than by divine command. In Shia Islam, by contrast, the imam is a divinely appointed guide who preserves and interprets the faith. Ismaili teaching holds the imam vital to understanding the outward and inner meanings of the Quran, and in Twelver doctrine the imams are members of the Prophet's family.

Disputes over the line of imams split the Shia. Twelver Shi'ism, the largest branch, recognises twelve imams and holds that after the death of the eleventh, Hasan al-Askari, in 874, his son entered a state of occultation and will return as the Mahdi to restore justice. After the death of Ja'far al-Sadiq, the Ismailis recognised his eldest son, Isma'il ibn Ja'far, or Isma'il's son as the rightful imam and built a rich esoteric philosophy around the office. The Zaydis reject divine designation and infallibility: any pious, learned descendant of Muhammad who rises against tyranny may become imam.

Many states took the name. The Zaidi Imams of Yemen held political leadership from 897 until 1962, and a Nizari Ismaili state stood in the Middle East from 1090 until 1273. Other traditions used the title as well: the Ibadi Rustamid Imamate ruled in North Africa from 767 until 909, the Imamate of Futa Jallon in West Africa from 1725 until 1896, and the Imamate of Nejd, the Second Saudi State, from 1824 to 1891. The Caucasian Imamate held the Eastern Caucasus in the early and mid-19th century.
imar: Ímar, Ívarr in Old Norse, is called in the later Fragmentary Annals of Ireland a son of the king of Lochlann, named there as Gofraid, and a brother of Amlaíb Conung and Auisle. Lochlann is often identified with Norway, but several historians hold that in early times it meant the Norse lands of the Hebrides, the Isle of Man, the Northern Isles and parts of mainland Scotland. Modern scholars treat the annals' genealogy with caution, and Donnchadh Ó Corráin calls it a political construct of limited historical value.

Ímar first appears in contemporary Irish annals in 857, four years after Amlaíb is recorded arriving in Ireland, and Auisle joined them before 863. The annals call the three kings of the foreigners; modern historians call them kings of Dublin, after the Viking settlement at Áth Cliath that was the base of their power.

His first recorded war was against Máel Sechnaill, overking of the Southern Uí Néill and the most powerful king in Ireland, perhaps over control of Munster and its resources. In 858 Ímar and Cerball, King of Ossory, routed a force of Norse-Irish at Araid Tíre, and the next year the allies raided Meath, until Cerball made peace with Máel Sechnaill. Ímar and Amlaíb then allied with Áed Findliath, overking of the Northern Uí Néill. After Máel Sechnaill died in 862 the brothers raided Brega in 863 and sought to extend their power into the lands of the Southern Uí Néill.

Ímar is absent from the Irish annals between 864 and 870, the years in which Ivar the Boneless was active in England with the Great Heathen Army; Clare Downham concludes that they were the same man, though there is no scholarly consensus. In 867 Auisle was killed by kinsmen, a killing the Fragmentary Annals attribute to Amlaíb and Ímar. After the four-month siege of Dumbarton Rock in 870, Ímar and Amlaíb returned to Dublin in 871 with 200 ships and many captive Angles, Britons and Picts.

According to Ó Corráin, Ímar's kingdom at his death included Man, the Western Isles, Argyll, Caithness, Sutherland, Orkney and parts of the coast of Ross and Cromarty and Inverness. Three of his sons, Bárid (d. 881), Sichfrith (d. 888) and Sitriuc mac Ímair (d. 896), ruled as kings of Dublin, and later rulers such as Sitric Cáech and Ragnall ua Ímair were styled his grandsons. The Uí Ímair dominated the seaports of Ireland and held power in Northumbria and the Isles through the tenth century; their power declined after the Battle of Clontarf in 1014, and the Crovan dynasty of Mann and the Isles is generally held to descend from him.
imbangala: The origins of the Imbangala are still debated, though historians agree that they were not the Jagas who attacked the Kingdom of Kongo under Alvaro I. In the 1960s Jan Vansina and David Birmingham read Lunda oral traditions as tracing them to the Lunda Empire under a leader named Kinguri; another view makes them a local people of southern Angola, from the Bie Plateau or the coast west of the highlands. The first eyewitness account came from the English sailor Andrew Battell, who lived among them for 16 months around 1600 to 1601 just south of the Kwanza River and whose story Samuel Purchas published in 1614 and 1625.

Battell describes bands that moved every few months, killing or enslaving those who could not flee. Children born inside the kilombo, the fortified camp, were killed so that kinship could not replace initiation, and the bands grew by capturing adolescents, trained daily in combat. A boy wore a collar until he had killed a man in battle. Fighters anointed themselves with maji a samba, believed to make them invulnerable as long as they kept codes demanding infanticide, cannibalism and absolute courage; Battell reports that cowards were killed and eaten.

The fighting men, ngunza, formed twelve squadrons, each under a captain called a musungo, and a kilombo had twelve gates, one for each. In the field they attacked with a right horn, a left horn and a vanguard in the centre, armed with bows, knives, swords and, above all, the war club or hatchet.

Portuguese governors of Luanda, fought to a standstill by Ndongo, hired Imbangala bands from 1615, above all after Luis Mendes de Vasconcelos's assault on Ndongo in 1618, despite the protests of Álvaro II of Kongo. The bands proved hard to control. Kasanje's broke away and settled along the Kwango, while Kaza's joined Ndongo and then betrayed Queen Njinga Mbande in 1629; she later formed or joined a band of her own in Matamba. Other bands served as Portuguese auxiliaries or were destroyed, and south of the Kwanza they gradually joined states such as Bihe, Huambo and Bailundu, their customs moderating in the 18th century.
imbros: Imbros, officially Gökçeada since 29 July 1970, is the largest island of Turkey, in Çanakkale Province. It lies in the north-northeastern Aegean Sea at the entrance of Saros Bay, and Cape İncirburnu is the westernmost point of Turkey. The island has an area of 286.8 square kilometres and some wooded areas. It is mainly of volcanic origin, and its highest peak, İlyas Dağ, is an extinct stratovolcano. It lies just south of the North Anatolian Fault, and a severe earthquake struck it on 21 August 1859.

Herodotus records Pelasgians as the original inhabitants, who worshipped the Cabeiri and Hermes. Imbros and Lemnos were sacred to Hephaestus, and an ithyphallic Hephaestus appears on the island's ancient coins. In classical antiquity Imbros was an Athenian cleruchy, a colony whose settlers kept Athenian citizenship. The Iliad mentions the island and a lord of Imbros named Eëtion. The island was primarily inhabited by ethnic Greeks from the Iron Age until about the 1960s.

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Byzantine forces left, and the Ottomans took the island not by force but by a policy of conciliation. Michael Critoboulos, a leading Imbriot and later a chronicler of Mehmet II, arranged its peaceful surrender. In return for taxes and loyalty the island kept a degree of autonomy under a local administrator, and in 1479 it came under definitive Ottoman rule. The islanders lived in relative peace and prosperity until the 20th century and took no part in upheavals such as the Greek War of Independence.

In 1915 Imbros was a staging post for the Allied Mediterranean Expeditionary Force during the Gallipoli campaign, with a field hospital and an airfield, and General Ian Hamilton had his headquarters there. A naval action, the Battle of Imbros, was fought nearby on 20 January 1918. From November 1912 to September 1923 the island was under Greek naval administration. Article 14 of the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 exempted Imbros and Tenedos from the population exchange between Greece and Turkey.

After Turkish authorities took over in October 1923 the elected island government was dismissed. Law 1151 of 25 June 1927 abolished local administration and closed the Greek schools. Many Greeks left from the 1960s, and settlers from the mainland now make up most of the population. A Greek school reopened in September 2015. The main industries are fishing and tourism. Çınarlı is the only town, and the island is one of Turkey's cittaslow towns.
imhotep: Imhotep, whose name means the one who comes in peace, was chancellor to King Djoser, a possible architect of his step pyramid and high priest of the sun god Ra at Heliopolis. Little is known of him as a historical figure. Two contemporary inscriptions on the base of one of Djoser's statues establish him as chancellor, and a graffito on the enclosure wall of Sekhemkhet's unfinished step pyramid suggests that he outlived Djoser by a few years and worked on that king's pyramid, which was abandoned because Sekhemkhet reigned briefly.

He held the unique title bity sensen, literally the King of Lower Egypt, the two brothers, which has been read as meaning he was the king's twin; with no comparable holders the reading remains speculative. If not a relative, he may have been the king's confidant or childhood friend.

Egyptologists, following much later legends, credit Imhotep with the design and building of the Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, built during the 3rd Dynasty. He may also have been responsible for the first known use of stone columns to support a building. Stone had appeared sporadically in the Archaic Period, but nothing as large as the step pyramid had been built wholly of stone; earlier kings were buried in mastaba tombs. The ancient Egyptians themselves never credited him as designer of the step pyramid or inventor of stone architecture. Manetho, in the Ptolemaic period, credited him with inventing the method of dressed-stone building under Djoser.

The location of his tomb is unknown. No text from his lifetime mentions skill in medicine or wisdom writing, and none names him for 1,200 years after his death. The first surviving text to name him dates to the time of Amenhotep III and mentions libations poured to him, and his cult in the New Kingdom was distinct from offerings to other commoners. Imhotep is one of fewer than a dozen non-royal Egyptians deified after death, with his cult centred at Memphis.

Healing powers are first attached to him from the Thirtieth Dynasty, about 2,200 years after his death, and the Greeks equated him with Asklepios. The Famine Stela of the Ptolemaic period credits him with ending a seven-year famine under Djoser. A demotic papyrus of the 2nd century CE from Tebtunis tells a long story of him that includes a magical duel with an Assyrian sorceress.
imjin-war: Ming China and Joseon Korea both emerged in the fourteenth century after the fall of the Yuan dynasty and faced similar threats from Jurchen raiders and the wokou. By the last decade of the sixteenth century Toyotomi Hideyoshi had unified Japan. A man of relatively humble origins who owed his position to his military might, he sought military power to legitimise his rule. It has also been suggested that he meant to fulfil the dreams of his late lord Oda Nobunaga and to keep the new state united against a common enemy, easing the threat of disorder from idle samurai and ambitious daimyos.

Japanese tanegashima matchlock arquebuses proved effective in land combat and sieges, while Korea was a manufacturing hub for cannons and ships, so Japanese strength lay on land and Korean strength at sea.

On 23 May 1592 about 7,000 men of the First Division under Konishi Yukinaga reached Busan from Tsushima. After the fall of Busan and the fortress of Dongnae, where about 3,000 were killed and the Japanese took no prisoners, they advanced north. Koreans were enraged rather than cowed and raised militias called righteous armies; by summer 1592 about 22,200 guerrillas tied up much of the Japanese force. At sea, Yi Sun-sin destroyed Japanese ships carrying troops and supplies, and Japan, short of arms and men, changed its aim from conquering China to occupying Korea.

Ming forces under Li Rusong, with 43,000 Chinese alongside Koreans, guerrillas and warrior monks, retook Pyongyang. In July 1593 Ukita Hideie led 90,000 Japanese troops against Jinju, the largest force of the war for a single operation. After talks the Japanese withdrew to the Busan area and a ceasefire followed, with little fighting for three years.

Hideyoshi launched a second invasion in 1597, no longer aiming at China. The Japanese were again halted in the south. Hideyoshi died in 1598, the Council of Five Elders ordered the withdrawal, and the Japanese fleet was attacked at the Battle of Noryang on 16 December 1598, the final, largest and bloodiest battle of the war.

These were East Asia's first regional wars of massed armies with modern weapons, with Japanese armies of up to 200,000 and Ming armies of 80,000. Hideyoshi's order for the second invasion called for everyone to be mown down, young or old, and the heads sent to Japan. The war weakened the Toyotomi clan and, since the forces came mostly from western daimyos, strengthened Tokugawa Ieyasu, who became shogun in 1603 after the Battle of Sekigahara. Later Japanese leaders cited the invasions to justify the annexation of Korea.
immanuel-kant: Immanuel Kant was born Emanuel on 22 April 1724 in Königsberg, East Prussia, into a Lutheran family. His father, Johann Georg Kant, was a harness-maker from Memel, and his mother was Anna Regina Reuter. He was the fourth of nine children, six of whom reached adulthood. The household stressed Pietist values of religious devotion, humility and a literal reading of the Bible, and his early schooling was strict, with an emphasis on Latin and religious instruction. He changed the spelling of his name to Immanuel after learning Hebrew.

Kant received a licence to lecture at Königsberg in 1755 and taught mathematics, physics, logic and metaphysics. In 1757 he began lecturing on geography, one of the first to teach it as a subject of its own. His Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens (1755) set out the nebular hypothesis, in which the Solar System formed from a cloud of gas. He also suggested that other distant nebulae might be other galaxies. In 1756 he published three papers on the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, among the first systematic attempts to explain earthquakes in natural terms. He became a professor in 1770.

The Critique of Pure Reason appeared in 1781, with a heavily revised second edition in 1787. The Critique of Practical Reason followed in 1788 and the Critique of the Power of Judgment in 1790. In 1792 the King's censorship commission opposed the publication of part of his work on religion. He published the book through the University of Jena, which earned him a royal reprimand, and a royal order later required him never to publish or speak publicly about religion. He died in Königsberg on 12 February 1804, saying Es ist gut, 'It is good'.

In the Critique of Pure Reason Kant argues for transcendental idealism: space and time are forms of intuition that structure all experience, and we know only appearances, not things in themselves. He compared this to a Copernican Revolution, proposing that objects of experience conform to the mind's forms of intuition and categories, not the reverse. His aim was to secure both knowledge and morality against scepticism and determinism, and he wrote that he had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.
imo-incident: After the Treaty of Ganghwa opened Korea, King Gojong's government pursued a policy of enlightenment, taking up Western technology while keeping Korean values. In 1881 Gojong and Queen Min invited the Japanese military attaché Lieutenant Horimoto Reizō to help create a modern army, and a unit of eighty to one hundred young men, the Pyŏlgigun or Special Skills Force, was given Japanese training. In January 1882 the old five-army garrison structure was reorganised into two garrisons.

Regular soldiers resented the new unit, which was far better equipped and treated. More than 1,000 men had been discharged in the reorganisation, and the rest had not received their pay in rice for 13 months. Meanwhile China, under Li Hongzhang, encouraged Korea to sign the treaty with the United States concluded at Incheon on 22 May 1882, hoping to offset Japanese influence.

The riot broke out on 23 July 1882 when the soldiers found sand and bad rice in their rations. They wrecked the house of Min Gyeom-ho, whom they suspected of swindling them, seized weapons from an armoury and freed prisoners, and the poor of Seoul joined them. Rioters stabbed Lieutenant Horimoto to death, and a crowd of some 3,000 surrounded the Japanese legation; the minister Hanabusa Yoshitada had it set on fire and escaped with his staff to Incheon and then to sea, where the British survey ship HMS Flying Fish picked them up. Six Japanese were killed during the flight.

On 24 July the rioters forced their way into the royal palace and killed Min Gyeom-ho and about a dozen high officials, among them Heungin-gun Yi Choe-Heung, the Daewongun's elder brother. They searched for Queen Min, who escaped disguised as a court lady, carried on the back of a guard.

Japan sent Hanabusa back with warships and soldiers, while China sent ships of the Beiyang Fleet and about 4,500 troops under General Wu Changqing. After seizing the Daewongun, Li Hongzhang had him confined for three years near Beijing. China then stationed troops in Seoul, sent advisers including Paul Georg von Möllendorff, set up a Korean Maritime Customs Service in 1883 and had Yuan Shikai train new Korean units. In Japan the crisis convinced leaders to expand the armed forces, and rivalry over Korea led on to the failed coup of 1884 and the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894.
imola: Imola is a city and comune in the Metropolitan City of Bologna, on the river Santerno in the Emilia-Romagna region. It is traditionally considered the western entrance to the historical region of Romagna. Its Roman name was Forum Cornelii, the Forum of Cornelius, after the dictator Sulla, who founded the city around 82 BCE. It was an agricultural and trading centre, notable for its ceramics. The name Imola was first used in the 7th century by the Lombards, who applied it to the fortress now known as the Castellaccio.

According to Paul the Deacon, Imola was in 412 the scene of the marriage of Ataulf, king of the Visigoths, to Galla Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius the Great. With the exarchate of Ravenna it passed under papal authority. In the 10th century and after, it saw incessant wars against Ravenna, Faenza and Bologna, and out of these conflicts came the city's republican constitution. In the contest between pope and emperor it was generally Ghibelline. Pope Benedict XII made Lippo II Alidosi pontifical vicar, and his family held power until 1424, when the condottiero Angelo della Pergola gained the upper hand.

In 1426 the city was restored to the Holy See, and it was conferred on the Sforza, dukes of Milan, in 1434, 1438 and 1470. It was later bestowed as a dowry on Caterina Sforza, bride of Girolamo Riario, nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, and under the Riarii it was embellished with palaces and works of art. Pope Alexander VI deprived Girolamo's son Ottaviano of power, and on 25 November 1499 the city surrendered to Cesare Borgia. In 1504 Imola submitted to Pope Julius II. It remained papal, apart from the years after 1797, until it joined the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

Imola is best known for the Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, opened in the 1950s. Among its older buildings are the Rocca Sforzesca, built under Girolamo Riario and Caterina Sforza, the cathedral dedicated to San Cassiano, erected between 1187 and 1271, and Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1726 and 1738 and since 1981 a civic art museum.
imperial-airways: The airline was meant to speed colonial government and trade by making travel to and from the colonies quicker than by ship. Facing heavily subsidised French and German airlines, the government's Hambling Committee under Sir Herbert Hambling recommended in February 1923 that four airlines merge: the Instone Air Line Company, British Marine Air Navigation, the Daimler Airway and Handley Page Transport. A subsidy of £1 million over ten years was offered. Sir Eric Geddes became chairman, and the airline, based at Croydon Airport, dropped its predecessors' services north of London to concentrate on international and imperial routes.

After a dispute with its pilots, services began on 26 April 1924 with a daily London–Paris flight in a de Havilland DH.34. In its first year the company carried 11,395 passengers and 212,380 letters. Alan Cobham flew route surveys to Cape Town in 1925–1926 and to Melbourne in 1926. A London to Karachi service started on 30 March 1929, taking seven days and including stretches by train, and was extended to Delhi that December. From October 1932 the eastern route ran along the Arabian side of the Persian Gulf. Services reached Calcutta in July 1933, Singapore in December 1933 and, with Qantas flying the last sector, Brisbane in December 1934, while a London to Cape Town mail route opened on 20 January 1932.

From 1937 Short Empire flying boats offered a through service from Southampton, and the Empire Air Mail Programme, started in July 1937, carried mail anywhere on the routes for 1½d an ounce. Shortly before war broke out on 1 September 1939, the aircraft of Imperial Airways and British Airways Ltd were moved to Bristol (Whitchurch) Airport to be operated jointly by National Air Communications.

Most aircraft seated fewer than twenty passengers, and about 50,000 people flew with the airline in the 1930s, mostly men in colonial administration, business or research. Its crews, about 3,000 by the end of the decade and all male on the flight deck, in the cabin and on the ground, were stationed along the routes and expected to act as ambassadors for Britain and the Empire. Accidents were frequent: in the first six years 32 people died in seven incidents, and on 28 March 1933 an Armstrong Whitworth Argosy burned and crashed at Diksmuide, killing all fifteen aboard in what is suspected to be the first sabotage in the air.
imperial-aramaic: The term was coined by Josef Markwart in 1927, in German as Reichsaramäisch. In 1955 Richard N. Frye observed that no surviving edict gave any language the status of an official language, and he described Imperial Aramaic instead as the lingua franca of the Achaemenid territories. Because every phase of it can be called imperial, some scholars prefer more specific names: Neo-Assyrian Aramaic and Neo-Babylonian Aramaic for the older phases and Achaemenid Aramaic for the later one. The alternatives Official Aramaic and Standard Aramaic have been criticised as unspecific, and all these terms are still used in different ways.

Aramaic spread as Arameans settled in great numbers in Babylonia and Upper Mesopotamia under the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian Empires, and it became the lingua franca of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. After their conquest of Mesopotamia in 539 BCE the Achaemenids made it the imperial standard for written communication between the regions and peoples of their empire, a choice cited as one reason for their success in holding that empire together for centuries.

Its spelling followed the language's own historical roots rather than any spoken dialect, so it was highly standardised across the empire. It was written in a lapidary form, carved on stone monuments, and in a cursive form; the cursive became far more common, and the lapidary style disappeared by the 3rd century BCE. Outside Egypt the language is known mostly from inscriptions on stone and pottery spread over a wide area, and a group of leather and wooden documents, the Bactria Aramaic documents, was found more recently in Bactria.

After the fall of the Achaemenid Empire the unity of the script was lost and it divided into a number of cursives. Its spread led to the Aramaic alphabet being used for Hebrew in place of the Paleo-Hebrew alphabet, and the two languages borrowed words from each other. The Nabataeans wrote in Imperial Aramaic rather than their native Arabic, and their Nabataean alphabet developed into the alphabet of Arabic. The Pahlavi scripts of the Arsacid and Sassanian empires kept Aramaic spellings, called Aramaeograms, as signs for Iranian words, and the Manichaean script also grew from it. The Brahmi script, the ancestor of Devanagari and the other Brahmic scripts, most likely descends from Imperial Aramaic.
imperial-conference: The meetings began as Colonial Conferences, gatherings of government leaders from the self-governing colonies of the British Empire, held in 1887, 1894, 1897 and 1902. Until then they had taken place while overseas statesmen were visiting London for royal occasions such as jubilees and coronations. The conference of 1907 renamed them Imperial Conferences and agreed that they should henceforth meet regularly, rather than whenever such an occasion brought the leaders together.

Imperial Conferences met in 1907, 1911, 1921, 1923, 1926, 1930, 1932 and 1937. They had been instituted to emphasise imperial unity, but in time they became the main forum in which dominion governments pressed to remove the remaining traces of their colonial status. The Balfour Declaration of 1926 described the dominions as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.

The conference of 1930 decided to end the legislative supremacy of the British Parliament as expressed in the Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865 and other imperial acts. The statesmen recommended a declaratory act of Parliament, passed with the dominions' consent, which became the Statute of Westminster 1931, although some dominions did not ratify it until years later. The 1930 conference was also attended by Southern Rhodesia, although it was a self-governing colony rather than a dominion.

As World War II drew to a close, the Imperial Conferences gave way to Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conferences, of which seventeen were held between 1944 and 1969, all but one of them in London. In 1971 these became the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meetings, held every two years with the hosting rotating among the members of the Commonwealth.
imperial-examination: Tests of skill such as archery contests existed from the Zhou dynasty, and the Confucian character of the later examinations owed much to the reign of Emperor Wu of Han. Before the Sui dynasty most official posts were filled through recommendation, based on qualities such as social status, morals and ability. The original purpose of the examinations under the Sui was to strike a blow against the hereditary aristocracy, whose power in the period of Northern and Southern dynasties had seriously constrained the emperor, and to centralise power around him.

In 622 the first Tang emperor let men nominate themselves, and throughout the Tang the vast majority of males were eligible. Oral interviews were meant to be unbiased but in practice favoured candidates from the elite clans of Chang'an and Luoyang. Empress Wu Zetian created military examinations in 702.

Under the Song dynasty the examinations became the primary method of recruiting officials and took the form of a rough ladder of local, provincial and court examinations. By the mid-12th century 100,000 candidates registered for the prefectural examinations each year, and by the mid-13th more than 400,000. The Liao and Jin dynasties held examinations for their Han subjects, while the Yuan ended them after the defeat of the Song in 1279, since Kublai Khan believed that Confucian learning was not needed for government posts. The Ming retained and expanded the system. In 1370 the Hongwu Emperor declared that the examinations would follow the Neo-Confucian canon of Zhu Xi, and the first palace examination of the dynasty was held in 1385.

From the 1830s and 1840s officials proposed adding Western technology, and in 1888 international commerce was added. The system lasted about 1,300 years until its abolition in the late Qing reforms in 1905.

By the Ming the degrees formed a ladder of success, with the jinshi, awarded at the palace level, regarded as the mark of success. Candidates spent up to three days and two nights in an isolated cell, writing eight-legged essays; guards searched them for hidden texts. The passing rate among the two or three million annual applicants was about 1%. The top three palace graduates were appointed directly to the Hanlin Academy. The exams were written in Classical Chinese, which spread as an educational standard to Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

The problem of surplus graduates became acute from the 18th century, when a long peace let many candidates prepare and examiners found their papers of similar quality. Reformers charged that the eight-legged essay stifled original thought. European missionaries and diplomats described the system, and in 1855 Britain adopted a similar testing system for its civil servants.
imperial-general-headquarters: The headquarters was set up by Imperial Decree 52 on 22 May 1893 as part of the Supreme War Council, a central command over the Imperial Japanese Army General Staff Office and the Imperial Japanese Navy General Staff. Under the Meiji Constitution the emperor was both head of state and supreme commander, and he headed it, assisted by officers of both services. It was wholly independent of the civilian government: Itō Hirobumi was admitted to its meetings by order of Emperor Meiji during the First Sino-Japanese War, but Katsura Taro was refused entry during the Russo-Japanese War.

After the Lugouqiao Incident of July 1937 it was abolished by Imperial Decree 658 of 18 November 1937 and at once reconstituted under Military Decree 1, with command over military operations in peace as well as war. That month Emperor Hirohito created a Liaison Conference within it to bring the army and navy chiefs closer to the government. Agreements between the services were each written down in a document called a Central Agreement, and final decisions were approved at Imperial Conferences over which Hirohito presided.

From November 1937 it also broadcast war news, fairly accurate at first but less so after the defeat at Midway, so that after the war the phrase daihon'ei happyou, announcement from the Imperial General Headquarters, came to mean any dubious official announcement. After the firebombing of Tokyo it moved to an underground site in the mountains outside Nagano, and the Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers ordered it abolished on 13 September 1945.

It had an Army Section, of the Chief of Army General Staff, his chief of operations and the Army Minister, and a Navy Section on the same pattern, with the Inspector-General of Military Training and the emperor's aide-de-camp as members. Relations between the services were never cordial. The army saw the Soviet Union as the main threat and favoured the Hokushin-ron, the Strike North concept of interests on the Asian continent; the navy saw the United States as the main threat and favoured the Nanshin-ron, a turn south to Southeast Asia and the Pacific islands.
imperial-royal-landwehr: The name Imperial-Royal might seem to join the two halves of the monarchy, but here Royal refers to the Kingdom of Bohemia, a crownland of the Austrian half to whose kingship the Habsburgs remained formally entitled. Calls on all able-bodied men to defend the country go back to the 16th century, and an imperial decree of 9 June 1808 created a standing Landwehr to complement the regular army; it was used in 1809 and in 1813/14 and abolished in 1859. Beethoven's March No. 1 of 1808, written for the Bohemian Landwehr, is now known as the Yorck March.

After the war with Prussia, the Compromise gave Hungary the right to its own Royal Hungarian Landwehr, the Honvéd, and the Austrian Landwehr was set up as its counterpart in the kingdoms and lands represented in the Reichsrat. The Defence Act of 1889 tasked it in war with supporting the army and defending the homeland and, by exception in peacetime, with keeping order, and set its yearly intake at 10,000 men. Conscripts served from 21 to 32, two or three years on active duty, and then passed to the Landsturm militia.

In 1914 it had 37 infantry regiments, 6 regiments of lancers, 8 field artillery and 8 field howitzer battalions, and mountain troops that included four Tyrolean rifle regiments, renamed Kaiserschützen in January 1917. On 11 April 1917 its infantry units were renamed Schützen, rifles. In September 1915 Emperor Franz Joseph I granted it colours for its achievements in the war, to be presented after the war; they were never issued under the monarchy, and only later passed to traditional units, as those of the 2nd Linz regiment did on 8 June 1924.

The Landwehr reported to the Imperial-Royal Ministry of Defence in Vienna, independent of the joint Ministry of War, and had its own barracks, depots and officer training; its officers trained at the Franz Joseph Military Academy in Vienna. Its regiments had three battalions instead of the four of the Common Army but were often better equipped, since the parliaments were readier to fund their own troops. Each bore the name of its staff's garrison town, as in the 6th Eger Landwehr Infantry Regiment, and its uniforms are shown in the Military History Museum in Vienna.
imperialism-the-highest-stage-of-capital: Lenin wrote the work between January and June 1916 and sent it to Parus, a Petrograd publishing house founded by the writer Maxim Gorky. It was meant to belong to a series of popular surveys of the West European countries involved in the war, edited by the Marxist historian Mikhail Pokrovsky, but Gorky issued it in addition to the regular series. It was announced in Gorky's magazine Letopis and published by Zhizn i Znaniye in mid-1917, with a preface by Lenin dated 26 April and with his criticisms of Karl Kautsky removed.

After the war Lenin added a new preface, dated 6 July 1920, for the French and German editions; it first appeared in the Communist International, No. 18, in 1921. The preface to those editions held that revolt against the capitalist world system would come through the colonies and semi-colonies, with their "thousand million people", rather than through the urban workers of Western Europe.

The book has ten chapters. The first three trace how the concentration of production produces monopolies, how banks cease to be mere intermediaries and come to control industry, and how the merger of bank and industrial capital creates finance capital and a financial oligarchy. The fourth chapter argues that surplus capital is exported to less developed countries in search of higher profits, and the fifth and sixth describe the division of the world into colonies and spheres of influence, which Lenin dated to the final partition between 1876 and 1900.

Lenin held that older powers such as Britain and France had taken most colonial possessions while newer ones such as Germany grew faster, and that only a war of redivision could resolve the contradiction. In the seventh chapter he attacked Kautsky's ultra-imperialism, the idea that international cartels would soften rivalry among the powers. The eighth chapter describes the parasitism of rentier states and the bribing of an upper layer of the working class with monopoly profits. The last chapters survey attitudes to imperialism and call it a moribund, transitional stage of capitalism.

Lenin expected to put the theory into practice through the Third International (1919-1943), whose conferences of July and August 1920 he dominated intellectually and politically. The 1920 edition cited the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of 1918 and the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 as proof that empire and hegemony, not nationalism, lay behind the First World War. Kwame Nkrumah took inspiration from the text for his work on neocolonialism, and the title of his book Neo-Colonialism, the Last Stage of Imperialism alludes to it. Editions appeared in London in 1948, in New Delhi in 2000 and as a Penguin Classic in 2010.
imphal: Imphal lies in the Imphal Valley in the extreme east of India, surrounded by nine ranges of hills, at an average elevation of 786 metres. Its climate is humid subtropical, with cool, dry winters and a slightly hot monsoon season. The name comes from two Meitei words, yum, meaning house, and phāl, meaning plenty or beautiful.

Tradition holds that King Pakhangba established Kangla Fort, once the capital of Manipur, in 33 CE. The kingdom had earlier been ruled by kings of the Khaba clan; the Ningthouja dynasty began to rule after the ascension of Nongda Lairen Pakhangba and came to dominate the region in politics and war. Kangla Palace was built by King Khagemba and his son Khunjaoba. In the reign of Maharaja Bhagyachandra there were a number of Burmese invasions, and the kingdom survived with the help of Maharaj Gambhir Singh.

Imphal remained peaceful until 1891, when disputes within the royal family led the British to send J. W. Quinton, and an order to arrest the prince Senapati Tikendrajit angered the people. The resulting Anglo-Manipur War was won by the British. The king, Maharaja Kulachandra, was sentenced to imprisonment and sent to the Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Tikendrajit and Thangal General were hanged. The British destroyed Kangla Palace in the war. The region merged with India in 1949.
The Battle of Imphal was fought between March and July 1944. The Japanese had invaded in order to destroy the Allied forces and then invade India, but were defeated and forced to retreat.

Imphal is the capital of the Indian state of Manipur, with a population of 277,196 at the 2011 census; most people speak Manipuri. Hinduism is the majority religion and Sanamahism the second largest, and the Pakhangba temple stands within Kangla Fort, whose ruins are surrounded by a moat. The Ima Keithel, or Mothers' Market, was established in the 16th century and is run by women vendors. The Imphal War Cemetery commemorates Indian and British soldiers who died in 1944.
impi: Before Shaka, warfare among the peoples of KwaZulu Natal was frequent but of low intensity, fought over cattle, personal insults or grazing land. Many battles were arranged in advance, with women and children watching from a distance, and consisted of ritual taunts, single combats and tentative charges by men armed with several thin throwing spears, the assegai, and small cowhide shields. Casualties were usually light, and the defeated might pay in land or cattle. The quick raid was the most frequent action.

In the early 19th century rising populations, white settlement and slaving, and ambitious new men changed this pattern. According to historians such as Donald Morris, Dingiswayo of the Mthethwa built a relatively light hegemony by diplomacy and judicious force that reduced feuding among the clans. Shaka, serving in his iziCwe regiment, designed the short stabbing spear, the iklwa, with a broad blade 25 centimetres long, and a larger shield, the isihlangu, and discarded sandals so that his men could run faster.

After their 20th birthdays young men were sorted into amabutho and built their ikhanda, a stockade of huts around a cattle corral, where they gathered when summoned. Boys trained from as early as six and went on campaign as porters, carrying rations, cooking pots and sleeping mats. A regiment might number 400 or 4000 men under an inDuna, and regiments were grouped into corps named after their military kraals. Each ibutho had its own headdress and shield colouring: junior regiments carried largely dark shields, senior ones lighter, and Shaka's own Fasimba white.

The impi attacked in the buffalo horns formation. The two horns, usually younger troops, encircled and pinned the enemy; the chest, the prime fighters, delivered the decisive blow; the loins, often older veterans, waited in reserve, sometimes with their backs to the battle. Encirclement was not new in the region; what set the Zulu apart was the degree of organisation, the consistency with which they used these tactics and the speed of their execution.

Shaka's brother and successor, Dingane kaSenzangakhona, reintroduced greater use of the throwing spear, perhaps against Boer firearms. At Ndondakusuka, two decades before the Anglo-Zulu War, Cetshwayo deployed 30,000 men. After Isandlwana the Zulus captured many Martini–Henry rifles but lacked training and used them ineffectively. The attacks on Rorke's Drift and Kambula, both bloody defeats, seem to have been made against Cetshwayo's orders, and massed attacks were broken by rifles, Gatling guns and artillery, finally at Ulindi.
impressionism: In the middle of the 19th century, as Napoleon III rebuilt Paris, the Académie des Beaux-Arts dominated French art. It valued historical and religious subjects and portraits, and preferred carefully finished pictures whose brush strokes were blended to hide the artist's hand. Its annual juried show, the Salon de Paris, decided prizes and commissions. By the 1850s some artists, notably Gustave Courbet, had drawn attention and censure by depicting contemporary realities without idealisation. The Impressionists also learned from painters such as Eugène Boudin and Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot, who worked from nature in a direct and spontaneous style, and followed Eugène Delacroix and J. M. W. Turner in letting freely brushed colour take precedence over line.

Impressionism began with a group of Paris-based artists whose independent exhibitions brought them to prominence in the 1870s and 1880s. They painted outdoors, en plein air, to capture the momentary effects of sunlight, and portrayed overall visual effects rather than details. They used short, broken strokes of colour set side by side with as little mixing as possible, and placed wet paint into wet paint.

They chose subjects such as middle-class leisure, cafés, theatres, train stations and the widened avenues of Paris, and included factories in their landscapes. Among the central figures were Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Alfred Sisley, Edgar Degas, Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt; Pissarro was the only one to take part in all eight Impressionist exhibitions. Women were excluded from much of the social life of the boulevard and café where ideas were shared.

The name comes from Monet's Impression, Sunrise. The critic Louis Leroy coined it in a mocking review of the First Impressionist Exhibition of 1874 in Le Charivari, writing that wallpaper in its embryonic state was more finished than that seascape. The artists earned little from the exhibitions, but the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel kept their work before the public and arranged shows in London and New York. Renoir had a great Salon success in 1879, Monet became financially secure in the early 1880s and Pissarro by the early 1890s, while Sisley died in poverty in 1899.

The style spread to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia and the Netherlands, and analogous movements arose in music and literature. In the 1880s Vincent van Gogh, Paul Gauguin, Georges Seurat and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec developed different ideas of colour and form, and their work is called post-Impressionism.
imre-nagy: Imre Nagy was born on 7 June 1896 in Kaposvár, in the Kingdom of Hungary, to a family of peasant origin. His father was a carriage driver and later an unskilled worker. After a poor record at the gymnasium he trained as a locksmith and metal fitter.

Conscripted into the Austro-Hungarian Army in 1914, he was wounded on the Italian Front and again on the Eastern Front, where Russian forces took him prisoner in July 1916. In Siberia he joined a Marxist discussion group, and in 1918 he joined the Communist Party of the Foreign Workers of Siberia and fought in the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. He joined the Russian Communist Party in 1920.

Sent by the Hungarian Communist Party to Hungary in 1921, Nagy worked on underground networks and was arrested several times. From 1930 he lived in the Soviet Union, where he did agricultural research and, from 1933 to 1941, served the NKVD as an informer under the codename Volodia.

After the Second World War he returned to Hungary and was Minister of Agriculture, distributing land to the peasants, then Interior Minister. As prime minister from 1953 to 1955 he promoted his New Course, easing the harshest parts of Mátyás Rákosi's Stalinist regime, but Rákosi's influence prevailed and he was dismissed on 18 April 1955, losing his party posts.

After Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech of February 1956, criticism of Rákosi grew, and he was forced out in July. On 23 October a student demonstration in Budapest called for Nagy's return, and the revolt began. Nagy was named prime minister on 24 October. On 28 October he negotiated a ceasefire with Soviet representatives and announced the dissolution of the ÁVH secret police.

By 30 October he promised a multi-party system, and on 1 November he announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and appealed to the UN for recognition of its neutrality. Soviet forces attacked Budapest on 4 November, and Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav Embassy.

Despite János Kádár's written safe conduct, he was arrested on 22 November as he left the embassy and taken to Romania. He was secretly tried in Hungary for treason and the organisation of the overthrow of the republic, and hanged on 16 June 1958; his burial was in an unmarked grave in the prison yard. In June 1989 he and other figures of the revolution were rehabilitated and reburied with full honours, an event that played a key part in the fall of the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party regime.
imre-thokoly: Imre Thököly was born in Késmárk, now Kežmarok in Slovakia, on 25 September 1657, the fifth son of Count István Thököly and the only one to survive childhood. His father was among the wealthiest nobles of Upper Hungary. He studied at the Lutheran lyceum in Eperjes from 1668. In 1670 his father was accused of joining the aristocrats' conspiracy against Leopold I and died during the siege of Árva Castle on 4 December; accounts differ on how the son got away to Transylvania.

His estates in Hungary were confiscated, but he kept his Transylvanian lands and continued his studies at the Reformed college of Nagyenyed. Meanwhile Leopold I appointed a Directorium in 1673 that pursued a violent anti-Protestant policy, and refugees, called kuruc, raided the borderlands of Royal Hungary.

The princely council appointed him to command the Kuruc army on 26 September 1677, after a treaty at Warsaw in which Louis XIV promised an annual subsidy. He joined the Kuruc at Derecske on 27 November. In 1678 he captured Szendrő and Murány and the mining towns of the Garam valley, and he kept control of thirteen counties of Royal Hungary after a defeat at Barsszentkereszt.
