Muhammad Shah's order of 1327 moving much of Delhi's Muslim population to Daulatabad carried it to the Deccan, where the Bahmani Sultanate, founded in 1347 by Hasan Gangu, kept festivals such as Nowruz and recruited Persian officials such as Mahmud Gawan; rivalry between these newcomers and the Dakhani elite led to Gawan's execution in 1481 and massacres of foreigners. In Bengal Persian was an official language from 1204 to 1837, and the poet Hafez corresponded with Sultan Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah.

The synthesis shaped daily life as well as courts. Mughal kitchens produced Mughlai cuisine and dishes such as biryani; Hindustani classical music, the khyal and tarana and the Sufi qawwali drew on Iranian elements, many credited to Amir Khusrau; architecture joined domes, iwans and gardens with Indian corbelled arches and jali, and Sikh and Vijayanagara builders used it too. Hindustani, the ancestor of Hindi and Urdu, grew from these contacts.

After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 and Nader Shah's sack of Delhi in 1739, Persian culture declined, though it still found patrons in regional courts such as that of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Under British rule Persian lost its place as an official language, and the dethroning of Bahadur Shah Zafar in 1857 is often taken to mark the end of the Indo-Persian era. Persian still had readers afterwards, as in the poetry of Muhammad Iqbal, and British architects borrowed its forms for the Indo-Saracenic style.
indo-scythians: The Indo-Scythians, also called Indo-Sakas, were nomadic people of Iranian Scythian origin. Saka is more a generic term than the name of one state: Saka tribes were part of a cultural continuum of early nomads across the steppe, Iranian-speaking horse nomads who buried their dead in mound tombs called kurgans. Chinese sources record that after the Xiongnu defeated the Yuezhi, the Yuezhi moved west and displaced the Saka, who migrated south toward Bactria and present-day Afghanistan. Many settled in Drangiana, later called Sakastan or Sistan, from which the Indo-Scythian kingdom and its vassal states arose.

Maues is the first Saka king in the Indian subcontinent. Petroglyphs at river crossings in Chilas and on the Sacred Rock of Hunza mark the route across the Karakoram that he used to capture Taxila from the Indo-Greek king Apollodotus II. In 55 BCE Azes I took control of north-western India after his victory over Hippostratos. In the east the Indo-Scythians held Mathura from about 60 BCE under satraps such as Hagamasha, Hagana and Rajuvula, called the Northern Satraps. After Azes, the Indo-Parthian ruler Gondophares ended Indo-Scythian rule in the north-west, and the Kushans later regained the region, taking the Mathura area about 100 CE.

The Western Satraps ruled Kathiawar and Gujarat until the fifth century. Rudradaman I is known from the Junagadh rock inscription, which records his conquest of the Yaudheyas and his defeat of the Satavahana empire. The last Western Satrap, Rudrasimha III, was defeated by the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II in 395 CE.

Indo-Scythian coinage is generally of high quality, between Indo-Greek and Kushan work, and may have benefited from Greek coin-makers. The coins use the Greek alphabet on the obverse and Kharoshthi on the reverse, show the king on horseback or seated cross-legged, and often show Greek gods on the reverse. The Indo-Scythians seem to have supported Buddhism. Kharahostes and Rajuvula are named on the Mathura lion capital, which records the gift of a stupa with a relic of the Buddha, and coins of Azes were found in the Bimaran casket, one of the earliest representations of the Buddha. Indian texts such as the Mahabharata name them Shakas and list them among warlike tribes of the north-west.
indochinese-communist-party: The party began as the Vietnamese Communist Party, founded on 3 February 1930 by uniting the Communist Party of Indochina, which despite its name was active only in Tonkin, and the Communist Party of Annam, active only in Cochinchina; the Communist League of Indochina, active in central Annam, joined soon after. The Comintern held that the movement should cover the whole of French Indochina, Cambodia and Laos included, and at its urging the party took the name Indochinese Communist Party in October 1930. In return for financial aid, the Communist International had considerable control over the party's policies and leadership.

Its programme of action had ten points: the overthrow of French imperialism, Vietnamese feudalism and the reactionary bourgeoisie; complete independence for Indochina; a worker-peasant-soldier government; the confiscation of the imperialists' banks, enterprises and plantations and the distribution of property to the poor; an eight-hour working day; the abolition of the poll tax and other unjust taxes; democratic freedoms; education for all; and equality between men and women.

The party's outlook was Marxist-Leninist, adapted to colonial Indochina. Much of the population was rural, and it saw the peasantry as well as the workers as agents of revolution, while stressing the unity of Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos in the struggle for independence. It directed the Viet Minh and sought to coordinate revolution across the region. In Cambodia it set up the League for National Salvation of Vietnamese Residents of Kampuchea in March 1947 as its front among Vietnamese living there; Vietnamese sources claimed in 1950 that it had 50,000 members.

After its nominal dissolution on 11 November 1945 the party continued in secret under the name Institute for Studying Marxism in Indochina. It was publicly re-established as the Workers' Party of Vietnam in February 1951 and became the Communist Party of Vietnam in 1976. Its members in Cambodia and Laos helped shape the movements of those countries: the Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party, which became the Cambodian People's Party, and the Lao People's Revolutionary Party, which with the Pathet Lao took power in 1975 and established the Lao People's Democratic Republic.
indonesia: Indonesia is an equatorial archipelago of coastal plains, mountains and volcanic islands, extending 5,120 kilometres from east to west across three time zones and 1,760 kilometres from north to south. Published counts of its islands range from 13,000 to 25,000, and the most widely cited official count is 17,508, with about 6,000 inhabited.

Its five main islands are Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Borneo and New Guinea. Strategic shipping routes between the Indian and Pacific oceans run through the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits. The country lies on a complex plate-boundary zone, with at least 127 active volcanoes and a high exposure to earthquakes and tsunamis; the Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago was one of the largest known.

Java has yielded hominin fossils generally attributed to Homo erectus, and narrative cave art in Sulawesi has been dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years. From the third millennium BCE Austronesian-speaking communities moved south from Taiwan through the Philippines into the archipelago, and from around 500 BCE regional trading networks connected it with South and East Asia.

In the early centuries CE some coastal communities in Borneo, Sumatra and Java developed into trading ports, and Indian merchants and religious specialists brought Sanskrit literacy, Hindu and Buddhist practices and models of kingship that local rulers adopted. Srivijaya, founded in southeastern Sumatra in the late 7th century, became a maritime trading polity and a centre of Buddhist learning.

Rulers in central Java supported the building of Borobudur and Prambanan between the 8th and 10th centuries. Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late 13th century after Raden Wijaya used a Mongol expedition to defeat his rivals and then forced the Mongols to withdraw.

Its rulers claimed suzerainty over ports across the archipelago, although beyond Java this authority was often exercised indirectly through tributary, ritual and commercial relationships. Islamic states grew from the late medieval period, and European powers competed to monopolise trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku. Dutch commercial and colonial control expanded from the 17th century and covered most of the archipelago by the early 20th century.

Indonesia proclaimed its independence in the aftermath of World War II. After the fall of Suharto in 1998, decentralisation transferred substantial lawmaking powers to provincial, regency and city governments, and constitutional amendments between 1999 and 2002 introduced direct presidential elections, which began in 2004. The country is a presidential republic of 38 provinces.

The Javanese are the largest ethnic group, at about 40%. More than 700 languages are spoken, and Indonesian, a standardised variety of Malay adopted as a language of unity through the 1928 Youth Pledge, is the official language. Its motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, comes from the 14th-century poem Sutasoma.
indonesia-raya: While living in Jakarta, Wage Rudolf Supratman, a musician and young reporter, read an essay in Timbul magazine that challenged Indonesian music experts to compose a future national anthem. He took up the challenge, and the song, titled Indonesia, was completed in Bandung in 1924. According to Tempo the words were revised after Supratman was reportedly inspired by Tan Malaka's book Massa Actie, published in 1926, and the song went through several revisions before reaching its final form in 1928.

That year youths from across Indonesia held the first Indonesian Youth Congress to push for independence. Supratman asked the organisers for access to report on it, and they asked him not to publish, for fear that the Dutch authorities would ban the event. Encouraged by the leader Sugondo Djojopuspito, he played the song on the violin on 28 October 1928, at the Second Indonesian Youth Congress, hoping it would one day become the national anthem.

After the congress many political and student organisations distributed the text, and the press played a key part. The daily Soeloeh Ra'jat Indonesia published the words on 7 November 1928, and the Chinese Indonesian weekly Sin Po followed on 10 November, an act of defiance towards the Dutch. In 1929 Supratman retitled the song Indonesia Raya, Great Indonesia, and printed pamphlets himself; all one thousand copies sold quickly. The businessman Tio Tek Hong issued the first records that year, but in 1930 the Dutch colonial authorities banned the song and confiscated the unsold records.

The first stanza was chosen as the national anthem when independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945, and the constitution and a state gazette of 1958 confirm that only that stanza serves as the anthem. It is played at flag-raising ceremonies in schools every Monday, and at the main ceremony on 17 August each year.

The song marked the birth of the archipelago nationalist movement that aimed to end Dutch colonial rule. Because there was no orchestral version, the Indonesian government asked the Dutch arranger Jozef Cleber in 1950 for a symphonic one. President Sukarno found his first recording too frilly and wanted something solemn like the Dutch Wilhelmus. Cleber considered that impossible, saw some of the character of the Marseillaise in the tune, and made a second arrangement marked maestoso con bravura, which Sukarno approved. It remained in use for 47 years, until a remastered version by Addie MS in 1998.

Supratman died in 1938, and his four surviving sisters inherited the rights. The state became owner when the song became the national anthem, and in 1958 the government obtained the sole right from his family, rewarding each sister with 250,000 rupiah in 1960.
indonesian-independence: In 1918 the Dutch authorities set up a partly elected People's Council, the Volksraad, which gave Indonesian nationalists a voice for the first time. In 1927 Sukarno turned his study club into the Indonesian Nationalist Association, which became the Indonesian National Party in May 1928, aiming at independence through mass non-cooperation. Sukarno was arrested in 1929 and again in 1933, and Mohammad Hatta and Sutan Sjahrir were exiled to the Boven Digul camp, which effectively ended the non-cooperation movement.

Japan invaded the Dutch East Indies in January 1942, and the Dutch surrendered on 8 March. Seeking to mobilise the population, the Japanese freed Sukarno from exile in 1943, and he and Hatta cooperated with them while keeping independence as their aim. On 7 September 1944 Prime Minister Kuniaki Koiso promised independence for the East Indies later on. After Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed, Sukarno and Hatta were flown to Dalat on 9 August 1945, where Field Marshal Hisaichi Terauchi promised independence.

Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945. Younger activists, the pemuda, urged Sukarno and Hatta to declare independence at once and without the Japanese-formed Preparatory Committee. When the two refused, pemuda leaders took them on 16 August to Rengasdengklok, but they still would not proclaim without assurances from the Japanese. Achmad Soebardjo brought them back to Jakarta, and they met committee members at the house of Rear-Admiral Tadashi Maeda.

Sjahrir's pemuda had drafted a text declaring that government organs would be seized by the people. Sukarno and Hatta rejected it as likely to spark violence, and Sukarno drafted a version speaking of an orderly transfer of power in the shortest possible time. Only Sukarno and Hatta signed it. At 10:00 on 17 August 1945 Sukarno, with Hatta beside him, read the proclamation. Latief Hendraningat raised the red-and-white flag, and the attendees sang Indonesia Raya.

Youths spread the news across Java by Japanese news and telegraph facilities, and in Bandung it was broadcast by radio. Many ordinary Indonesians doubted it or saw it as Japanese deception, and in Sumatra only the republican elite of major cities knew of it by mid-September. On 18 August the committee elected Sukarno president and Hatta vice-president and ratified the constitution. The Dutch regarded the republicans as collaborators with the Japanese and wished to restore colonial rule, which began a four-year war. The Netherlands acknowledged Indonesian independence in 1949.
indonesian-national-armed-forces: Before the Republic of Indonesia existed, military authority in the Dutch East Indies lay with the Royal Dutch East Indies Army and the Royal Netherlands Navy. They did not directly form the later Indonesian forces and were mainly the enemy during the Indonesian National Revolution of 1945 to 1949, but the Army had given military training to some future officers. It recruited Ambonese, Kai Islanders, Timorese and Minahasan people, and in 1940 it opened to large intakes of Javanese, among them the future officers Suharto and Abdul Haris Nasution.

The forces themselves were formed during the Revolution, when they fought a guerrilla war alongside informal militia. They began as the People's Security Agency on 22 August 1945, became the People's Security Forces on 5 October 1945 and then the Armed Forces of the Republic of Indonesia in January 1946. The name Tentara Nasional Indonesia was first used on 3 June 1947. Later names included the War Forces of the Republic of Indonesia (1950 to 1962) and the Armed Forces of the Republic of Indonesia, ABRI (1962 to 1999). The name Tentara Nasional Indonesia was restored on 1 April 1999.

The Army, Navy and Air Force have long been organised along territorial commands, a legacy of the guerrilla war and of the need for internal security. Seven commands were established by 1958, and no central reserve formation existed until 1961. Only after the attempted coup of 1 October 1965 and General Suharto's rise to the presidency did it become possible to integrate the services and develop a joint operations structure. A 1985 reorganisation separated the Ministry of Defense and Security from the ABRI headquarters, leaving the commander in chief in command of the forces and a member of the cabinet.

The military philosophy is civilian-military defence, called Total People's Defence. It foresees three stages: a short period in which an invader defeats the conventional army, a long period of territorial guerrilla warfare, and a final expulsion, with the army as a rallying point from village level upwards. The Armed Forces Enters the Village programme, begun in 1983, is held three times a year to build civilian projects. Indonesia has also sent forces to UN peacekeeping missions, including in Lebanon and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The President of Indonesia is Supreme Commander. Each service has a chief of staff, but only the commander of the armed forces holds command authority over all three. Special forces include the army's Kopassus and the navy's Kopaska. After the Surabaya bombings of 2018 President Joko Widodo agreed to revive a joint special operations command, and in July 2019 he formed the Armed Forces Special Operations Command. In January 2021 a regulation created a reserve component, with voluntary membership.
indonesian-national-party: The party grew out of the Algemeene Studie Club that Sukarno, then an engineering student at the Bandung Technical College, founded in November 1925 on the model of a club Soetomo had started in Surabaya. Reformed in July 1927 as the Indonesian National Association, it took the name Indonesian National Party in May 1928. Its aim was economic and political independence for the archipelago, and by the end of 1929 it had 10,000 members.

Sukarno and seven other leaders were tried as a threat to public order and sentenced in September 1930 to one to three years, Sukarno receiving the longest term. Rival successors followed, among them Partindo and Sutan Sjahrir's Indonesian Nationalist Education, the New PNI, which Mohammad Hatta led from 1932.

Two days after the declaration of independence in August 1945, a state party of the same name was set up as a continuation of the wartime Jawa Hokokai, but its ties to the Japanese occupation made it unpopular and it was dissolved within weeks. On 29 January 1946 the PNI was revived as a popular party without Sukarno, who as president stood above politics. During the National Revolution it opposed negotiating with the Dutch and drew support from the administrative officers of the republic.

The party took 22.3% of the vote and 57 of the 257 seats in the 1955 general election, ahead of Masyumi, the Nahdlatul Ulama and the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI). Its members Wilopo and Ali Sastroamidjojo headed cabinets in the 1950s. Under Guided Democracy it moved left, and in 1963 its congress defined its ideology of Marhaenism as Marxism adapted to Indonesian conditions.

After the coup attempt of 30 September 1965 the army forced out the party's left wing. Weakened, the PNI came third in the 1971 elections with less than 7% of the vote, and in 1973 it was merged into the Indonesian Democratic Party. After the fall of Suharto several parties claimed its name; in the 1999 election two of them won one seat each.
indonesian-national-revolution: Indonesian nationalism grew rapidly in the first half of the 20th century. The independence movement is dated to 20 May 1908, commemorated as the Day of National Awakening. Budi Utomo, Sarekat Islam, the Indonesian National Party and the Indonesian Communist Party took different paths, some cooperating with the Volksraad in hope of self-rule, others refusing to cooperate.

The Japanese occupation of three and a half years during the Second World War was a crucial factor. The Netherlands could hardly defend its colony, and within three months the Japanese held it. In Java and, to a lesser extent, Sumatra they encouraged nationalist sentiment for their own advantage, elevated leaders such as Sukarno and destroyed much of the infrastructure built by the Dutch.

Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945, and radical youth groups, the pemuda, pressed Sukarno and Hatta to proclaim independence on 17 August. The next day Sukarno was elected president and Hatta vice-president. The Netherlands, weakened by the war, did not return as a significant military force until early 1946, and Allied forces under British command acted as caretakers in the interval.

In November 1946 the British brokered the Linggadjati Agreement, under which the Netherlands recognised the Republic as the de facto authority over Java, Madura and Sumatra. Neither party was satisfied. At midnight on 20 July 1947 the Dutch launched Operatie Product, a major offensive to regain economically valuable areas, which they described as police actions. Republican forces were confined to the Yogyakarta region. Alongside the war came social revolutions against aristocrats and village heads, and in East Sumatra the sultanates were overthrown and many aristocrats killed.

Resistance and diplomacy turned world opinion against the Dutch, and the second police action was a diplomatic disaster for them. The United States, threatening to cut off economic aid, pushed the Netherlands into negotiations. At the Round Table Conference at The Hague, from 23 August to 2 November 1949, the Netherlands agreed to recognise a federal United States of Indonesia over all the former Dutch East Indies except Dutch New Guinea, and Indonesia took on a colonial debt of 4.5 billion guilders. Sovereignty was transferred on 27 December 1949.

Estimates of Indonesian deaths in fighting and among civilians range from 97,421 to 100,000, and more than 4,000 Dutch soldiers died. The revolution ended Dutch colonial administration and reduced the power of many local rulers, but did not significantly improve the fortunes of most of the population.
indra: Indra is of ancient but unclear origin, and the roots of his name have been contested among scholars since the 19th century. Aspects of him resemble other Indo-European thunder gods, such as Zeus, Thor and Perun, who are linked to rain and thunder and share parts of his heroic mythology. A tablet from Boghaz-köi, dated to about 1400 BCE, records a treaty that names Mitra, Varuna, Indra and Nasatya among its gods. Modern scholarship suggests that the name arose at the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, where the Aryans lived before settling in India.

More than a quarter of the 1,028 hymns of the Rigveda mention Indra, which makes him the deity referred to most often. The commonest theme is his killing, with his thunderbolt, of the serpent Vritra, which held back the rains; the rivers are thereby released. In the Rigveda he is armed with a thunderbolt, the vajra, rides a chariot and has golden hair. In later art he rides a four-tusked white elephant, Airavata, and the rainbow is called his bow. His abode is Amaravati, the capital of Svarga.

In post-Vedic texts his importance declines and he is shown as an intoxicated, hedonistic god, a minor figure beside Vishnu, Shiva or Devi. The Puranas, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata make him a son of the sage Kashyapa and of Aditi, and husband of Shachi. According to the Vishnu Purana, Indra is a title borne by the king of the gods, which changes with each Manvantara, a cyclic period of time in Hindu cosmology.

In Buddhism Indra, called Śakra or Sakka, rules over the Trāyastriṃśa heaven above Mount Sumeru, one of the realms of rebirth, and Buddhist texts reduce him to a figurehead who himself suffers rebirth. In Jainism he is not the king of the gods but the king of superhumans in Svarga-Loka, and Jain literature knows sixty-four Indras who attend the five auspicious events in the life of a Tirthankara. In Iranian religion the roles were reversed, and the Vendidad names Indra as a relatively minor demon. Tamil Sangam literature describes a month-long festival for Indra, the Indra Vila, held for want of rain.
indra-jatra: Indra Jatra is the largest religious street festival of the Kathmandu Valley, and its name in Nepal Bhasa, Yenya Punhi, refers to the full-moon day of Yenla, the eleventh month of the Nepal Sambat calendar. Tradition credits King Gunakamadeva with starting it to commemorate the founding of Kathmandu in the 10th century. The chariot festival of Kumari, Kumari Jatra, which coincides with it, was started in 1756 during the reign of Jaya Prakash Malla. As the celebrations follow the lunar calendar, their dates change from year to year.

According to legend, Indra came down to earth disguised as a farmer to gather night jasmine for a ritual of his mother Basundhara. The people caught him plucking the flowers at Maru and bound him like a thief, and released him once they learned who he was. His mother then promised enough dew through the winter to ensure a rich crop, and the foggy mornings of Kathmandu are said to begin from the festival onwards.

The celebrations last eight days. They open with the raising of the Yosin pole at Kathmandu Durbar Square, a tree stripped of branches and bark, brought from a forest near Nala, 29 km east of the city, and dragged there by men pulling on ropes. On three days chariots carrying human representations of Ganesh, Bhairava and Kumari are pulled through the southern, northern and central parts of the city; since 2012 an all women's team has pulled the chariot of Kumari on the third day.

Families honour relatives who died in the past year by offering butter lamps along the route, and many follow the procession of Dagin, which re-enacts Indra's mother searching for her son. Images of Indra with his hands bound are shown at Maru and Indra Chowk, and masks of Bhairava, among them Sweta Bhairava at Durbar Square, are displayed throughout. Masked dances such as Pulu Kisi, the wicker elephant of Indra, and the demon Majipa Lakhey move through the streets. The festival ends when the pole is taken down.

Bhaktapur and Patan keep their own traditions. In Bhaktapur poles representing Yama are raised, the goddess Indrayani is carried to Siddha Pokhari, and the masked Mupatra and Pulu Kisi keep apart, since local tradition holds that their meeting could bring a confrontation. The season is also one of open air theatre, the Dabu Pyakhan, with plays of satire and comedy on the sidelines.
indrapura-champa: The name Indrapura means City of Indra in Sanskrit, after the Hindu god of storm and war and king of the gods in the Rig Veda; the modern place name is Đồng Dương. Chinese and Vietnamese sources rendered the city as Fóshì, or Phật Thệ in Vietnamese. Earlier scholars took Fóshì to be a transcription of Vijaya, a reading later rejected. The historian Michael Vickery suggests that colonial-era scholars made that link to support the posited empire of Srivijaya in present-day Indonesia.

The city was built around 875 by Indravarman II (r. 875–890), a Buddhist king who founded the Bhrgu dynasty of Champa, and under that dynasty it served as the chief capital for about a century. Indravarman II built a Mahayana Buddhist temple complex named Lasmindra Lokesvara there, and his successors raised further Buddhist temples around it. A high-ranking Cham court official made a Buddhist pilgrimage from Indrapura to Java around 911–912, and Buddhist temples spread as far north as Quảng Bình.

The rise of Đại Cồ Việt in the north and the Khmer Empire in the west weakened Champa, which fought the Khmer in 945 and Đại Cồ Việt in 979. In 982 the Vietnamese emperor Lê Hoàn led armies into northern Champa in the Cham–Vietnamese War, and the Cham king Paramesvaravarman I was killed. In 983 a Vietnamese named Lưu Kế Tông dethroned the ruling king of Champa, and in 986 he proclaimed himself king, seeking recognition from Song China, while many Cham fled to Hainan Island. In 988 a new Cham king, Harivarman II, sent an envoy to the Song. Power passed to Vijaya in Binh Dinh by the 12th century.

Đồng Dương and My Son were struck by USAF carpet bombs in August 1969, which left both sites in ruins. Research on Champa resumed in the late 1980s and 1990s, and the site has since been excavated again. Its remains include an eroded citadel, the royal palace area, watch towers, the ruins of the monastery, paved roads, bridges and a sewer system, signs of a well-organised city whose other buildings were probably of wood or bamboo.
indus: The Indus is 3,180 kilometres long. It rises in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, where it is known as Sengge Zangbo, flows northwest through Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan, and bends sharply to the left after the Nanga Parbat massif. It then runs south-by-southwest through Pakistan and empties into the Arabian Sea near Karachi. Its left-bank tributary on the plains is the Panjnad, formed by the successive confluences of the five Punjab rivers: the Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Its principal right-bank tributaries are the Shyok, Gilgit, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal.

Its headwaters, with those of the Yarlung Tsangpo to the east, follow the suture where the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate about 50 million years ago. Its traditional name in Sanskrit and Tibetan is Sindhu, a word for river, and the English name derives through Greek and Old Persian from the same root, as do Hindustan and India.

The cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, date back to around 3300 BCE and were among the largest human settlements of the ancient world. The civilisation reached from northeast Afghanistan to Pakistan and northwest India, and over 1,052 cities and settlements have been found, mainly around the Ghaggar-Hakra River and its tributaries; only about 40 sites lie on the Indus and its tributaries. Its people were the first to build irrigation canals in the valley, and the Kushan and Mughal empires later built canals too.

In the 2nd millennium BCE the Punjab was called Sapta Sindhu in the Rigveda and Hapta Həndu in the Avesta, both meaning seven rivers. Early kingdoms of the valley included Gandhāra and Sindhu-Sauvīra. The river became known to the western world when King Darius of Persia sent his Greek subject Scylax of Caryanda to explore it, about 515 BCE. In 1850 the British East India Company introduced modern irrigation and restored old canals, and the British supervised the building of one of the most complex irrigation networks in the world.

The Indus is the chief supplier of water to the plains of Punjab and Sindh, where rainfall is meagre, and it is the backbone of agriculture in Pakistan. The river is sacred to Hindus, and the Sindhu Darshan Festival is held on its banks at Leh. The Indus River dolphin is found only in this river.
indus-script: Early examples of the script come from pottery inscriptions and clay impressions of inscribed seals dated to about 2800–2600 BCE, in the Early Harappan period, where they appear alongside administrative objects such as seals and standardised weights. Excavations at Harappa show that some symbols developed from potters' marks and graffiti of the earlier Ravi phase, about 3500–2800 BCE. In the Mature Harappan period, from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, strings of signs are common on flat rectangular stamp seals and on pottery, tools, tablets and ornaments. At Harappa the use of the script largely ceased around 1900 BCE as inscribed seals went out of use, though it may have lasted longer in other regions, for example at Rangpur in Gujarat.

The signs are largely pictorial, depicting objects of the Harappan world and of nature, though many abstract signs have also been identified. Some are compounds of simpler signs, and some resemble tally marks and are often interpreted as numerals. The number of principal signs is over 400, which is considered too many for each to stand for a single sound, so the script is generally believed to be logo-syllabic. Iravatham Mahadevan listed 419 distinct signs in the 1970s, while in 2015 Bryan Wells estimated around 694. Just 67 signs account for 80 per cent of usage.

Most scholars agree that the script was generally read from right to left, though exceptions are known. The direction has been deduced from external evidence, such as signs crowded on the left side as if the writer were running out of space at the end of a row. Seals were small, mostly 2–3 centimetres on a side, and animals such as bulls and elephants often accompany the text.

The first publication of a seal with Harappan symbols dates to 1875, in a drawing by Alexander Cunningham. By 1992 about 4,000 inscribed objects had been found, some as far away as Mesopotamia. The script has not been deciphered. The inscriptions are very short, averaging around five signs, no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone has been found, and the language is unknown. Over 100 mutually exclusive attempts at decipherment have been published since the 1920s, without scholarly consensus. Some scholars, among them Asko Parpola and Iravatham Mahadevan, argue that the language was Dravidian, while others propose an Indo-Aryan or Munda language. Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel argued in 2004 that the signs were nonlinguistic, a view Parpola disputed.
indus-valley-civilisation: The civilisation lasted from 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE, and in its mature form from 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE, across much of Pakistan, north-western India and north-eastern Afghanistan. Its area was larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. It is called Harappan after Harappa, the first site excavated, in the 1920s. The early Harappan cultures grew out of Neolithic cultures, of which the best known is at Mehrgarh in Balochistan, one of the earliest sites of farming and herding in South Asia. A gradual drying of the region during the third millennium BCE may have stimulated urbanisation, and flood-supported farming produced surpluses that supported cities.

Over a thousand Mature Harappan sites have been reported, but there are only five major urban centres: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganeriwala, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa probably held 30,000 to 60,000 people each. The cities were noted for grid planning, baked-brick houses, covered drains and water supply, and merchants traded by caravan with Central Asia and the Iranian plateau.

Around 1900 BCE signs of decline appeared, and by about 1700 BCE most cities were abandoned. In 1953 Sir Mortimer Wheeler proposed that Aryan invaders caused the end, but scholars rejected this because the skeletons he cited belonged to a later period. Many now point to drought, a weakening monsoon and a decline in trade with Egypt and Mesopotamia. After 1900 BCE the number of sites in India rose from 218 to 853, as people moved east.

Archaeology gives no direct answer about who ruled the cities. The consistency of weights and measures and the uniform planning suggest some central authority, and theories range from a single state to self-governing city states. An ivory scale from Lothal has a smallest division of about 1.704 millimetres. Craftsmen worked copper and bronze alloyed with tin, arsenic and lead. Between 400 and 600 distinct symbols of the undeciphered Indus script are known, and typical inscriptions are about five characters long. Interpretations of Indus religion are largely speculative. Mohenjo-daro was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980 and Dholavira in 2021.
industrial-revolution: Several factors enabled industrialisation: high agricultural productivity, as in the British Agricultural Revolution, which supplied surplus labour and food; managerial and entrepreneurial skills; ports, rivers, canals and roads that moved raw materials and goods cheaply; natural resources such as coal, iron and waterfalls; political stability and a legal system that supported business; and capital available to invest. Innovations such as Jethro Tull's seed drill of 1701 and Andrew Meikle's threshing machine of 1784 cut the labour that farming required. Before the change, most manufacturing took place in China and India, and India, China and parts of the Middle East produced most of the world's cotton cloth.

The textile industry was the first to use modern production methods. In 1750 Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton, mostly spun and woven by hand in Lancashire homes and workshops. By 1787 raw cotton consumption was 22 million pounds, most of it spun on machines, and in 1800 the industry used 52 million pounds. Mechanised spinning powered by water and later steam raised output per worker by a factor of around 500, and the power loom by a factor of 40.

Coke replaced charcoal in iron making: in 1720 Britain made 20,500 tons of charcoal iron and 400 tons with coke, and in 1806 coke cast iron reached 250,000 tons. John Roebuck's lead chamber process of 1746 began large-scale chemical production. Steam supplied an estimated 10,000 horsepower in Britain by 1800 and 210,000 by 1815, though water and wind supplied most industrial power early on. William Murdoch's gas lighting reached London between 1812 and 1820, and steam locomotives came in the early 19th century. Mechanised production spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.

Historians debate the precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution and the pace of its changes. Growth slowed from the late 1830s as markets for the early innovations matured, and revived after 1870 with the steel-making, assembly-line and electrical innovations of the Second Industrial Revolution. The earliest recorded use of the term Industrial Revolution was in 1799, by the French envoy Louis-Guillaume Otto, and Arnold Toynbee's lectures of 1881 are credited with popularising it.

Output and population grew at unprecedented rates. Visible poverty, a growing population and new wealth caused tensions between rich and poor, which led to ideas such as socialism, communism and anarchism. Children as young as eight worked in textile mills. Economists such as Robert Lucas Jr. hold that for the first time the living standards of ordinary people began sustained growth, while others say they did not improve meaningfully until the 20th century. After the Industrial Revolution most manufacturing took place in North America and Western Europe.
indutiomarus: Indutiomarus was a leading aristocrat of the Treveri, the people of the area around present-day Trier, at the time of Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul. He headed the anti-Roman party among them and contended with his pro-Roman son-in-law Cingetorix for the highest power in the state.

In 54 BCE Indutiomarus prepared for war against the Romans and sent the non-combatants of his people away to the Ardennes. When Caesar arrived in the territory of the Treveri on his way to Britain, however, many of his leading supporters deserted him, and he submitted in the hope of keeping his position. Caesar accepted the submission and took 200 hostages, among them several of his close relatives, but he also used the occasion to raise Cingetorix to power among the Treveri at Indutiomarus's expense.

Deprived of much of his power, Indutiomarus became a still more bitter enemy of the Romans and waited for an opportunity. That winter Caesar divided his troops among winter quarters spread across Gaul to secure their food supplies. Indutiomarus urged Ambiorix and Cativolcus, chiefs of the Eburones, to attack the legion stationed in their country, and soon afterwards marched against Titus Labienus, who was encamped among the Remi, immediately west of the Treveri. Warned of Caesar's victory over the Nervii, he withdrew into his own country and raised fresh troops.

Through the winter Indutiomarus sent ambassadors to the Germans in search of allies, while the Senones, the Carnutes, the Nervii and the Aduatuci sent envoys to him of their own accord. Emboldened, he had Cingetorix declared an enemy of the state and his property confiscated, then marched against Labienus a second time and surrounded the Roman camp.

Almost every day he rode around the camp with his cavalry, both to reconnoitre and to intimidate the Romans inside. Labienus secretly brought a large body of auxiliary cavalry into the camp, and during one of these rides the auxiliaries surprised the Treveran horsemen with a sudden sally. In the rout that followed, Indutiomarus was killed while crossing a river.
ine-of-wessex: Ine was born around 670, the son of Cenred and grandson of Ceolwald. His brother Ingild was named in the royal genealogies as the ancestor of King Egbert of Wessex and the later kings of England. His sister Cuthburh married King Aldfrith of Northumbria, and Ine himself married Æthelburg. Bede calls him 'of the blood royal', meaning the royal line of the Gewisse, the early West Saxon tribe. He came to the throne after Cædwalla abdicated and left for Rome to be baptised, and there is some uncertainty about the transition. He may have ruled for a time alongside his father, who was still reigning according to a surviving land grant.

Ine's predecessor Cædwalla had made himself overlord of most of the southern kingdoms, but by the end of Ine's reign Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex had slipped out of West Saxon control. Ine made peace with Wihtred of Kent in 694, when Wihtred paid compensation for the death of Cædwalla's brother Mul. He kept control of the Isle of Wight and what is now Hampshire, and in 710 he fought with Nothhelm of Sussex against Geraint of Dumnonia, whom John of Worcester says was killed. In 721 he killed one Cynewulf, and in 722 his queen destroyed Taunton, which he had built around 710. In 722 he invaded Sussex because of the exile Ealdberht, and three years later he invaded again and killed him.

His code of laws, issued in 694 or shortly before, was the first by an Anglo-Saxon king outside Kent and survives because Alfred the Great appended it to his own. It addresses baptism, tithes and church dues as well as civil matters such as straying cattle, giving the earliest documentary evidence of open-field farming. It sets fines for neglecting military service and gave Britons half the weregild of Saxons of the same rank. Ealdormen and shires are first mentioned in his reign. The trading settlement of Hamwic, now part of Southampton, grew to a population estimated at 5,000. Ine patronised religious houses and, at Bishop Aldhelm's suggestion in 705, built the church that later became Wells Cathedral.

In 726 Ine abdicated, with no obvious heir, and left the kingdom, in Bede's words, to younger men. He travelled with Æthelburg to Rome, where both died. Roger of Wendover says that Ine founded the Schola Saxonum there in 727, though tradition also gives that role to Offa of Mercia. His successor Æthelheard faced a rival claim from the ætheling Oswald.
infamous-decade: The period began with the coup d'état of 1930 against President Hipólito Yrigoyen. José Félix Uriburu ruled as dictator until 1932, intervening in every province except San Luis and Entre Ríos and treating the anarchists as public enemies; in 1931 three anarchists, the prisoners of Bragado, were tortured and given life sentences in a show trial that caused international indignation. Power then passed to the Concordancia, a lasting alliance of the National Democratic Party, the former conservatives, with the Antipersonalist Radical Civic Union and the Independent Socialist Party.

Agustín P. Justo was president from 1932 to 1938. His minister Federico Pinedo created boards for grain, meat, cotton, yerba mate, wine and dairy, policies that protected large producers at the expense of smaller ones. In 1935 Senator Lisandro de la Torre began an investigation of the meat trade, during which his disciple, the senator-elect Enzo Bordabehere, was murdered on the Senate floor. The CHADE electricity concession, whose company was accused of bribing politicians, became the symbol of the decade.

Roberto M. Ortiz was elected by fraud in 1938 but tried to clean up elections, ordering federal intervention in the Province of Buenos Aires. Diabetes left him nearly blind, and from 1940 his vice-president Ramón S. Castillo governed, restoring fraud and keeping Argentina neutral after the attack on Pearl Harbor, when he declared a state of siege to stop pro-Allied demonstrations. Against him the Democratic Union of 1942 joined the Radical Civic Union, the Democratic Progressive Party, the Socialist Party and the Communist Party.

On 4 June 1943 the Grupo de Oficiales Unidos, a nationalist faction of the army whose members included Colonel Juan Domingo Perón and which sympathised with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, overthrew Castillo and made General Pedro Ramírez chief of state. The Great Depression had ruined many small rural landowners and pushed the country towards import substitution industrialization. Farmers and rural workers moved to the outskirts of the cities, creating the first villas miseria, and Buenos Aires grew from 1.5 million inhabitants in 1914 to 3.5 million in 1935. These newcomers would form the social base of Peronism. The period was also the golden age of tango.
inferno-dante: Dante probably began work on the Comedy around 1306, although some modern scholars argue that the composition of the Inferno began as late as 1313, and early commentators proposed start dates before 1302. He had been exiled from Florence in 1302 after his faction, the pro-empire White Guelphs, was defeated by the pro-papal Black Guelphs, and he spent nearly all of the last fifteen years of his life on the Comedy. Many scholars agree that the Inferno was begun in 1306–1307 and completed in 1309–1310, though revisions probably continued. Giovanni Boccaccio and some other early commentators held that Dante composed the first seven cantos before his exile.

The poem describes the journey of a fictionalised Dante through Hell, guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil. Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment within the Earth, culminating at the centre, where Satan is held in bondage. As an allegory, the Divine Comedy represents the journey of the soul toward God, and the Inferno the recognition and rejection of sin. Each punishment is a contrapasso, a symbolic instance of poetic justice: fortune-tellers, for example, must walk with their heads on backward because they tried to see the future by forbidden means.

The poem begins on the night of Maundy Thursday in 1300, when Dante, aged 35 and "midway in the journey of our life", finds himself lost in a dark wood. His way is blocked by three beasts, a leopard, a lion and a she-wolf. Virgil explains that he has been sent by Beatrice, and the two enter the gate of Hell, which bears the inscription ending "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here".

The circles are Limbo, for the unbaptised and the virtuous pagans; lust; gluttony; greed; wrath; heresy; violence; fraud; and treachery. The eighth circle, Malebolge, is a funnel of stone with ten concentric ditches, and the ninth is a frozen lake, Cocytus, where traitors are held in ice according to their guilt. Among the damned are historical persons and figures of Dante's own Florence, such as the Ghibelline leader Farinata degli Uberti and Emperor Frederick II, both in flaming tombs among the heretics.
inflanty-voivodeship: The name Inflanty comes through Polonization from Livland, the German name for Livonia. Zygmunt Gloger, in his Historical Geography of the Lands of Old Poland, describes the land as inhabited by Latvians, whose language is close to Lithuanian, and says that it and Courland were conquered in the 13th century by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. The voivodeship was one of the few territories of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth ruled jointly by Poland and Lithuania: since the Union of Lublin had made Livonia a joint possession, royal bills for the province bore both Polish and Lithuanian stamps.

Pressed by Muscovy, Sweden and the Commonwealth, Master Gotthard Kettler turned to the Polish king, and a document signed at Vilnius on 28 November 1561 made Livonia a Polish–Lithuanian fief. A long struggle with Muscovy and later Sweden followed. After the victories of King Stephen Báthory, Commonwealth rule was confirmed in 1582 and the province divided into three presidencies centred on Dorpat, Wenden and Parnawa, which King Sigismund III Vasa renamed voivodeships in 1598.

Sweden took most of the Duchy of Livonia in the Polish–Swedish War of 1621–1625, and the Inflanty Voivodeship was formed in the 1620s from what was left of the Wenden Voivodeship. The Treaty of Oliwa of 1660 left the Commonwealth about one fifth of Livonia, despite the efforts of Jan Zamoyski and Jan Karol Chodkiewicz to hold it.

The Warsaw Sejm of 1677 gave the province the right to name three senators: the Bishop, the Voivode and the Castellan of Inflanty. Local sejmiks met at Dyneburg, and starostas resided at Dyneburg, Lucyn, Rzezyca and Marienhaus. Of its six deputies to the Sejm only two came from Inflanty; the king named the other four in memory of the lost part of Livonia. Its noble families included descendants of German knights, such as the Borch, Plater and Tyzenhaus, and Polish or Lithuanian settlers.
ingapirca: The name comes from the Kichwa Inka Pirka, Inca wall. The site lies high in the mountains, where the weather can turn within minutes from calm sunshine to rain, wind and cold at any time of year. Its builders, worshippers of the sun and moon, sought to be as close to their gods as they could, and they held that this was the place their gods had led them to. An underground aqueduct system carried water to the whole compound.

The area had long been settled by the Cañari people, who called it Hatun Cañar. As the Inca Empire spread into southern Ecuador, the Inca Túpac Yupanqui found them hard to conquer and turned to political means: he married a Cañari princess and enlarged the Cañari city of Guapondelig as Tumebamba, the present-day Cuenca. The two peoples settled their differences and lived side by side, each keeping its own customs; although the Inca were more numerous, they did not demand that the Cañari give up their autonomy. The observatory was built under the Inca Huayna Capac.

The castle complex is of Cañari and Inca origin and its purpose is uncertain, but it served as a fortress and as a storehouse for supplying Inca troops on their way to northern Ecuador. The people held many festivals there and prepared large amounts of a local fermented drink for the rituals. Charles Marie de La Condamine, who visited in 1739 during his expedition to South America, was the first European to describe Ingapirca scientifically.

Ingapirca is also the name of a town in Cañar Province near the ruins. The partial ruins of the Temple of the Sun survive. Like most of the complex it was built in the Inca manner without mortar, from stones chiselled to fit closely, around a large rock. It was aligned so that at the solstices sunlight fell through the centre of the doorway of the small chamber at its top, most of which has since fallen.
ingelheim-am-rhein: Ingelheim lies on the left bank of the Rhine in the north of Rhenish Hesse, in the bend of the river west of Mainz. The Rhine forms its northern limit, and to the south the town stretches into the valley of the Selz, which flows into the Rhine at Frei-Weinheim. The ending -heim in the name probably goes back to Frankish times, as far as the fifth or sixth century. The name is recorded as Ingilinhaim in 782, and since 1269 a distinction has been made between Nieder-Ingelheim and Ober-Ingelheim, Lower and Upper Ingelheim.

The area was settled in prehistoric times, but it became important only under Charlemagne and his successors. Charlemagne had the Ingelheim Imperial Palace built after 785, and in the time that followed synods and imperial diets were held there. The palace served emperors and kings as lodging and ruling seat until the eleventh century. Charlemagne held court at Ingelheim in 807, and his son and successor Emperor Louis the Pious died there on 20 June 840, in a summer tent on an island in the Rhine off the town.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the importance of the Palatinate, and with it Ingelheim, shrank. The Ingelheimer Oberhof, the Ingelheim Upper Court, is of particular importance in German legal history, since a unique collection of its judgments from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries has survived. The Dutch writer Multatuli, Eduard Douwes Dekker, lived in Ingelheim in the late nineteenth century. In 1939 the formerly self-governing municipalities of Nieder-Ingelheim, Ober-Ingelheim and Frei-Weinheim were merged into the town of Ingelheim am Rhein.

Ingelheim is the seat of the Mainz-Bingen district in Rhineland-Palatinate. Remnants of the Imperial Palace can be seen beside the Museum bei der Kaiserpfalz, which has an exhibit on the palace, with archaeological finds, architectural sculpture and a model of the building. A golden solidus found in 1996 is so far the only gold coin known to have been struck with Charlemagne's effigy. The town also has a Carolingian aqueduct and the Ohrenbrücker Tor, a gate of the town wall first mentioned in the thirteenth century.
ingiloys: The Ingiloys call themselves Heretians, and their homeland is Saingilo, formerly Hereti, a region of 4,780 square kilometres. Tradition derives the name from the patriarch Heros, son of Thargamos, who founded the city of Hereti, later Khoranta, on the Alazani River. As Caucasian Albania declined the area passed to the Iberian kingdom as one of its duchies, and through the 5th century its peoples were assimilated into the Georgians. Under Arab occupation Hereti was a separate kingdom, then part of the Kingdom of Kakheti and Hereti, which was annexed to the Georgian Kingdom in 1104.

In the 15th century the name Hereti gave way to Kakheti. Early in the 17th century Shah Abbas I took the land from the king of Kakheti and granted it to Dagestani feudal clans. Raids by Avar and Tsakhur bands, the Lekianoba, made the Ingiloys serfs paying tribute, and after the founding of the Sultanate of Elisu the conquerors undertook the Islamization of the region. Russian rule came in 1803. Both the Democratic Republic of Georgia and Azerbaijan claimed Saingilo from 1918 to 1920, and Moscow transferred it to the Azerbaijan SSR in 1922. Missionaries converted some to Christianity in 1860, but most returned to Islam by 1863.

Most Ingiloys are Sunni Muslims, and three Georgian Orthodox churches are active in Qakh district. The 2009 census counted 9,900 Georgians in Azerbaijan, most in Qakh. There are seven Georgian schools in Saingilo and a Georgian drama theatre at Alibeyli. Houses, mostly of brick and stone, follow the Georgian darbazi type in the erdoiani-akariani form, and carved wooden gates, the darvaza, stand at the farmsteads. Women's dress, kept up into the 1930s, resembles that of the neighbouring Azerbaijanis, Tsakhurs and Avars.
ingolstadt: Ingolstadt is an independent city on the Danube in Upper Bavaria. The old town stands about 374 metres above sea level in a wide, flat basin, where the river Schutter reaches the Danube from the west. The Ingolstadt basin borders the foothills of the Franconian Jura, and lowland forests of the Danube reach into the urban area. The river there is between 80 and 100 metres wide and flows from west to east past the old town.

The place was first mentioned in a document of Charlemagne of 6 February 806 as Ingoldes stat, the place of a person named Ingold. It was granted city status around 1250. In the late Middle Ages it was one of the capitals of the Bavarian duchies, alongside Munich, Landshut and Straubing. Louis VII, Duke of Bavaria ordered the building of the New Castle and of the Church of Our Lady, a Gothic hall church begun in 1425 as the intended burial place of the dukes of Bavaria-Ingolstadt.

The university founded in 1472 became an influential defender of the Catholic Church in the Reformation era, led by scholars such as Johann Eck. In 1516 William IV, Duke of Bavaria wrote and signed the Bavarian Reinheitsgebot in the city. On 30 April 1632 the German field marshal Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly died there during a Swedish siege. Ingolstadt was the first fortress in Germany to hold out for the whole length of a Swedish siege, and the Swedes withdrew. A cannon inside the fortress shot the horse from under King Gustavus Adolphus, and its remains are kept in the city museum.

Adam Weishaupt, who founded the Order of Illuminati in the city in 1776, was born there in 1748. After the French invasion of 1799 the fortress was demolished and the university was moved to Landshut. The Bavarian fortress, in use from 1537 to 1930, held the future French president Charles de Gaulle as a prisoner of war during the First World War. In 1945 the car maker Auto Union arrived, and it was formally re-founded in Ingolstadt in 1949, with Marshall Plan aid. It became the modern Audi company after Volkswagen took it over in 1964.

The historic old town has been preserved, with Gothic buildings such as the old ducal castle of about 1255, the Kreuztor of 1385 and the Old City Hall. The New Castle and the Tilly redoubt house the Bavarian Army Museum, the oldest museum in the city. The Old Anatomy building of 1723 to 1736 holds the German Museum of Medical History, and Mary Shelley set part of Frankenstein in the city. The city has two universities and Audi is the largest employer in the region.
ingria: Ingria, also called Ingermanland, takes in the area around the Neva River, the south-eastern shore of the Gulf of Finland and the south-western shore of Lake Ladoga. Its historical boundaries reached the Narva River in the west and the Sestra River in the north. The Votians and Izhorians, both Baltic Finnic peoples, are among its indigenous peoples. The origin of the name is uncertain. One explanation derives it from the River Inger, a tributary of the Neva; another from Eymund's saga, which says that the Swedish princess Ingegerd Olofsdotter received Ladoga and its lands from Yaroslav the Wise on her marriage in 1019, so that the region became Ingegerd's land.

From the 750s Ladoga served as a bridgehead on the Varangian trade route to Eastern Europe. In the 12th century western Ingria was absorbed by the Novgorod Republic, and centuries of wars followed, chiefly between Novgorod and Sweden. Ingria became a Swedish dominion in the 1580s and was returned to Russia by the Treaty of Teusina in 1595. Russia ceded it to Sweden in the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, after the Ingrian War of 1610 to 1617. Sweden valued it as a buffer for the Karelian Isthmus and Finland and as a toll on Russian Baltic trade.

Under Swedish rule the province remained sparsely populated, about 15,000 in 1664. Efforts to introduce Lutheranism met repugnance among the Orthodox peasantry, but Lutheran Finns from Savonia and Karelia settled voluntarily, and they made up 73.8 per cent of the population in 1695. Russia reconquered the region in the Great Northern War and founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 near Nyen. Sweden formally ceded it in the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. In 1919 and 1920 the short-lived Republic of North Ingria held a small area near the Finnish border, returned to Soviet Russia by the Treaty of Tartu in 1920.

Historic Ingria covers about the same area as the city of Saint Petersburg and seven districts of Leningrad Oblast. Under the Soviet Union the Ingrian Finns were deported and dispersed from the late 1920s, and both they and the Izhorians all but disappeared from the region, outnumbered by Russian immigration. The 1926 census recorded 114,831 Ingrian Finns, and the Soviet census of 1989 counted 829 Izhorians.
ingrian-finns: Ingria is the historical region that corresponds to the central part of today's Leningrad Oblast. During Swedish rule in 1617 to 1703 its population changed drastically. After the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, and especially after the War of Rupture of 1656 to 1658, much of the Orthodox population fled to Russia, largely in response to heavy taxation and to Swedish pressure to convert to Lutheranism. Lutheran migrants from Finland settled the empty lands, mainly the Äyrämöiset from the Karelian Isthmus and the Savakot from Savo. For many the region was a frontier that offered an escape from taxes and military service. The movement was mostly voluntary, though some Forest Finns from Närke were forced to move.
Finns made up 41.1 percent of the population in 1656 and 73.8 percent in 1695, and by the end of the century they were about three quarters of a rural population of some 60,000.

Russia conquered Ingria in 1702 to 1703 and founded Saint Petersburg in 1703. Under Russian rule the Ingrian Finns became serfs, forbidden to move, but they kept their Lutheranism while Orthodox Christianity became dominant among a growing Russian population. After serfdom ended in 1861 many became independent peasants. The Kolppana seminary for teachers and cantors was founded in 1863, a first library opened in 1850 and the first Finnish-language newspaper, Pietarin Sanomat, began in 1870. There were 130,413 Ingrian Finns in 1897 and more than 140,000 by 1917.

After the 1917 revolution Ingrian Finns on the southern Karelian Isthmus seceded from Soviet Russia and formed the Republic of North Ingria with Finnish backing. The Treaty of Tartu of 14 October 1920 returned it to Soviet Russia. From 1928 to 1939 North Ingria's Finns formed the Kuivaisi National District, with Finnish as its official language.

Collectivisation began in 1928, and between 1929 and 1931 18,000 people from North Ingria were deported to East Karelia, the Kola Peninsula and Central Asia. Further deportations followed in 1935 and 1936 as the Soviet Union planned border zones free of the Finnic peoples, whom it considered politically unreliable. In 1941 Moscow decided that Ingrian Finns were unreliable, and in 1942 most of those left in Ingria were relocated to Siberia. After the Continuation War, most of those evacuated to Finland were returned to the Soviet Union and dispersed in Central Russia, though nearly 4,000 stayed in Finland.

From 1991 to 2010 about 25,000 Ingrian Finns moved to Finland under its Law of Return, which the government stopped applying in 2010. Many Ingrian Finns in Russia belong to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Ingria.
ingrian-war: During Russia's Time of Troubles, Tsar Vasily IV was besieged in Moscow by supporters of False Dmitry II. Driven to despair by Polish intervention, he allied with King Charles IX of Sweden, who was also at war with Poland. Under the Treaty of Vyborg of 1609 the tsar promised to cede the Korela Fortress to Sweden and renounced all Russian claims on the Baltic coast. The Swedish commander Jacob De la Gardie joined the Russian commander Mikhail Skopin-Shuisky in the De la Gardie campaign.

Sweden's involvement gave King Sigismund III Vasa of Poland a pretext to declare war on Russia. After Skopin-Shuisky died suddenly, the Poles defeated the combined Russo-Swedish force at the Battle of Klushino on 4 July 1610. The tsar was deposed by the Seven Boyars and the Poles occupied the Moscow Kremlin. De la Gardie then sought to control the Russian north-west so that the Poles could not threaten Sweden's Baltic territories.

In July 1611 De la Gardie captured Novgorod and compelled its people to acknowledge the Swedish king as their patron and to choose one of his sons, Carl Filip or Gustavus Adolphus, as monarch. Gustavus Adolphus then came to the Swedish throne and pursued his brother's claim to the Russian crown, even after a patriotic uprising expelled the Poles from Moscow in 1612 and Mikhail Romanov was elected tsar.

In 1613 the Swedes besieged Tikhvin but were repelled, and a Russian counteroffensive failed to retake Novgorod. In 1614 the Swedes captured Gdov, and thousands of soldiers freed by the peace of Knäred were shipped over. The following year Gustavus Adolphus besieged Pskov, which the Russian generals Morozov and Buturlin defended. Negotiations began on 9 March 1617.

Under the Treaty of Stolbovo of 1617 Sweden received Ingria with Ivangorod, Jama, Koporye and Nöteborg, and Kexholm in Karelia, while restoring Novgorod and Gdov. Russia renounced claims to Estonia and Livonia, owed 20,000 rubles in reparations and was denied access to the Baltic for about a century, which raised the importance of Arkhangelsk for trade. Sweden recognised Michael Romanov as tsar.

Most sources regard the war as a Swedish victory. The treaty was considered humiliating in the Soviet era, but recent Russian historiography notes that it freed forces to face Poland. German Zamyatin argues that Sweden suffered a diplomatic defeat in failing to secure Novgorod and Gdov, and Gennady Kovalenko calls it a mutually beneficial compromise.
ingush-people: The Ingush call themselves Ghalghai, a name most often linked to the word ghāla, tower or fortress, so that it means people of towers. Georgian sources knew them as Gligvi and Dzurdzuks, and Russian sources as Kists. Their ethnonym Ingush comes from the medieval village of Angusht, which by the end of the 17th century was a large settlement in the Tarskoye Valley.

In the early Bronze Age the territory of Ingushetia lay where the Maykop and Kuro-Araxes cultures met, and the Koban culture, dated from the 12th to the 4th century BCE, is usually tied to the origins of the proto-Ingush. Late in the 1st millennium BCE Koban tribes formed a large union known as Malkh or, in Georgian sources, Dzurdzuketi, which controlled the Darial Gorge. It was defeated at the beginning of the 2nd century BCE by the Seleucid king Antiochus III.

From the late 9th to the early 13th century the Ingush belonged to the kingdom of the Alans, and some Ingush researchers place its capital, Magas, on the territory of present-day Ingushetia. On 4 to 6 March 1770, 24 Ingush elders swore an oath of allegiance to the Russian Empire at Barta-Bos, near Angusht, although each side treated such oaths as a union treaty and relations stayed much the same.

In the 19th century the Ingush resisted Russian expansion in the Caucasian War and were considered half-conquered. In 1860 their lands formed the Ingushskiy Okrug of the Terek Oblast, and the 1897 census counted 47,409 Ingush in the empire.

In the Soviet period an Ingush alphabet based on the Latin script was introduced in 1923 and the first newspaper in the language, Serdalo, appeared that year. The 1939 census counted 92,120 Ingush. They were exiled en masse in 1944. In 1992 the Republic of Ingushetia was formed within the Russian Federation, and armed clashes with Ossetians over the Prigorodny district of North Ossetia killed 583 people according to the Russian prosecutor's office. The capital Magas was founded in 1995.

The Ingush are predominantly Sunni Muslims and speak the Ingush language. Their society was traditionally classless, built on clans and unwritten law, with about 350 clans in Ingushetia today. Villages were governed by senior family members and acted together only in great danger, and the Ingush had no titles giving civil authority over others. Their stone architecture is tied to life in the mountains: a family had a tower, a church and a necropolis. Combat towers usually had five or six levels and a stepped pyramidal roof, with the entrance on the second floor.
inhambane: Inhambane, also known as Terra de Boa Gente, 'Land of the Good People', lies on Inhambane Bay, 470 km north-east of Maputo. The settlement owes its existence to a deep inlet into which the small Mutamba River flows. Two protective sandy headlands shelter the harbour and form a sandbank. The sister town of Maxixe stands across the bay, and motor and dhow taxis sail between the two. Inhambane has one of the largest working fleets of dhows on the Swahili Coast.

Inhambane is one of the oldest settlements on Mozambique's eastern coast. It is recorded as a city-state that submitted to successive powers, beginning with the Kilwa Sultanate, then the Gaza Empire, and finally Portuguese Mozambique. Dhows traded here as early as the 11th century, and Muslim and Persian traders, the first outsiders to arrive by sea, dealt in pearls and ambergris. The area was known for cotton spinning and production by the Bitonga. Before the Portuguese came, the Karanga had invaded and formed a number of local chiefdoms, dominating the Tonga cotton workers and profiting from the trade with Muslim merchants.

Vasco da Gama put in to replenish stocks and explore, and named the place Terra de Boa Gente. In 1505 a ship sent by Francisco de Almeida was wrecked south of the town, and the Portuguese gained a first meeting with the Karanga chiefs. They established a permanent trading post in 1534, and in 1560 Inhambane was chosen as the first Jesuit mission to Southeast Africa. The port grew as an ivory and slave trading centre, particularly in the 18th century under mostly Indian control.

Soshangane destroyed it in 1834, but it grew rapidly in the second half of the century as a town of Portuguese East Africa, and the old cathedral and old mosque were built in that period. In the 20th century its standing declined, as Maputo, called Lourenço Marques before 1975, became the main centre.

Inhambane is the capital of Inhambane Province. The census of 2017 gave it a population of 79,724, up from 54,157 in 1997. The Cathedral of Our Lady of Conception, about 170 years old, stands in the old quarter, and the city has a museum and a central market, the Mercado Central, on its main boulevard. The beaches of Tofo and Barra lie nearby.
inigo-arista: Íñigo Arista, Eneko in Basque, was a Basque chieftain and the first king of Pamplona. His origin is obscure, and even his father's name is disputed: a charter preserved at Leyre calls him Íñigo son of Jimeno, another document Íñigo Garcés, commonly called Arista, while the chroniclers Ibn Hayyan and Al-Udri indicate that his father was also named Íñigo. The nickname Arista appears as early as the 10th century and may come from the Basque Aritza, the oak, or the Latin Aresta. His mother married the muwallad lord Musa ibn Fortun, bearing Musa ibn Musa, who became head of the Banu Qasi and ruler of Tudela. Because of this kinship Íñigo and his kin often acted in alliance with Musa.

The family rose through struggles over Frankish and Córdoban influence. In 816, according to Ibn Hayyan, a Córdoban campaign routed the pro-Frankish Velasco the Gascon, lord of Pamplona, and killed him, which appears to have allowed the anti-Frankish Íñigo to come to power. In 820 he is said to have ejected the Frankish vassal Aznar I Galíndez from the County of Aragon in favour of García Galíndez, who became his son-in-law.

In 824 a Carolingian force under the counts Aeblus and Aznar Sánchez was defeated at the second battle of Roncesvalles. Tradition has this crown Íñigo as king, though there is no direct evidence of his part in the battle, and Arab chroniclers give him the same title of lord of Pamplona as Velasco.

In 840 an attack by Abd Allah ibn Kulayb, wali of Zaragoza, drove Musa ibn Musa to rebel against the Emirate of Córdoba, and Íñigo's son García, as regent, and Íñigo's brother Fortún Íñiguez joined him. Abd-ar-Rahman II launched reprisals. In 843 Fortún was killed, and the next year Íñigo's son Galindo went over to Córdoba. A peace followed in 845, and in 850 Musa rebelled again with Pamplona's support.

Íñigo died after a long illness, during which his son García Íñiguez was already governing, and was reported buried at the monastery of Leyre, which he is said to have granted the town of Yesa in 842, though the grant's authenticity is disputed. The dynasty he founded reigned for about 80 years until a rival dynasty supplanted it in 905. Because of intermarriage, later kings of Navarre descended from him, and he is remembered as the founder of Navarre.
inisfallen: Innisfallen, in Irish Inis Faithlinn, Faithlinn's island, lies about midway in Lough Leane. It covers some 8.5 hectares (21 acres), mostly wooded, with undulating hills and many slopes, and lies within Killarney National Park. The monastery is thought to have given the lake its name: Loch Léin is rendered in English as Lake of Learning.

The monastery was founded around 640. Scholars identify its founder, traditionally a Saint Finian, either as Finian Lobhar, a disciple of Columba, or as Finan Cam of Corca Dhuibhne. Nothing survives of its earliest buildings, which were probably of wood. According to tradition the High King Brian Boru was educated there under Maelsuthain O'Carroll, who has been credited as the possible originator of the Annals of Innisfallen. The Annals record Irish history from 433 to 1450, with further material on earlier times, and they tell of Viking raids and of an attack in 1180 by the O'Donoghue clan, who carried off valuables from the church.

After the Norman invasion of Ireland in the late 12th century the monastery came under Augustinian control and was renamed the Priory of Saint Mary. The community was dissolved in 1582 under Elizabeth I, and the island passed through several hands before becoming part of the Kenmare estate. In 1973 it was transferred to the state and made part of Killarney National Park.

The ruins date mainly from the 10th to the 12th centuries. Near the shore stands an oratory with a Romanesque doorway carved in a Hiberno-Norman style, and the larger church may reuse stone from earlier Irish-built churches. A small early church, domestic buildings of the monastery and a bullaun stone also survive.

The island appears in 19th-century works such as Thomas Moore's song Sweet Innisfallen and in William Allingham's poem The Abbot of Innisfallen, first published in Macmillan's Magazine in 1864. Geoffrey Molyneux Palmer's setting of the poem won the cantata prize at the 1908 Feis Ceoil in Dublin, and Sean O'Casey took a line of Moore's, Inishfallen, Fare Thee Well, as the title of the fourth volume of his autobiography.
inishowen: Inishowen covers 884.33 square kilometres at the northern end of the island of Ireland. The Atlantic Ocean bounds it on the north, Lough Foyle on the east and Lough Swilly on the west, and it joins the rest of the island at the south. After the last ice age it was an island. Most of the population lives round the coast, while the interior is low mountain country, mostly bogland, rising to Slieve Snaght at 619 metres.

Most of the peninsula lies in County Donegal, but its south-eastern part lies in County Londonderry, having been transferred from Donegal at the request of the London companies in the Plantation of Ulster in the early 17th century. Lough Swilly is a fjord-like lough that was of strategic importance to the British Empire as a deep-water harbour, and it is the departure point of the Flight of the Earls. Lough Foyle is shallower and leads to the river Foyle and the city of Derry.

The area was named Inis Eoghain after Eógan mac Néill, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, and the name was also used for Tyrone. It was the homeland of the Meic Lochlainn, descended from the tribe of Eoghan, a clan that grew formidable enough that a king from Limerick came north to Aileach and ordered the fort destroyed, each of his soldiers carrying away a stone so that it could not be rebuilt. Ptolemy's Geography of the second century describes a point called Wenniknion, which probably referred to Inishowen.

After the decline of the Meic Lochlainn the Norman Earldom of Ulster expanded into Inishowen and founded Greencastle. In 1196 the Anglo-Norman knight John de Courcy defeated the king of the Cenél Conaill, and two years later he returned to devastate Inishowen, but he was defeated in later campaigns by Clan O'Neill under its chief Áed Méith. After the Bruce invasion of the early 14th century the Ó Dochartaigh clan gradually conquered the peninsula, having lost their own homeland in the Laggan. In 1608 Sir Cahir O'Doherty, lord of Inishowen, began O'Doherty's Rebellion by burning Derry, and after its defeat most of the clan's territory was awarded to Arthur Chichester.

Inishowen includes Malin Head, the most northerly point of Ireland. The census of 2016 counted 40,544 people, of whom 6,785 lived in the urban area of Buncrana, the largest town. Its monuments include the Grianán of Aileach, a ringfort restored in the nineteenth century, and the castle ruins at Greencastle, Buncrana, Elagh and Inch and Carrickabraghey on the Isle of Doagh. The peninsula is a starting or ending point of the Wild Atlantic Way.
injo-of-joseon: Injo, personal name Yi Jong, was born on 7 December 1595, the eldest son of Prince Jeongwon and a grandson of King Seonjo. Without the support of any political faction, he lived as Prince Neungyang. Gwanghaegun, though an able administrator and diplomat, was unpopular among many politicians, scholars and aristocrats because he was not the first-born and was the son of a concubine.

In 1623 the ultra-conservative Westerners Kim Chajŏm, Kim Ryu, Yi Kwi and Yi Kwal launched a coup that dethroned Gwanghaegun, who was exiled to Jeju Island. They crowned Injo, but almost all power stayed with them. In 1624 Yi Kwal, who thought his reward too small, rebelled with 12,000 troops, took the capital and enthroned Prince Heungan on 11 February. General Chang Man defeated him, and Yi was murdered by his bodyguard. The rebellion exposed the weakness of royal authority and gave the aristocrats more power.

Gwanghaegun had kept a neutral policy between the Ming and the rising Jurchens. The Westerners took a hard line against the Later Jin and kept the Ming alliance. In 1627 a Manchu cavalry force of 30,000 invaded and Injo fled to Ganghwa Island, but peace soon followed, and the two states were declared brother nations.

Injo then gave refuge to the Ming general Mao Wenlong, which prompted a further invasion. In 1636 Hong Taiji renamed his dynasty Qing and invaded in person with an army of 128,000 men, which reached Hansŏng before Injo could escape to Ganghwa and drove him to Namhan Mountain Fortress. Short of food after the Manchus cut his supply lines, Injo surrendered, bowing nine times to Hong Taiji, and agreed to the Treaty of Samjeondo, under which his first and second sons were taken to China as captives. Joseon became a tributary of the Qing.

After the Qing took Beijing in 1644 the princes returned. Crown Prince Sohyeon brought western goods and ideas, including Christianity, and urged reform, but Injo persecuted him for bringing in foreign Catholicism and Western science. Sohyeon was found dead in the king's room, bleeding from the head. Injo ordered an immediate burial and a reduced funeral, had Sohyeon's wife executed for treason, and exiled Sohyeon's three sons to Jeju, from which only the youngest returned alive. Injo died in 1649. He is regarded as a weak and indecisive ruler, though credited with reforming the military and expanding the nation's defences.
inkatha-freedom-party: Mangosuthu Buthelezi, a former member of the ANC Youth League, founded the Inkatha National Cultural Liberation Movement on 21 March 1975. It was built on Inkatha, meaning crown in Zulu, a cultural organisation of the 1920s established by his uncle, the Zulu king Solomon kaDinuzulu. The movement began in what is now KwaZulu-Natal, and branches soon appeared in the Transvaal, the Orange Free State and the Western Cape. Because of Buthelezi's former place in the African National Congress, the two organisations were at first close and supported each other in the anti-apartheid struggle.

By the early 1980s Inkatha was regarded as a thorn in the side of the ANC, which wielded more political force through the United Democratic Front. As a Bantustan leader, Buthelezi's power depended on the South African state, and critics increasingly regarded him as a government puppet.
