In the Philippines the Iranun live mainly in Maguindanao del Norte, at Barira, Buldon, Parang and Matanog, and in parts of Cotabato, Lanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Bukidnon and Zamboanga del Sur, including Pagadian City. When an Iranun woman marries an outsider, the customs of her family tend to prevail, so that the husband may come to be regarded as an Iranun man, although in many cases this does not happen.
iraq: Iraq lies in West Asia, bordered by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Iran, Kuwait, Jordan and Syria, with a coastline of 58 kilometres on the northern Persian Gulf. The Tigris and Euphrates run south through the country into the Shatt al-Arab and then the Persian Gulf. Fertile alluvial plains lie between and beside the two rivers, which carry about 60,000,000 cubic metres of silt a year to the delta, and marshlands flank the estuary.

Rocky deserts cover about 40 percent of Iraq and another 30 percent is mountainous, with the northwestern end of the Zagros range. Summer temperatures average above 40 °C for most of the country, and most places receive less than 250 millimetres of rain a year.

Iraq largely coincides with ancient Mesopotamia. Sumer emerged between 6000 and 5000 BCE during the Neolithic Ubaid period, and is recognised as the world's earliest civilisation. The territory includes the heartlands of the Akkadian, Neo-Sumerian, Babylonian, Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires. After the Achaemenid conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great adopted titles such as King of Babylon and King of Sumer and Akkad, and Aramaic became the lingua franca of the empire.

Babylon surrendered without resistance to Alexander the Great in 331 BCE, and after his death in 323 BCE Seleucia became the imperial capital in Mesopotamia. Cuneiform writing and temple institutions continued under Seleucid rule. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Iraq became the centre of the Abbasid Caliphate, and the name Iraq came into use for the region. The Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and from the 16th century until the 20th Iraq was governed within the Ottoman system.

Iraq became independent in 1932. A military coup led by Abdul Karim Qasim overthrew the monarchy in 1958, and the Ba'ath Party took power in 1968. The country fought a war with Iran from 1980 to 1988, invaded Kuwait in 1990, and was invaded by a U.S.-led coalition in 2003. Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic.

Oil was nationalised in 1972. The 2021 population estimate was 43,533,592, and most Iraqis are Arabs, with Kurds, Turkmens, Assyrians, Yazidis and others. Arabic and Kurdish are the official languages.
irineu-evangelista-de-sousa-viscount-of-: Sousa was born on 28 December 1813 on his father's ranch in the village of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Arroio Grande, near the southern border of Brazil, then part of Jaguarão in the captaincy of São Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul. He was the second son of João Evangelista de Ávila e Sousa and Mariana de Jesus Batista, a family of small ranchers with ancestry from the Azores; his paternal grandfather, Manuel Jerônimo de Sousa, had held a land grant from the Portuguese crown.

In 1818 his father was murdered while travelling with a herd of cattle, and the family's income fell. When his mother married again in 1821 her new husband would not take her children, and at about nine Irineu was taken to Rio de Janeiro by his uncle José Batista de Carvalho, a ship's captain. His mother had taught him to read and count; whether he had any schooling is doubtful, as his biographers Anyda Marchant and Cláudio Ganns note. Left in Rio while his uncle sailed to India, he worked as a clerk in a warehouse.

Sousa became one of the richest men in the world: by 1867 his wealth exceeded the annual budget of the Brazilian Empire, and in 1871 The New York Times called him the Rothschild of the South American continent. At his peak he controlled eight of the ten largest companies in the country, the other two being state-owned, and his banking interests reached Britain, France, the United States and Argentina. He established the modern Banco do Brasil, founded the first bank in Uruguay, Banco Mauá y Cia, and financed much economic activity, above all coffee planting.

He began the Mauá Railroad in 1852, ran steamboats on the Amazon and Guaíba rivers, commissioned the first submarine telegraph cable between South America and Europe, and installed gas street lights in Rio de Janeiro. He was made baron in 1854 and viscount with grandeur in 1874. His fortunes declined with the Empire after the Paraguayan War, and by his death on 21 October 1889 he had lost most of his wealth.

In an economy led by landowners who relied on slavery and exports, Sousa defended the free market, liberalism, industrialisation and the abolition of slavery. He is the patron of the Ministry of Transport, Brazil's merchant navy day falls on his birthday for his work at the Ponta d'Areia shipyard, and Praça Mauá in Rio de Janeiro and the Baron of Mauá International Bridge between Jaguarão and Río Branco, Uruguay, bear his name.
irish-confederate-wars: The rising of October 1641 was planned as a swift and mainly bloodless seizure of power by a small group of conspirators led by Phelim O'Neill, who meant to take Dublin Castle and win an end to anti-Catholic discrimination, more Irish self-government and a rollback of the Plantations of Ireland. The plot was betrayed at the last minute, and the rising turned into attacks on Protestant settlers in Ulster: around 4,000 Protestants were massacred and a further 12,000 may have died of privation. Settlers and the Dublin government answered with massacres of Catholics, as on Rathlin Island.

By the end of 1642 the Confederation based at Kilkenny controlled two-thirds of Ireland, and it later supported some 60,000 men under professionals such as Thomas Preston and Owen Roe O'Neill. The Adventurers' Act of March 1642 had funded the war with loans to be repaid from rebel land, committing the English to confiscation. A ceasefire with the Royalists on 15 September 1643 was followed by years of raids in which all sides destroyed crops. Owen Roe O'Neill defeated Robert Munro's army at Benburb on 5 June 1646, but defeats in 1647 and a treaty with the Royalists divided the Confederates.

Oliver Cromwell landed in August 1649 with the New Model Army and secured the east coast, massacring the defenders of Drogheda and Wexford. Kilkenny fell in March 1650 and Galway in May 1652, and guerrillas known as Tories fought on until the last organised force surrendered in Cavan in April 1653. The English answered with evictions and the destruction of crops, and famine and bubonic plague followed.

William Petty, who made the Down Survey in the 1650s, put the dead at between 400,000 and 620,000 in a population of about 1.5 million; the lowest estimate is about 200,000, about two-thirds of them civilians. Ireland was annexed by the English Commonwealth, Catholicism was repressed, and tens of thousands were sent to the Caribbean or Virginia as indentured servants or joined Catholic armies in Europe. After the Act for the Settlement of Ireland of 1652, the share of land owned by Protestants rose from 41% in 1641 to 78% in 1660, and Irish poetry long lamented the Confederates' disunity.
irish-declaration-of-independence: The declaration, in Irish Forógra na Saoirse, followed from the Sinn Féin election manifesto of December 1918 and was adopted at the Dáil's first meeting in the Mansion House. Texts were adopted in three languages, Irish, English and French. By it the Dáil ratified the Proclamation of the Irish Republic of Easter 1916, which had been issued not by an elected body but by the Easter rebels, claiming to act in the name of the Irish people. Unlike the proclamation, the declaration was followed by the setting up of some political organs in fact.

Its central line had the elected representatives of the ancient Irish people ratify the establishment of the Irish Republic and pledge themselves to make it effective by every means at their command. It called foreign government in Ireland an invasion of the national right and demanded the evacuation of the English Garrison. This was the nearest the Republic came to declaring war on Britain, but London regarded the wording as meant for an Irish audience, and when shots were fired the same day at Soloheadbeg, County Tipperary, the British treated them as a police matter. The Dáil had no claim to control the Irish Republican Army until the IRA swore allegiance to it in August 1920.

The declaration spoke of seven hundred years of Irish resistance to foreign usurpation, reaching back before the Anglo-Norman invasion of 1168-71 and counting the risings of 1594-1603, 1641-50, 1689-91, 1798, 1803, 1848, 1867 and 1916 as one continuing effort. It also claimed the recognition of every free nation, an aim of the 1918 manifesto, which hoped for a hearing at the peace conference after the First World War.

The Republic claimed jurisdiction over all 32 counties of Ireland, in rivalry with the British administration of the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and it gained legitimacy in the eyes of most Irish people as the war went on. Almost all states then followed the constitutive theory of statehood and did not recognise it. In June 1920 a draft treaty with the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic circulated in Dublin, though the historian E. H. Carr judged that neither side took the talks very seriously. The Irish Free State took over from the Republic in 1922, after the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
irish-home-rule-bills: Under the Act of Union 1800 the kingdoms of Ireland and Great Britain were merged on 1 January 1801. The term Home Rule, first used in the 1860s, meant an Irish legislature with responsibility for domestic affairs, and from the 1870s it was seen as part of a federal system for the United Kingdom, with the Parliament at Westminster keeping imperial affairs. Isaac Butt founded the Home Government Association in 1870, which became the Home Rule League in 1873. In 1882 Charles Stewart Parnell turned the League into the Irish Parliamentary Party, which won 85 of the 103 Irish seats in 1885. Republicans such as the Fenians sought total separation, while Unionists feared a Dublin parliament dominated by the Catholic Church.

Four bills were introduced to grant self-government to Ireland. The Government of Ireland Bill 1886 was defeated in the Commons. The Government of Ireland Bill 1893 passed the Commons but was defeated in the Lords. The Government of Ireland Act 1914, the third bill, passed under the Parliament Act 1911 and received royal assent on 18 September 1914, but the Suspensory Act 1914, signed the same day, deferred it. The Government of Ireland Act 1920 replaced it and created separate parliaments for Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland.

William Ewart Gladstone, impressed by Parnell, had come to believe that the Irish people were fitted for self-government. The defeat of the first bill by 30 votes split the Liberal Party, since the Liberal Unionists allied with the Conservatives, and was followed by serious riots in Belfast in 1886. The second bill passed the Commons with a majority of 30 and was defeated by the Lords. After the removal of the Lords' veto in 1911, the third bill was introduced in 1912 and was fiercely opposed by Ulster unionists under Edward Carson and James Craig, who organised the Ulster Covenant and the Ulster Volunteers. In the south the Irish Volunteers were formed to restrain Ulster.

After the Easter Rising of 1916 public support moved from the Home Rule movement to Sinn Féin, and in the 1918 general election the Irish Parliamentary Party fell to six seats. The Parliament of Northern Ireland was established in 1921, but that of Southern Ireland never functioned. Under the Anglo-Irish Treaty, twenty-six of the thirty-two counties became the Irish Free State in December 1922.
irish-parliamentary-party: The party grew out of the Home Rule League, which Isaac Butt founded after leaving the Irish Conservative Party in 1873. After the 1874 general election forty-six Home Rule members met in Dublin and formed a separate group in the Commons, but Butt could win no major party to bills for Ireland. Younger members led by Charles Stewart Parnell, Joseph Biggar and John Dillon turned in 1876–1877 to parliamentary obstructionism, proposing amendments to almost every bill, which revived the group and brought Parnell to the fore.

Parnell became president of Michael Davitt's Irish National Land League in 1879. The Kilmainham Treaty of April 1882, a truce with the government in which he undertook to move against agrarian crime, marked a turning point in his leadership, though it lost him the support of John Devoy's Irish-American Fenians.

Parnell's party was tightly disciplined; one author described it as a regiment led by Parnell and Michael Davitt.The party pledge of 1884 bound every member to sit, act and vote with it, under a whip, Richard Power. Members were paid expense allowances from party funds long before other MPs received state pay in 1911, which let middle-class men such as William O'Brien and D. D. Sheehan sit in parliament. By the early 1890s more than half of the Irish members came from the professions.

William Ewart Gladstone's first Home Rule Bill was defeated in 1886 by 341 votes to 311. In 1890 Parnell was named co-respondent in Katharine O'Shea's divorce, and the party split; Gladstone's second bill passed the Commons in 1893 but was rejected by 419 peers to 41. The factions reunited in 1900 under John Redmond, and the party pressed for land purchase, local government and labourers' housing acts.

After the Parliament Act 1911 curbed the Lords, a Home Rule bill introduced in 1912 was passed but suspended when the First World War began. Redmond's call for the Irish Volunteers to support the war split them, over 142,000 forming the National Volunteers. In the 1918 election the party won 220,837 votes but only 6 seats, losing 78 of its 84, and Dillon lost his own. Its remnants formed the Nationalist Party in Northern Ireland under Joe Devlin.
irish-sea: The Irish Sea separates the islands of Ireland, the Isle of Man and Great Britain. Scotland lies to the north, England to the east, Wales to the south-east, and Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland to the west. St George's Channel links it to the Celtic Sea in the south, and the North Channel to the Inner Seas off the West Coast of Scotland in the north. Anglesey is its largest island, followed by the Isle of Man.

The western side is a deeper channel about 300 km long and 30 to 50 km wide, with depths from 80 to 275 metres, while the bays to the east are shallow. During the last ice age the central part of the sea was probably a long freshwater lake, which reconnected to the sea as the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago.

The sea was formed in the Neogene era. In the Roman Empire it was called Mare Hibernicus. Several invasions of Ireland from Britain crossed it. The Norman invasion of Ireland took place in stages during the late 12th century, from Porthclais near St Davids in Wales to Wexford Harbour in Leinster. The Tudors crossed it in 1529 in caravels and carracks to invade.

Because no tunnel or bridge joins Ireland to Great Britain, most heavy goods are carried across the sea by ship. Ferries run from Fishguard and Pembroke to Rosslare, from Holyhead to Dublin and Dún Laoghaire, and from Cairnryan to Belfast and Larne. The sea has also seen shipwrecks, among them the SS Mesaba, sunk by the German submarine U-118 in 1918, and HMS Mercury, which sank in 1940.

The sea lies off Scotland, England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, and is used for trade, shipping and transport, for fishing and for power generation. Oil and gas fields lie in Liverpool Bay and in the basins of Cardigan Bay and Caernarfon Bay.
irish-war-of-independence: Since the 1870s the Irish Parliamentary Party had demanded home rule, while small groups such as Arthur Griffith's Sinn Féin argued for immediate independence. The Easter Rising of April 1916 proclaimed an Irish Republic and was put down within a week, with over four hundred dead. The execution of its leaders and the arrest of thousands of activists then raised support for Sinn Féin, and the Conscription Crisis of 1918 added to it. In the general election of 1918 Sinn Féin took 73 of the 105 Irish seats, and 91 per cent of those outside Ulster.

Its members met as the First Dáil at the Mansion House in Dublin on 21 January 1919, reaffirmed the 1916 proclamation and issued a declaration of independence. The Irish Volunteers were reconstituted as the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

On the day the Dáil met, Seán Treacy, Séumas Robinson, Seán Hogan and Dan Breen, acting on their own initiative, shot two Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC) constables at Soloheadbeg in County Tipperary. The IRA, organised in flying columns of 20 to 100 men, claimed 70,000 members but only about 3,000 were active fighters. Michael Collins built an intelligence network and a group of gunmen called the Squad.

The British reinforced the RIC with the Black and Tans, about seven thousand mostly ex-soldiers, and the Auxiliaries, who gained a reputation for indiscipline and reprisals against civilians. On Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920, fourteen British intelligence operatives were killed in Dublin and the RIC fired on a crowd at Croke Park, killing fourteen civilians. A week later the IRA killed seventeen Auxiliaries at Kilmichael. Martial law followed and the centre of Cork was burnt. About 1,000 people died between January and July 1921, and 4,500 republicans were interned. In the north-east the conflict had a sectarian aspect, and in Belfast almost 500 people were killed, most of them Catholics.

A truce began on 11 July 1921 after a stalemate and growing British criticism at home and abroad. The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed on 6 December 1921 and ratified by the Dáil on 7 January 1922. The Irish Free State was created as a self-governing Dominion on 6 December 1922, while Northern Ireland, created by the Government of Ireland Act in May 1921, remained in the United Kingdom.

One count puts the dead at 2,346: 919 civilians, 523 police, 413 British military personnel and 491 IRA volunteers. Disagreement over the Treaty among republicans led to the eleven-month Irish Civil War from June 1922.
irk-bitig: The manuscript, shelfmark Or.8212/161, is a booklet of 58 folios folded in half, each page about 13.1 by 8.1 cm, turning to the right. The Old Turkic text fills 104 pages, in horizontal right-to-left lines running down the page, written in black ink with red word dividers; the colophon is in red. Chinese Buddhist verses fill the first and last folios and overwrite the start and end of the Turkic text, so the Turkic was written first. Copying errors and omissions suggest a copy of an earlier text, probably in the Old Uyghur script.

The colophon dates the copy to the 15th day of the second month of a year of the tiger, at the Taygüntan monastery, made for General İtaçuk. Louis Bazin suggests 930 or 942, while Gerard Clauson and Talat Tekin date it to the 9th century.

Each omen is headed by three groups of one to four red circles, thought to be the pips of a four-sided wooden die thrown three times. There are only 64 such combinations, and the book's 65 omens include two missing and several duplicated. The short stories draw on the nomads' world: wild animals fighting or hurt and domestic animals mistreated or stolen are bad omens, animals giving birth good ones. The sky god Tengri appears as a kindly rescuer of lost animals, a god of the road favours travellers, and a khan sets up a royal camp or goes hunting. The book ends: everyone is master of his own fate.

Stein entrusted the manuscript and three other Old Turkic runic manuscripts to Vilhelm Thomsen, who published the first edition in 1912 with a transliteration, an English translation, notes and a word list. Annemarie von Gabain called its language a Manichaean dialect, but Clauson noted that it is virtually identical to that of the Orkhon Valley inscriptions. The text mixes prose and poetry and, without a fixed metre, uses parallelism, alliteration and rhyme.
irkutsk: Irkutsk lies on the Angara River, a tributary of the Yenisei, 72 kilometres below its outflow from Lake Baikal, about 850 kilometres south-east of Krasnoyarsk and about 520 kilometres north of Ulaanbaatar. The Irkut River, from which the town takes its name, joins the Angara directly opposite the city. The city stands among rolling hills in the thick taiga typical of Eastern Siberia. The Trans-Siberian Highway and the Trans-Siberian Railway connect it to other regions of Russia and to Mongolia.

In 1652 Ivan Pokhabov built winter quarters near the site for gold trading and for collecting fur taxes from the Buryats. Yakov Pokhabov built an ostrog, a small fort, nearby in 1661, and it gained official town rights in 1686. Its position at the crossroads of colonisation, trade and industrial routes gave it a larger role in the history of Eastern Siberia than its military importance would suggest. It became the administrative centre of the large Irkutsk province in 1731. The first road connection between Moscow and Irkutsk, the Siberian Route, was built in 1760, and goods imported from China via Kyakhta, including silk and tea, became widely available.

In 1821, under Mikhail Speransky's reforms, Siberia was divided at the Yenisei and Irkutsk became the seat of the Governor-General of East Siberia. In the early 19th century many artists, officers and nobles were exiled to Siberia for their part in the Decembrist revolt against Tsar Nicholas I. Irkutsk became the main centre of their intellectual and social life, and they built wooden houses with ornate hand-carved decoration, many of which survive. By the end of the 19th century there was one exiled man for every two locals. A fire in July 1879 destroyed three-quarters of the city, including about 4,000 houses. The first train arrived on 16 August 1898, and by 1900 the city had the nickname of the Paris of Siberia.

During the Russian Civil War Irkutsk saw fierce fighting between the White movement and the Bolsheviks. In 1920 Aleksandr Kolchak, commander of the largest anti-Bolshevik force, was executed there, which effectively ended anti-Bolshevik resistance. The Irkutsk Region KGB estimated that 15,000 to 17,000 victims of the Great Terror were buried on the city outskirts, and the burial area was explored only after 1989.

Irkutsk is the largest city and administrative centre of Irkutsk Oblast, with a population of 587,891 at the 2010 census. Its historic centre is on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites. The Savior Church, laid in stone in 1706, and the Epiphany Cathedral are among the oldest stone buildings in Siberia.
irminsul: The Old Saxon compound Irminsûl means great pillar. Its first element, Irmin, meaning great, is cognate with terms elsewhere in Germanic mythology: in Old Norse the form Jörmunr is one of the names of Odin. Sacred trees and groves were widely venerated by the Germanic peoples, and the oldest chronicle describing an Irminsul calls it a tree trunk erected in the open air.

Older scholarship inferred from the name a god Irmin, presumed to have been the national god or demi-god of the Saxons. Irmin could also have been an aspect or epithet of another deity, most likely Wodan, or perhaps of Ziu. The view that Odin replaced Tyr as chief god, favoured by early 20th-century Nordicist writers, is not generally considered likely today.

According to the Royal Frankish Annals, in 772 Charlemagne repeatedly ordered the destruction of the chief seat of the Saxon religion, an Irminsul, during the Saxon Wars. It is described as not far from Heresburg, now Obermarsberg. Jacob Grimm argued that strong reasons place it about 24 km away in the Teutoburg Forest.

The Benedictine monk Rudolf of Fulda, writing in 865, described a great wooden pillar erected and worshipped beneath the open sky, whose name signified a universal, all-sustaining pillar. Clive Tolley has argued that Widukind of Corvey, in his Deeds of the Saxons of about 970, describes an Irminsul put up to celebrate a Saxon victory over the Thuringians in 531: an altar to a god of victory depicted by wooden columns, whose name Widukind gives as Hirmin.

Under Louis the Pious in the 9th century a stone column was dug up at Obermarsberg and moved to Hildesheim cathedral, where it was reportedly used as a candelabrum until at least the late 19th century. In the 13th century Hildesheim still commemorated the destruction on the Saturday after Laetare Sunday, when youths on the cathedral square tried to knock over a wooden object on top of a pole with sticks and stones. The custom is described elsewhere in Germany too, notably at Halberstadt.

The twelfth-century Kaiserchronik mentions an Irminsul three times, showing that the concept persisted in Christian times. Scholars have compared it with Tacitus's Pillars of Hercules and the Jupiter Columns of the Rhine, though Rudolf Simek notes the latter were Gallo-Roman monuments found outside the area of Eresburg. In 1929 Wilhelm Teudt proposed that a bent tree on the Externsteine relief was an Irminsul, an idea that became a symbol for anti-Christian völkisch movements.
irnerius: Irnerius, sometimes called lucerna juris, the lantern of the law, was born in Bologna about 1050. At the urging of Countess Matilda of Tuscany he turned to jurisprudence, taking the code of Justinian I as his guide. Law had been taught at Bologna before him by Pepo and a few others, and a tradition of legal study had grown up at Pavia since the mid-ninth century. After teaching briefly in Rome he returned to Bologna and founded a new school in 1084 or 1088, which came to rival the law school of Ravenna.

His teaching followed the methods used for Scripture: he read aloud a section of the civil law, which the students copied, and added his commentary and explanatory glosses. At first these were brief notes between the lines, but as they grew too long he wrote them in the margins, and the marginal gloss later came into general use. The Bolognese text of Justinian's Pandects, the Littera Bononiensis, spread across Europe as students went home, with copies traced to Paris, Padua, Leipzig and the Vatican.

Few works can be securely given to him. An old opinion, much disputed, makes him the author of the Authentica, an epitome of Justinian's Novellae, and his Formularium tabellionum, a guide for notaries, and Quaestiones are lost. The Summa Codicis, credited to him in Herman Fitting's edition of 1894, is now widely dated to between 1130 and 1159, and the Quaestiones de juris subtilitatibus was taken from him after Hermann Kantorowicz published a manuscript from the British Museum.

Irnerius also served the emperor. After the death of Pope Paschal II he defended the rights of Emperor Henry V in the papal election and upheld the election of the imperial antipope Gregory VIII, and after 1116 he seems to have held an imperial office. He died perhaps under Lothair II, certainly before 1140. Largely forgotten for centuries, he was revived by German historians of the later 19th century and the celebration of the University of Bologna's eight hundredth anniversary, though Anders Winroth has questioned much of the received account.
iron-age: The Iron Age is the final epoch of the three-age system of technology, after the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. The concept was devised for Iron Age Europe and the ancient Near East. Meteoric iron had been used for thousands of years earlier; the earliest known artifacts are nine small beads dated to 3200 BCE from burials at Gerzeh in Lower Egypt.

The beginning of the Iron Age is defined locally by archaeological convention, when smelted iron, especially steel tools and weapons, replaces bronze in common use. Smelting iron requires temperatures above 1,250 °C, impractical to reach commonly until the end of the second millennium BCE, and it also required procedures for removing impurities and regulating carbon content.

The three-age system was first used for the archaeology of Europe in the first half of the 19th century and was introduced to Scandinavia by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in the 1830s; its name recalls Hesiod's Ages of Man. The earliest tentative evidence for iron-making is a few iron fragments with suitable carbon content from Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey, dated to 2200 to 2000 BCE. A long-held view that a Hittite monopoly on ironworking underlay Hittite success no longer represents scholarly consensus.

Modern evidence identifies the start of large-scale global iron production about 1200 BCE, which marks the end of the Bronze Age. Anthony Snodgrass suggests that a shortage of tin and disrupted Mediterranean trade about 1300 BCE forced metalworkers to look for an alternative; once tin returned, iron was cheaper, stronger and lighter.

The Iron Age varies by region. In the ancient Near East it is considered to last from about 1200 BCE, the Bronze Age collapse, to about 550 BCE, with the Achaemenid Empire traditionally the end date. Iron working spread through the Mediterranean and to South Asia between the 12th and 11th centuries BCE. In Central and Western Europe the Iron Age lasted from about 800 BCE to about 1 BCE, ending with Roman conquest, and in Northern Europe it began about the 5th century BCE.

In China, writing developed first, so Bronze Age China passes almost directly into the Qin dynasty. Many parts of Africa passed directly from stone to iron, and some archaeologists believe iron metallurgy developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa; the Nok culture may have smelted iron from about 1000 BCE. Indigenous cultures of the Americas did not develop an iron economy before European contact.
iron-crown-of-lombardy: According to tradition, St. Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, had the crown forged for her son around a beaten nail from the True Cross, which she had found. Pope Gregory the Great is said to have given it to Theodelinda, princess of the Lombards, as a diplomatic gift, although he mentions no such donation among his recorded gifts, and Theodelinda gave it to the church at Monza in 628.

Scholars have long debated its origin, since no contemporary sources record its making. Radiocarbon analysis in the late 20th century identified at least two phases: the oldest components, including organic materials used to set the gemstones, date to between the 5th and 6th centuries, and others to between the late 7th and 10th centuries. The gold plates are consistent with late Roman and Byzantine craftsmanship, and some scholars think the crown was once part of a ceremonial helmet or diadem.

The crown has an outer circlet of six hinged segments of beaten gold, partly enamelled and set with 22 gemstones in relief, in the form of crosses and flowers. Inside is a band about one centimetre wide that is said to have been beaten from a nail of the crucifixion.

In 1993 the University of Milan tested it with X-ray fluorescence and radiocarbon dating. The band was found to be pure silver, with no iron. A note in the Roman Ceremonial of 1159 suggests the name came from a lamina of iron once laid over the crown, probably as an arch, rather than inside it. Beeswax under three enamel plates dated to around 500 and that under the others to around 800, consistent with a more ancient crown decorated under Theoderic and extensively restored under Charlemagne.

The Lombard kings did not use it, being acclaimed by the people in arms with the spear as symbol of royal power. Critical scholarship identifies only a limited number of the coronations that 17th-century writers attributed to it, the first confirmed being that of Otto III in 996 at Pavia, followed by Conrad II in 1026. Later confirmed uses include Charles IV in 1355, Sigismund in 1433 and Charles V in 1530 at Bologna, the last coronation performed by a pope.

On 26 May 1805 Napoleon crowned himself King of Italy in Milan Cathedral with it, saying, God has given it to me, woe to him who touches it. After being taken to Vienna, it was returned to Italy in 1866 and restored to Monza Cathedral. It is kept in the Chapel of Theodelinda there.
iron-curtain: The phrase was used before the Cold War: Queen Elisabeth of Belgium used it in 1914 for a barrier descending between her people and Germany. Perhaps the first recorded application to Soviet Russia is in Vasily Rozanov's 1918 polemic The Apocalypse of Our Time.

Winston Churchill's first recorded use was in a telegram of 12 May 1945 to President Harry S. Truman, expressing concern about Soviet actions, and he repeated it on 4 June and in the House of Commons on 16 August 1945. On 5 March 1946, at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, with Truman attending, he said that from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic an iron curtain had descended across the continent.

The antagonism behind the term had several origins. The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of August 1939 contained a secret agreement to split Poland and Eastern Europe between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany, and the Soviets then occupied eastern Poland, the Baltic states and northern Romania. Between 1945 and 1949 the Soviets converted East Germany, Bulgaria, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania and Albania into satellite states, while Yugoslavia turned away from the Soviet Union in the late 1940s.

The curtain took physical shape as border defences, among the most heavily militarised areas in the world, particularly the inner German border. In Hungary a double barbed-wire fence was set 50 metres from the border with mines between the fences, later replaced by an electric signal fence, guard towers, a sand strip to track violations and patrols authorised to use weapons to stop escapees. Emigration from east to west was effectively halted after 1950, after more than 15 million people, mainly ethnic Germans, had left Soviet-occupied countries in the five years following the war.

Churchill's speech was not well received at the time, and much of the Western public still regarded the Soviet Union as a close ally. The phrase gained popularity as a shorthand for the division of Europe as the Cold War progressed, and the curtain served to keep people in and information out.

Its end began with the fall of communism in Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Romania. East Germany reunited with West Germany on 3 October 1990, the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 and Czechoslovakia in 1992. The fall of the curtain was accompanied by a large rise in east–west migration.
iron-gate-central-asia: The Iron Gate, known in Uzbek as Buzgalaxona and in Persian as Darband, is a defile between Balkh and Samarkand that breaks through the mountains running south from the Hisar range towards the Amu Darya. It lies west of Boysun in the Surxondaryo Region. Its exact location is debated, but it is usually taken to be the pass of about 3 kilometres on the road from Samarkand to Balkh, close to the city of Qarshi. According to the historian Lev Gumilev its present name is Buzgala.

In ancient times the defile served as the passage between Bactria and Sogdia, and it was likely of great importance to any power in the region. Its name comes from the belief that an actual gate reinforced with iron once stood in it. The Chinese knew it as Tiěménguān.

Under the Göktürk Empire the medieval Turks controlled the Silk Road, an important source of revenue, and the Iron Gate, which they called temir qapïɣ, was a strategic point for that control. It is named several times in the Orkhon inscriptions of the 730s, raised for Bilge Khagan and his brother Kul Tigin, and in the Bain Tsokto inscriptions of their counsellor Tonyukuk, set up shortly before.

Kul Tigin's inscription says that an army was sent in the west over the Pearl River to the Iron Gate. Bilge Khagan's inscription says that Bumin Khagan annexed all the land from the Kadıgan forest in the east to the Iron Gate in the west, and Tonyukuk's inscription records that on a campaign of 701 his army reached the Iron Gate.
iron-gates: In the broad sense the Iron Gates are a route of 134 kilometres on the Danube, where the river separates the southern Carpathian Mountains from the north-western foothills of the Balkan Mountains. In the narrow sense the name means only the last barrier, just beyond the Romanian city of Orșova. The first narrowing is the Golubac gorge, 14.5 kilometres long, with a medieval fort on the Serbian bank. Next come Gospodjin Vir, with cliffs rising to 500 metres, and the Great and Small Kazan gorges. The Great Kazan is the narrowest, where the river is 150 metres wide and up to 53 metres deep.

The rapids and rocks in the riverbed made the passage infamous for shipping. Under Ottoman rule local pilots called kalauz guided ships through; under Prince Miloš Obrenović Serbs took over, with a Turkish title, dumendžibaša. The name Đerdap comes from Turkish girdap, meaning whirlpool, and the name Iron Gates translates the Turkish Demir-kapija.

The area has been inhabited for a very long time. The Iron Gates Mesolithic culture, dated about 13,000 to 5,000 years ago, is named after the gorge, and Lepenski Vir, unearthed in the 1960s, is often regarded as the most important Mesolithic site in south-east Europe. The Danube was part of the Roman frontier here, and the emperor Trajan had a bridge built by Apollodorus of Damascus east of the Great Kazan between 103 and 105, before his final conquest of Dacia.

The islet of Ada Kaleh, a Turkish exclave with about 400 to 500 people, changed hands between Austrians and Ottomans several times from 1669; the Treaty of Lausanne gave it to Romania in 1923. In the nineteenth century István Széchenyi drafted a plan in 1831 to make the passage navigable, and Hungarian engineers worked from 1889 on channels through the rocks. The Sip Canal was inaugurated on 17 September 1896 by Franz Joseph, Carol I of Romania and Alexander Obrenovich of Serbia.

A joint Romanian-Yugoslav project began in 1964. The Iron Gate I Dam opened in 1972 and Iron Gate II in 1984, each with a hydroelectric station and navigation locks. The river rose 35 metres near the dam, submerging old Orșova, Ada Kaleh and at least five other villages with 17,000 people, and the dams interrupted the spawning routes of several sturgeon species. The Đerdap National Park in Serbia dates from 1974 and the Porțile de Fier National Park in Romania from 2001.
ironclad: The ironclad became feasible and necessary through three developments of the first half of the nineteenth century: steam propulsion, shell guns and iron construction. Steam became suitable for major warships after the screw propeller was adopted in the 1840s, and the French built the first purpose-built steam battleship, Napoléon, in 1850. Explosive shells, developed by the French general Henri-Joseph Paixhans, were part of standard armament by the 1840s. Iron hulls began in the 1830s with the gunboat Nemesis, built for the East India Company in 1839.

France launched the first ocean-going ironclad, Gloire, in 1859. Her wooden hull was sheathed in iron plates 4.5 inches thick, and she carried thirty-six rifled guns. Britain responded and built the first completely iron-hulled warships, among them HMS Warrior, protected by wrought iron backed by 15 inches of teak.

Ironclads first fought in the American Civil War, notably at the Battle of Hampton Roads in 1862, where the Monitor and the Virginia met. Their performance showed that the ironclad had replaced the unarmoured ship of the line as the most powerful warship afloat. The first fleet battle between ironclads was the Battle of Lissa in 1866, between Austria and Italy, in which the Austrian flagship rammed and sank the Italian Re d'Italia.

The success at Lissa and the scant gun damage at Hampton Roads fuelled a ram craze from the 1860s to the 1880s, though few ships were actually sunk by ramming. Heavier guns, mounted in turrets and barbettes, replaced rows of broadside guns, and the torpedo added a threat from small craft. Early ironclads kept masts and sails, because early steam engines were inefficient and carried only a few days' coal.

Change was so rapid that many ships were obsolete almost as soon as they were finished. There is no clear end to the ironclad period, but in the 1890s navies settled on a standard pattern, the pre-dreadnought, and the terms battleship and armoured cruiser replaced the word ironclad. Ironclads were still in use in the First World War. Several survive as museum ships, among them HMS Warrior at Portsmouth and Huáscar at Talcahuano.
iroquoian-languages: The Iroquoian languages, occasionally called the Ogwehoweh languages, are a family of indigenous languages of North America. The family divides into Northern Iroquoian and Southern Iroquoian, or Cherokee. Northern Iroquoian includes the Iroquois Proper or Five Nations group of Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga, a Mohawk–Oneida group, the Huronian languages Wendat, Petun and Wyandot, and the Tuscarora–Nottoway group of Tuscarora, Meherrin and Nottoway. Susquehannock, Wenro, Neutral, Erie and Laurentian are unclassified. Cherokee has dialects in South Carolina and Georgia, in North Carolina and in Oklahoma. Several of these languages are extinct or dormant, including Wendat, Petun, Wyandot, Tuscarora, Meherrin and Nottoway.

The Iroquoian languages are polysynthetic and head-marking, and they are known for their general lack of labial consonants. Where labials occur they are largely restricted to borrowings, expressive vocabulary or variant pronunciations. In Cherokee, native vocabulary has them only in the words for water and salt. No member contrasts voicing, and most have oral vowels with no nasal counterparts and nasal vowels with no oral ones. Cherokee has lexical tone, which its relatives lack. Attempts to link Iroquoian, Siouan and Caddoan languages in a Macro-Siouan family are suggestive but remain unproven.

Several of the peoples are poorly documented. The languages of the Wenro, the Susquehannock or Conestoga Confederacy, the Neutral Nation and the Erie Nation are very poorly documented in print, and the Wyandot called the Neutral Atiwandaronk, meaning they who understand the language. By 1660 all of these peoples except the Conestoga and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy had been defeated and scattered, migrating to form new tribes or adopted into others. The Iroquoian peoples adopted valiant enemies, and captive women and children, to replace the dead.

Almost all surviving Iroquoian languages are severely or critically endangered, and some have only a few elderly speakers. The two languages with the most speakers, Mohawk in New York and Canada and Cherokee in Oklahoma and North Carolina, are spoken by fewer than 10 per cent of the populations of their nations. Programmes support revival: Syracuse University has a Certificate in Iroquois Linguistics for Language Learners, Six Nations Polytechnic in Ohsweken, Ontario offers diplomas and degrees in Mohawk or Cayuga, and from September 2017 the University of Waterloo has offered a credit course in Mohawk.
irpinia: Irpinia is centred on the stretch of the Apennines that runs from the Sella di Ariano in the north to the springs of the Sele River. Its land is a tangle of hills and valleys, mostly limestone with karst features, while in the lower north-east the rocks are chiefly sandstone. The highest peak of Irpinia proper is Mount Avella (1,591 m); to the south rise the Picentini Mountains, with Mount Cervialto (1,809 m). The Ofanto valley bounds it to the east, and to the north it merges with Sannio and Daunia.

The name comes from the Oscan word hirpus, wolf, still the region's symbol. Oscan groups migrated here from what is now Umbria in the 6th century BCE, and the Hirpini were already settled at the time of the First Samnite War (342 BCE). Their main centres included Maloenton (Benevento), Aeclanum (Mirabella Eclano), Aequum Tuticum (Ariano Irpino), Compsa (Conza) and Abellinum (Atripalda). They allied with the Samnites in 275 BCE, and the Romans, who took Maloenton early, renamed it Beneventum and made it a colony in 268 BCE. Caius Marius gave them Roman citizenship in 87 BCE, but Sulla stripped them of their privileges in 80 BCE.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Irpinia passed under Byzantine, Lombard, Hohenstaufen, Anjou, Aragonese and finally Spanish rule. Within the Kingdom of Naples it formed the land-locked province of Principato Ultra. Feudalism was abolished in 1806, the year Avellino became the provincial capital, and in 1861 Irpinia joined the Kingdom of Italy. The earthquake of 23 November 1980, of magnitude 6.9, killed between 2,483 and 4,900 people.

Irpinia produces the wines Fiano di Avellino, Greco di Tufo and Taurasi, along with scamorza and caciocavallo cheeses, chestnuts, hazelnuts and the black truffles of Bagnoli Irpino. Its historic towns include Ariano Irpino, with a medieval castle and romanic cathedral, Mirabella Eclano beside ancient Aeclanum, and Gesualdo, home of the composer Carlo Gesualdo. Montevergine and the Shrine of St. Gerard at Caposele are its best-known sanctuaries.
irrawaddy-river: The Irrawaddy rises where the N'mai and Mali rivers meet in Kachin State, both fed by Himalayan glaciers. The N'mai is the larger but cannot be navigated because of its current, while the Mali is navigable despite a few rapids. The drainage basin of about 400,000 square kilometres covers 61 per cent of the land area of Burma. Between Myitkyina and Mandalay the river runs through three defiles, then crosses the central Dry Zone, the ancient cultural heartland of the Bamar people, and is joined by the Chindwin before turning south.

The delta begins about 93 kilometres above Hinthada, with the Pathein River as its westernmost distributary and the Yangon River as its easternmost. Its fine silt is renewed by the river, and the delta surface extends into the Andaman Sea at about 50 metres a year. Monsoon rains between mid-May and mid-October make the flow vary greatly, with the highest water in August and the lowest in February.

The name comes from Pali, Irāvatī or Airāvatī being the name of the elephant mount of Indra. During the Age of Discovery European explorers also called the river the Pegu, after the Hanthawaddy kingdom whose main river it was. As early as the sixth century the river carried trade and transport, and by the twelfth century a developed network of canals supported flourishing rice cultivation. Later it became a key economic tool of British imperial interests, who set up trading ports along its shores.

The Irrawaddy is about 2,170 kilometres long and remains the most important commercial waterway of Myanmar. Commercial transport is maintained for about 1,300 kilometres, from Hinthada to Bhamo throughout the year, and rice from the delta, one of the major rice-growing areas of the world, is among the main goods carried, together with teak floated down in rafts and petroleum from the oil-field district at Chauk. Until the Ava Bridge, built by the British colonial government in 1934, the only way across was by ferry. The river gives its name to the Irrawaddy dolphin, and Rudyard Kipling's poem has led it sometimes to be called the Road to Mandalay.
irredentism: The term was coined from the Italian phrase Italia irredenta, meaning unredeemed Italy. It referred to territory in Austria-Hungary that was mostly or partly inhabited by ethnic Italians, in particular Trentino and Trieste but also Gorizia, Istria, Fiume and Dalmatia, during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. An Italian movement after 1878 claimed parts of Switzerland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Irredentism is tied to the rise of modern nationalism and the nation-state, which are often linked to the French Revolution of 1789, and it has been an influential force in world politics since the mid-nineteenth century. Some scholars argue that similar phenomena existed earlier, for example in the claim that the crusades aimed to liberate fellow Christians and redeem the Holy Land, but most see it as a recent development.

Irredentism is the desire of one state to annex territory of another, either because its population is ethnically similar to that of the parent state or because the territory once formed part of it. There is no consensus on its exact definition. Political theorists Naomi Chazan and Donald L. Horowitz distinguish two types: a state seeking to annex territory of a neighbour, as with Nazi Germany's claim on the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia, and a minority spread across several countries seeking to unite in a new state, as in the proposed Kurdistan. Not all theorists accept the second type.

It differs from secession, in which a territory breaks away to form an independent state, and from revanchism, which seeks territory in revenge for an earlier grievance. The word revanchism comes from the French revanche and was first used after the Franco-Prussian War for nationalists who wished to reclaim Alsace-Lorraine.

Among the cases often discussed are the Megali Idea, the Greek nationalist project that shaped Greek history from the War of Independence in the 1820s through the Balkan Wars and began to fade after the Greco-Turkish War of 1919 to 1922; the annexation of the Sudetenland in 1938, ceded to Germany under the Munich Agreement in an attempt to prevent a major war; Somalia's invasion of Ethiopia in 1977; and Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands in 1982.

International law is for the most part hostile to irredentism: the United Nations Charter calls for respect for established borders, as do the Organization of African Unity, the Organization of American States and the Helsinki Final Act. Irredentist movements often fail, and peaceful settlements usually bring mutual recognition of existing borders rather than territorial change.
irtysh: The Irtysh runs through China, Kazakhstan and Russia and is the chief tributary of the Ob and the longest tributary in the world. It rises as the Kara-Irtysh, or Black Irtysh, in the Mongolian Altai in Xinjiang, close to the border with Mongolia. It flows northwest through Lake Zaysan in Kazakhstan, meets the Ishim and Tobol and joins the Ob near Khanty-Mansiysk in western Siberia after 4,248 kilometres. Its name first appears in the epitaphs of the Turkic commanders Tonyukuk and Kul Tigin. Mahmud al-Kashgari derived it from ertishmak, a quick jump, while a legend told by al-Gardizi says a slave of the Kimak founder Prince Shad called out irtysh, meaning stop.

Mongol and Turkic peoples held the banks for many centuries. In 657 the Tang general Su Dingfang defeated Ashina Helu, qaghan of the Western Turkic Khaganate, at the Battle of Irtysh River, which ended the Khaganate. In 1208 the Mongol Empire fought an alliance of Merkit and Naimans near the mouth of the Bukhtarma. In the 15th and 16th centuries the middle and lower river lay within the Tatar Khanate of Sibir, whose capital Qashliq stood a few kilometres upstream from the mouth of the Tobol. The Russians conquered the Khanate in the 1580s and founded Tobolsk in 1587 and Tara in 1594.

In the 17th century the Dzungar Khanate controlled the upper river and became Russia's southern neighbour. Russia founded Omsk in 1716, Semipalatinsk in 1718, Ust-Kamenogorsk in 1720 and Petropavlovsk in 1752. The Qing Empire conquered Dzungaria in the 1750s, and the border between the two empires in the basin was roughly marked by chains of guard posts. The Convention of Peking of 1860 and the Protocol of Chuguchak of 1864 set a line close to China's present border, leaving Lake Zaysan on the Russian side, and the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881 adjusted it slightly in Russia's favour.

Ships navigate the river in Kazakhstan and Russia from April to October, and Omsk is the largest river port of Western Siberia. Hydroelectric plants stand at Bukhtarma, Ust-Kamenogorsk and Shulbinsk in Kazakhstan, and the lock at Ust-Kamenogorsk has a drop of 42 metres. The Irtysh–Karaganda Canal was built between 1962 and 1974 to supply the Kazakh steppe. Cities on the river include Oskemen, Semey and Pavlodar in Kazakhstan and Omsk, Tobolsk and Khanty-Mansiysk in Russia. The railway bridge at Omsk, opened in 1896 on the Trans-Siberian Railway, is the oldest on the river.
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa: Isa was born in Jasra to Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa and Mouza bint Hamad Al Khalifa, a member of the House of Khalifa. He succeeded his father as ruler upon his death in November 1961 and was installed on 16 December. On 8 May 1949 he had married his cousin Sheikha Hessa bint Salman Al Khalifa, the daughter of Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa. They had five sons and four daughters, and the eldest son, Hamad, succeeded him.

Isa ruled as Hakim until 1971 and as Emir for the remainder of his reign. In 1968 he visited Mohsin Al Hakim in Najaf to indicate his wish to strengthen relations with the Shia. Bahrain gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1971. The government at first considered joining the United Arab Emirates, but Isa withdrew his country, along with Qatar, because he was dissatisfied with the proposed constitution.

He then attempted to introduce a moderate form of parliamentary democracy, and men, though not women, were given the vote in parliamentary elections in 1973. In August 1975 he dissolved Parliament because it refused to pass the government-sponsored State Security Law of 1974. The parliamentary system was never restored in his lifetime, despite occasional protests from leftist and Islamist groups that reached their peak in 1994. During his reign the Emir had a diplomatic and ceremonial role by arrangement with his brother Sheikh Khalifa bin Salman, who controlled the government and economy as Prime Minister. In 1981 Isa was among the founders of the Dar Al Maal Al Islami Trust, initiated by Mohammed bin Faisal Al Saud, son of King Faisal.

During his 38 years as Emir Bahrain was transformed economically into a modern nation and a key financial centre of the Persian Gulf, though critics note that he also dissolved Parliament and took on absolute power. Isa died of a heart attack on 6 March 1999 at the Government House in Manama, at the age of 65, shortly after a meeting with the United States defense secretary William Cohen. The last function he attended was the funeral of King Hussein of Jordan, less than a month earlier. US President Bill Clinton expressed deep sadness, and UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan described him as a force for stability in the region. He was buried at the Al-Rifa'a cemetery.
isa-ibn-ali-al-khalifa: Isa bin Ali Al Khalifa was born on 27 November 1848 at Riffa Fort, the fourth son of Sheikh Ali bin Khalifa Al Khalifa. His father became ruler in 1868, after the British forced his brother Muhammad bin Khalifa Al Khalifa to abdicate over an alleged breach of the 1861 treaty against maritime depredations. In August 1869 a large force led by Nasir bin Mubarak invaded Bahrain and killed Sheikh Ali, and Nasir's cousin Mohammed bin Abdullah seized the throne. Isa fled to Zubarah, where the Al Noaim tribe remained loyal to him.

In December 1869 a British force under the Political Resident Lewis Pelly deposed the usurper, who died a captive in India in 1877, and Isa ruled from 2 December 1869. A treaty of 22 December 1880 bound him to make no treaty or engagement with any other foreign power without British consent. On his brother's death in October 1888 he became sole ruler, his title changing from Chief to Ruler of Bahrain, or Hakim. The treaty was confirmed and extended on 13 March 1892, Isa keeping for himself the management of Bahrain's internal affairs.

With his brother Sheikh Khalid bin Ali he fought off an attempted invasion by a maritime force of the Al Binali tribe in 1895. In 1923 the British political adviser Clive Kirkpatrick Daly forced him to abdicate, but Bahrainis never recognised the abdication and regarded his son Hamad only as vice-ruler. From 1926 the British adviser Charles Belgrave helped carry through administrative reforms, among them laws to regulate pearl fishing.

Isa died while saying the dawn prayers in his room in Muharraq on 9 December 1932, having held the title of ruler for 63 years, the longest such span in Bahrain's history, and was buried at the Muharraq cemetery. He was officially succeeded by his second son, Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, his eldest son Salman having died in 1893 on the way back from the Hajj. Among his honours were the Order of the Star of India in 1914 and a knighthood of the Order of the Indian Empire in 1919.
isa-khan: Isa Khan was born on 17 April 1536 into a zamindar family, the Dewans of Sarail, in the Bhati region of the Sultanate of Bengal. Accounts of his origins conflict. One tradition makes his grandfather Bhagirat a Bais Rajput from Oudh and his father, Sulaiman Khan, born Kalidas Gajdani, a convert to Islam, while Abu'l Fazl calls him Isa Afghan in the Ain-i-Akbari. His mother, Syeda Momena Khatun, was a daughter of Sultan Mahmud Shah. After the sultan's death Sulaiman claimed the succession, revolted against the Sur Empire and was killed in battle.

With the help of Taj Khan of the Karrani dynasty, Isa obtained an estate in Sonargaon and Maheswardi Pargana in 1564 as a Karrani vassal, and he built up his power in Bhati through alliances with other zamindars. In 1573 he helped Daud Khan Karrani in his expedition to Chittagong against Udai Manikya, the Maharaja of Tripura.

After Daud Khan's defeat at the Battle of Rajmahal ended Karrani rule, Isa led the local resistance. In 1577 he made Egarasindhur the political and trading centre of his realm, and in 1581-82 he declared himself ruler of Bhati, moving his administration from Sarail to Sonargaon and building forts at Katrabo, Kalagachhia and Khizrpur. In 1584 the Mughal subahdar Shahbaz Khan attacked Sonargaon, Katrabo and Egarasindhur; Isa held him off with pretended negotiations and then, with Masum Khan Kabuli, defeated him on water and land at Egarasindur and Bhawal.

When Shahbaz Khan returned in 1586 with reinforcements from Emperor Akbar, Isa gave his allegiance to Akbar and so averted an invasion. The English traveller Ralph Fitch, at Sonargaon late that year, called him the chief of all the kings of those countries. Man Singh, made subahdar of Bengal in 1594, set out against the delta on 9 December 1595. Allied with Raghudev of Koch Hajo, once his enemy, and Kedar Rai of Bhusna, Isa first lost Katrabo in the fighting of 1597 but defeated the Mughals on 5 September, when their commander Durjan Singh was killed.

Isa Khan died in 1599 and is buried in the village of Baktarpur in Kaliganj Upazila, Gazipur District. His son Musa Khan inherited Sonargaon and led the Baro-Bhuiyan landlords, resisting the Mughals until he submitted to Emperor Jahangir on 10 July 1610. In 1909 a farmer at Monwarbagh in Narayanganj unearthed seven cannons, some labelled Isa Khan and dated 1002 of the Hijri calendar, 1593 CE. A Bangladesh Navy base, BNS Issa Khan, bears his name, and Bangladesh issued a stamp in his honour on 15 September 1992.
isaac-ii-angelos: Isaac Angelos was possibly born in September 1156, the son of Andronikos Angelos Doukas, a general in Asia Minor under Manuel I Komnenos. Through his grandmother Theodora Komnene, a daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, he belonged to the extended imperial clan of the Komnenoi. During the regency of Andronikos I for Alexios II he joined a plot against Andronikos, fled by boat, and reached Damascus and Baghdad before settling at Acre. On 11 September 1185 Andronikos's lieutenant Stephen Hagiochristophorites tried to arrest him. Isaac killed him and took refuge in the Hagia Sophia, where a popular tumult proclaimed him emperor. Andronikos was killed on 12 September 1185.

Isaac began his reign with a victory over the Norman king William II of Sicily at the Battle of Demetritzes on 7 November 1185. He strengthened his position by marriage, wedding Margaret of Hungary, daughter of Béla III, in January 1186. His taxes, raised to pay his armies and finance the marriage, produced a Vlach-Bulgarian uprising late in 1185 and the empire under the Asen dynasty. His fleet failed to recover Cyprus from the rebellious noble Isaac Komnenos. He also faced several usurpers, among them Alexios Branas, who was killed outside Constantinople, and Theodore Mangaphas of Philadelphia.

In 1189 Frederick I Barbarossa asked to lead the Third Crusade through Byzantine territory. Isaac suspected his intentions, Barbarossa's army occupied Philippopolis, and in 1190 Isaac released the German emissaries and exchanged hostages. His campaigns against Bulgaria brought defeats at Tryavna in 1190 and Arcadiopolis in 1194. In April 1195 his older brother Alexios Angelos was proclaimed emperor as Alexios III while Isaac was away hunting, and had him blinded and imprisoned.

Isaac's son Alexis sought help in Venice, and the Fourth Crusade, diverted by Doge Enrico Dandolo, took Constantinople in July 1203. Isaac was freed after eight years of captivity and confirmed the Pact of Zara by chrysobull, and his son was crowned co-emperor as Alexios IV, the effective monarch because blindness and confinement had enfeebled Isaac. At the end of January 1204 Alexios Doukas seized the throne as Alexios V amid riots. Isaac died, allegedly of shock, and Alexios IV was strangled. Isaac has the reputation as one of the most unsuccessful rulers of the Byzantine throne, held responsible for the empire's troubles at the end of the 12th century.
isaac-komnenos-of-cyprus: Isaac Doukas Komnenos was a claimant to the Byzantine Empire, and contemporary sources commonly call him the emperor of Cyprus. His grandfather Isaac, bypassed in the succession by his younger brother Manuel I Komnenos, took the position of sebastokrator. The grandfather's daughter Irene Komnene married Doukas Kamateros and gave birth to Isaac of Cyprus around 1155. He married an Armenian princess.

Manuel I appointed him governor of Isauria and the town of Tarsus, where he began a war against the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia and was captured. Manuel died in 1180 and his successors did not at once try to rescue Isaac. In 1183 the new emperor Andronikos I Komnenos contributed to his ransom, as did Constantine Makrodoukas, Andronikos Doukas and the Knights Templar.

Released by the Armenians, Isaac used leftover ransom money to hire mercenaries and sailed to Cyprus, where he made himself ruler with the help of falsified imperial letters ordering the local administration to obey him. He took many Greeks into his service and created an independent patriarch of Cyprus, who crowned him emperor. Andronikos I had Makrodoukas and Andronikos Doukas arrested for treason, and a mob stoned them to death on 30 May 1185. Andronikos was killed in an uprising on 12 September 1185, and his successor Isaac II Angelos sent a fleet of 70 ships, which failed after Margaritus of Brindisi, admiral of William II of Sicily, captured the ships.

The chronicler Niketas Choniates, clearly not partial to Isaac, describes him as an irascible and violent man who plundered Cyprus and imposed cruel punishments. An apparent league with William II of Sicily helped him hold the island, and he was also closely connected to Saladin.

In early 1191, on the Third Crusade, Berengaria of Navarre, fiancée of Richard I of England, and Richard's sister Joan were shipwrecked on Cyprus and taken captive by Isaac. Richard conquered the island in retaliation, and Isaac is recorded shooting two arrows at him from horseback. The English took Isaac prisoner near Cape Apostolos Andreas. According to tradition he was kept in shackles of silver, since Richard had promised not to put him in irons, and he was handed to the Knights Hospitaller, who held him at Margat near Tripoli.

The conquest was a turning point in the history of Cyprus, leading to the Kingdom of Cyprus, which ruled the island for several centuries. Richard granted the town of Portsmouth the arms of Isaac Komnenos, in recognition of its part in the conquest. Isaac was later freed under the ransom agreement for Richard and went to the Sultanate of Rum to seek support against Emperor Alexios III Angelos. He died of poisoning in 1195 or 1196.
isaac-newton: Isaac Newton was born on 25 December 1642 (4 January 1643 in the modern calendar) at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. His father, also named Isaac Newton, had died three months before. Born prematurely, he was a small child; his mother, Hannah Ayscough, said that he could have fit inside a quart mug. When he was three she remarried and left him in the care of his grandmother. From about the age of twelve until seventeen he attended The King's School in Grantham. His mother tried to make him a farmer, an occupation he hated, until his uncle and the schoolmaster persuaded her to send him back to school.

Newton was a fellow of Trinity College and the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge, appointed at the age of 26. He refused to take holy orders in the Church of England. He served two brief terms as Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge, in 1689 to 1690 and 1701 to 1702.

In 1696 he moved to London as Warden of the Mint, a post obtained through the patronage of Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax. He took charge of England's great recoining. He became Master of the Mint in 1699, holding the post for the last 30 years of his life. These appointments were intended as sinecures, but Newton took them seriously, reforming the currency and punishing clippers and counterfeiters. He was president of the Royal Society from 1703 and was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705. He died on 31 March 1727, at the age of 84, and was the first scientist to be buried at Westminster Abbey.

Newton began his work on calculus, which he called fluxions, in 1664, and by 1665 had developed a systematic calculus unifying differentiation and integration. He was self-taught in mathematics. He later quarrelled with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz over priority. Both are now credited with developing calculus independently, though Newton came to it much earlier. Leibniz's notation, however, proved the more convenient. The Principia of 1687 set out his laws of motion and universal gravitation, and his Opticks appeared in 1704.

Newton was a devout but heterodox Christian who privately rejected the doctrine of the Trinity, and he devoted much time to biblical chronology and alchemy. Of an estimated ten million words in his papers, about one million deal with alchemy. Most of his writing in these fields stayed unpublished until long after his death. His library of 1,752 identified books held 477 on theology and 169 on alchemy.
isaac-the-armenian: Isaac came from the Kamsarakan clan and served as exarch, the emperor's governor at Ravenna. The sources disagree about one episode in his dealings with the Lombards. The Chronicle of Fredegar tells how Isaac killed Tasso, duke of Tuscany, by deceit, to please the Lombard king Arioald. Paul the Deacon instead names the patriarch Gregory as the killer and makes Tasso a duke of Friuli, who ruled with his brother Kakko.

In 638 Emperor Heraclius required the newly chosen Pope Severinus to sign the Ecthesis, a Monothelite profession of faith. When Severinus refused, Heraclius withheld recognition of the pope and sent an official, Maurikios Chartoularios, to negotiate in Rome. Maurikios seized the Lateran and urged Isaac to come to the city. Isaac stayed for a time in the Lateran, and the two men plundered the palace: part of the treasure was sent to Heraclius, and much of the rest went to the exarch.

Some time later Maurikios tried to repeat the seizure, and to avoid sharing the wealth he refused to recognise the exarch. Isaac had him captured and executed, ending the challenge to his authority in Rome.

Around 643 the Lombard king Rothari conquered all the imperial possessions in Liguria and much of Emilia. On the banks of the Panaro a Lombard army defeated the troops of the exarchate, and several thousand imperial soldiers were killed. Isaac probably died fighting the Lombards, although the author of the life of Pope Theodore in the Liber Pontificalis writes that he died of a stroke. A sarcophagus of Isaac survives, with depictions of Daniel, the adoration of the Magi and Lazarus.
isaac-watts: Isaac Watts was the eldest of nine children of Sarah Watts and Isaac Watts Senior, a nonconformist who had been imprisoned twice for his views. He was educated at King Edward VI School in Southampton, where he learned Latin, Greek and Hebrew, and he was said to have shown a gift for rhyme at seven. In 1690 he went to the Dissenting Academy at Stoke Newington. He then worked as a private tutor in the household of the Hartopp family and lived for a total of 36 years in the household of Sir Thomas Abney and Lady Mary Abney. He began preaching in 1698.

Watts held more ecumenical opinions than was usual among Congregationalists and cared more for education and scholarship than for any sect. He led a change in worship by adding new poetry on Christian experience to the older tradition of singing the Psalms. In his metrical psalter he adapted the Psalms with a Christian perspective, and he explained that where the Psalmist speaks of sacrificing goats and bullocks, he mentions the sacrifice of Christ. Many later poets followed his path.

His textbook Logick was first published in 1724 in four parts: perception, judgement, reasoning and method. It shows the influence of John Locke, and it treats logic as a practical art useful in any inquiry. It became the standard text at Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard and Yale, and was used at Oxford for well over 100 years. A supplement, The Improvement of the Mind, followed in 1741 and later inspired Michael Faraday.

Edinburgh gave Watts a Doctor of Divinity diploma in 1728. He lived at Abney Hall in Stoke Newington until his death in 1748 and was buried in Bunhill Fields. His papers were given to Yale University. His hymns influenced nonconformists and revivalists such as Philip Doddridge, who dedicated his best-known work to him. King Edward VI School in Southampton named one of its houses Watts and uses Our God, Our Help in Ages Past as its school hymn.
isabeau-of-bavaria: Isabeau was born into the House of Wittelsbach, the only daughter of Duke Stephen III of Bavaria-Ingolstadt and Taddea Visconti, a daughter of Bernabò Visconti, Lord of Milan. She was most likely born in Munich and baptised Elisabeth. In 1383 her uncle Duke Frederick of Bavaria-Landshut proposed her as a bride for King Charles VI of France, and the match was raised again at the Burgundian double wedding at Cambrai in April 1385. At 15 or 16 she was sent to France, and the couple wed three days after their first meeting. Her coronation on 23 August 1389 was marked by a lavish entry into Paris.

In 1392 Charles suffered the first attack of a lifelong mental illness. Although he demanded her removal from his presence during his illness, he consistently allowed her to act for him. She became regent to the Dauphin and sat on the regency council, with far more power than was usual for a queen consort. As rivalry grew between Charles's brother Louis I, Duke of Orléans, and the royal dukes of Burgundy, she acted as a peacekeeper. In 1401 she intervened between Orléans and Burgundy and prevented bloodshed, and in 1402 Charles gave her control of the treasury.

John the Fearless had Orléans assassinated in 1407, and the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War broke out in 1411. Isabeau shifted her allegiance in the interest of the heir. When she followed the Armagnacs the Burgundians accused her of adultery with Orléans, and when she sided with the Burgundians the Armagnacs removed her from Paris and imprisoned her. After Henry V of England's victory at Agincourt in 1415, she accompanied Charles to sign the Treaty of Troyes in May 1420, standing in for him because of his illness.

Isabeau lived in English-controlled Paris until her death on 24 September 1435. She had twelve children, of whom only her youngest son, Charles VII, reached adulthood among the sons. She was long portrayed as a spendthrift and philanderer and accused of giving away the crown at Troyes. Historians who re-examined the chronicles in the late 20th century concluded that many of these charges stemmed from factionalism and propaganda, in particular the pro-Burgundian writing of Pintoin. She was also a patron of goldsmiths, and in 1404 she gave Charles the gold statuette known as the Little Golden Horse Shrine.
isabel-de-clare-4th-countess-of-pembroke: Isabel was one of two known legitimate children of Richard de Clare, Earl Richard Strongbow, and Aoife MacMurrough, who married in August 1170, the day after Strongbow's forces captured Waterford. Her brother Gilbert, born in 1173, died a teenager soon after 1185, leaving her heir to great estates in England, Wales and Leinster, with a claim to the castles on Milford Haven, Pembroke Castle among them. She was said to speak French, Irish and Latin, and her personal seal shows her holding a falcon.

As a ward of King Henry II her inheritance was carefully watched, and in 1189 she was placed in the keeping of Ranulf de Glanville, chief Justiciar of England, at the Tower of London. Henry had promised her to William Marshal, and a month after his accession King Richard I kept the promise, arranging the marriage in August 1189.

The marriage made Marshal one of the richest men in the kingdom, giving him the overlordship of Leinster and the marcher lordships of Chepstow and Usk, and in 1199 King John revived the earldom of Pembroke for him on the basis of her hereditary claim. The couple first went to Ireland in 1200. Isabel stayed there while her husband fought in Normandy and may have ruled Leinster until 1203, with Geoffrey fitz Robert as her seneschal. She is credited with a major part in founding the borough of New Ross.

She ruled Leinster again in 1207-1208 while her husband was held at King John's court in England, and though pregnant she led the campaign that defeated the rebel barons of the province under Meiler FitzHenry. The couple had five sons and five daughters.

Within days of Marshal's death in 1219 Isabel asked for the delivery of her lands, and on 18 June 1219 the justiciar ordered them handed over to her. In July she did homage to King Philip Augustus in France for her Norman inheritance. She fell mortally ill at Chepstow in February 1220, died on 11 March according to the sources of Tintern Abbey, and was buried there beside her mother. Each of her sons became Earl of Pembroke and died without legitimate issue, a failure later attributed to a curse of the Bishop of Ferns, and the estates were divided among her daughters' husbands.
isabel-princess-imperial-of-brazil: Isabel was born on 29 July 1846 at the Paço de São Cristóvão in Rio de Janeiro, eldest daughter of Emperor Pedro II and Empress Teresa Cristina, of the Brazilian branch of the House of Braganza. After the deaths of her two younger brothers in infancy she was recognised as her father's heir presumptive, and the losses led Pedro II to see his position as that of a head of state for his own lifetime only. Her education began in 1854, and in 1856 the Countess of Barral became her aia, a role model for the young princess. In 1864 she entered an arranged marriage with the French prince Gaston, Count of Eu, with whom she had three sons.

Isabel served as regent three times, in 1871-1872, 1876-1877 and 1887-1888, while her father travelled abroad. In her first regency she signed on 27 September 1871 the Law of Free Birth, which freed all children born of slaves after that date. Her second regency was marked by election fraud and violence, tension between the Church and State and a drought in the north-east, and she and Gaston withdrew from public life, which left them isolated.

During the third regency, from 30 June 1887, she became convinced that more action was needed and pressed the Conservative prime minister, Baron of Cotegipe, to free more slaves. After the Rio police mishandled a pro-abolition demonstration in early 1888, she replaced him with João Alfredo Correia de Oliveira.

Isabel sponsored and signed the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law, in 1888, abolishing slavery in Brazil. Emancipation was widely welcomed but intensified opposition among landowners and political elites, and her prospective accession was contested because of gender prejudice, her strong Catholic faith and her marriage to a foreign prince. The military coup of 1889 overthrew the monarchy, and the family went into exile, settling at Cannes after the new government abolished their allowances. On the day after the coup she wrote that if abolition was the cause she did not regret it.

Isabel died in 1921 and was buried at Dreux, and in 1971 her remains and her husband's were interred in the Cathedral of Petrópolis. Historian Roderick J. Barman writes that posterity remembers her for acting decisively once, on the abolition of slavery.
isabella-i-of-castile: Isabella was born on 22 April 1451 at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, the daughter of King John II of Castile and his second wife, Isabella of Portugal. When her father died in 1454, her half-brother became King Henry IV, and she and her brother Alfonso were left in his care. On 19 October 1469 she married Ferdinand of Aragon in secret at Valladolid. Because they were second cousins they needed a papal dispensation, and the bull produced was supposedly Pope Pius II's, though he had died in 1464.

Henry IV denounced the marriage and in October 1470 declared his daughter Joanna his true heir. When he died on 11 December 1474, Isabella took refuge in the Alcázar of Segovia and was proclaimed Queen of Castile and León the next day. Supporters of Joanna planned to marry her to King Afonso V of Portugal. The war ended in a Castilian victory on land and a Portuguese victory at sea, and by the treaties of Alcáçovas, signed on 4 September 1479, Portugal gave up the Castilian throne and kept most of the disputed Atlantic territories, apart from the Canary Islands.

Isabella tackled the disorder left by her brother's reign and in 1476 created a police force, the Santa Hermandad. With Ferdinand she completed the Reconquista, ordered the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in the Alhambra Decree, began the Spanish Inquisition and financed Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage. The Granada War began in 1482, and it took ten years to conquer the Emirate of Granada. After a Muslim uprising in 1499, the monarchs broke the Treaty of Granada in 1502 and ordered Muslims to convert or leave.

Isabella withdrew from government on 14 September 1504 and died on 26 November at Medina del Campo. She is buried in the Capilla Real in Granada beside Ferdinand. Of her seven children five survived to adulthood, among them Joanna, Queen of Castile, and Catherine of Aragon. A cause for her beatification was opened in 1958 and she was named a Servant of God in 1974, but John Paul II suspended the cause in 1991 because of the expulsion of the Jews.
isabella-ii-of-jerusalem: Isabella II was born in late 1212 in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, then a rump state without the city of Jerusalem. She was the only child of Queen Maria of Montferrat, who died of complications of childbirth, and so inherited the kingdom within days.
