The French reacted to the manifesto with hostility, and after the Second World War they arrested nationalists including Balafrej, which led to demonstrations, violence and further arrests. Membership was estimated at three thousand in 1944 and ten thousand in 1947. After the French deposed Sultan Mohammed V, the Istiqlal presented his return as a religious duty. Al-Fassi, in exile in Cairo, called for armed struggle by radio, and the party founded a resistance group, the Secret Organisation.

After independence the party was the largest in the Moroccan majlis and sought a government of its own, which brought it into conflict with the monarchy. By 1956 a left wing around Ben Barka and a right wing around al-Fassi and Balafrej had formed. In 1958 Balafrej became prime minister. After the left wing broke away in the summer of 1958, Mohammed V made the trade unionist Abdallah Ibrahim prime minister, and the left formed the National Union of Popular Forces in 1959. Through the 1960s the Istiqlal was in opposition to Hassan II, though it supported the constitution of 1962. In 1998 it joined the Alternance government with the USFP.

The party's early leaders came largely from merchant families and religious scholars of Fes, joined by teachers and doctors and later by workers. Its ideology, which it calls Istiqlalism, was rooted in reformist Salafism and Arab nationalism, and Sufi orders and Berber tribal leaders regarded it with suspicion. After independence al-Fassi proposed the idea of Greater Morocco and published a map of it in the party newspaper Al-Alam in July 1956.
istituto-per-la-ricostruzione-industrial: From 1930 the Great Depression disrupted Italian credit, and the Fascist regime of Benito Mussolini, fearing mass dismissals and social unrest, began taking over the banks' stakes in large steel, weapons and chemical companies. IRI was meant as a temporary measure and was not intended to nationalize, yet it became the owner and operator of many major banks and firms. On 26 May 1934 Mussolini told the Chamber of Deputies that three-fourths of the Italian economy was in the hands of the State. By 1939 IRI and other agencies controlled over four-fifths of Italian shipping and shipbuilding and three-quarters of its pig iron. The historian Martin Blinkhorn judged that this gave Italy a public sector second only to that of Stalin's Russia.

After the war IRI kept its structure, since private firms could not easily make long-term investments. From 1950 Oscar Sinigaglia's plan for the steel industry gave it a new role in building national infrastructure, from steelworks to the telephone network and the Autostrada del Sole, begun in 1956. Other European governments, the British Labour government among them, admired the IRI formula of cooperation between public and private capital. Under Giuseppe Petrilli, president from 1960 to 1979, the group invested heavily in the south, at Taranto and Pomigliano d'Arco, and rescued failing private firms to protect jobs. Luigi Einaudi warned that a public company not run on economic criteria tended towards a hospice-type of charity.

Its presidents were always chosen by the Christian Democrats. In 1980 IRI was a group of about 1,000 companies with more than 500,000 employees, and in 1993 it was the world's seventh-largest company by revenue. It became a limited company in 1992, and after the Andreatta-Van Miert agreement the Treasury sold its operating companies, including the autostrada system and Alitalia, rather than privatizing IRI itself. Its name survives in Italian journalism for public investment made without business criteria.
istvan-bethlen: Bethlen was born on 8 October 1874, the only son of Count István Bethlen de Bethlen and Countess Ilona Teleki de Szék, with two elder sisters. His family was an old noble house of Transylvania. He was elected to the Hungarian Parliament as a liberal in 1901 and married his distant cousin, the author Countess Margarete Bethlen de Bethlen, on 27 June 1901. They had three sons.

The British historian C. A. Macartney described him as a poor public speaker, very reserved, with the assurance of a man whose family had been obeyed for centuries. He spoke Hungarian, English, French, German and Romanian. Macartney called him a conservative in the truest sense, who believed in the right of Hungary to rule the Danube basin through his own class.

After the attempt of King Charles IV to return to the throne in 1921, Horthy asked Bethlen to form a strong government. Bethlen disliked the House of Habsburg and, though he wanted Hungary to remain a monarchy, opposed a Habsburg restoration. Horthy appointed him as a compromise: as a Calvinist from Transylvania he was expected to follow a revisionist foreign policy, which suited the radicals, while his standing among the great aristocratic families satisfied the conservatives. He was prime minister until 1931.

From 11 October 1932 anti-Jewish demonstrations broke out at Hungarian universities, with Christian students complaining that Jewish students exceeded the quota of the numerus clausus law of 1920. Gömbös and his education minister Bálint Hóman supported the protests, and Gömbös used them to charge that Bethlen had failed to enforce the law during his decade in office.

Bethlen was increasingly sidelined, but he stood out as one of the few Hungarian voices opposed to an alliance with Nazi Germany. He objected that the Germans wanted Hungary to remain agrarian and supply them with cheap food and raw materials, and expected Britain to win the Second World War.
istvan-szechenyi: István Széchenyi was born in Vienna to Count Ferenc Széchényi and Countess Juliána Festetics de Tolna. The Széchenyis were an old and influential Hungarian noble family, traditionally loyal to the House of Habsburg. His father, an enlightened aristocrat, founded the Hungarian National Museum and the Hungarian National Library.

At seventeen he joined the Austrian army and fought in the Napoleonic Wars, distinguishing himself at the Battle of Raab on 14 June 1809 and carrying messages through enemy lines before the Battle of Leipzig in October 1813. He left the service as a captain in 1826, after a promotion to major was turned down, and from September 1815 to 1821 he had travelled in France, England, Italy, Greece and the Levant. The rapid modernisation of Britain fascinated him most.

Széchenyi organised the National Casino in 1827 as a forum for the patriotic nobility. His political writings, Hitel (Credit, 1830), Világ (Light, 1831) and Stádium (1833), condemned the nobility's conservatism and urged it to give up feudal privileges such as freedom from taxation and to lead modernisation. He envisioned reform within the Habsburg monarchy, opposed radicalism, and thought nationalism particularly dangerous in the multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary. In 1835 he established the Óbuda Shipyard, the first industrial-scale steamship builder in the Habsburg Empire. He led the Danube Navigation Committee, which finished its work in ten years, and was the first to promote steamboats on the Danube, the Tisza and Lake Balaton.

He backed the Chain Bridge, the first permanent bridge between Buda and Pest, as a symbol of their later union. He disagreed with Lajos Kossuth, whom he thought an agitator: in his pamphlet People of the East (1841) he argued for slow, careful reform to avoid Habsburg intervention, favouring laissez-faire and agriculture where Kossuth favoured protective tariffs and rapid industrialisation. In March 1848 he accepted the portfolio of ways and communications under Lajos Batthyány.

As the revolution of 1848 moved towards an attempt to break from Habsburg rule, contrary to his vision, Széchenyi suffered a breakdown in early September and was placed in Dr Gustav Görgen's asylum at Oberdöbling. He recovered enough to write Önismeret and Ein Blick, but never returned to politics. Still depressed, he shot himself on 8 April 1860, aged 68. All Hungary mourned, and more than 50,000 people visited his grave at Nagycenk in the three days after his funeral. A statue was unveiled in Budapest on 23 May 1880, and in 1898 the Chain Bridge was named the Széchenyi Chain Bridge in his honour.
istvan-tisza: Tisza was the son of Kálmán Tisza de Borosjenő, prime minister of Hungary from 1875 to 1890, and of Countess Helene von Degenfeld-Schonburg, a Hungarian-German aristocrat from Baden-Württemberg. He was raised in a puritanical and authoritarian Calvinist household, studied at home until the age of twelve and then attended the Calvinist Gymnasium of Debrecen. He studied law in Budapest, then international law at Heidelberg, economics in Berlin and political science at Oxford. After a year as a volunteer hussar he settled in Bihar County, and after five years overseeing the family estates he turned to politics, winning his first seat for the Liberal Party in 1886.

In the 1890s Tisza presided over the Hungarian Industrial and Commercial Bank and sat on many company boards. He resigned from all of them before his first term as prime minister, in 1903-1905, in which he had the remains of Prince Francis II Rákóczi brought back from Turkey and interred in Kassa, today Košice. When a railway workers' strike paralysed the economy on 19 April 1904, he had the organisers arrested and the strikers conscripted into the army. In Bihar the police dealt harshly with peasants at a Socialist gathering, leaving 33 dead and several hundred wounded.

He became prime minister again on 7 June 1913. His cabinet introduced the legal categories of defamation, libel and scare-mongering, which made the press actionable in the courts, and newspapers and journalists regarded this as a violation of freedom of the press. He promised to re-establish the Croatian Constitution, suspended in May 1912, and Croatian constitutional government was restored in November 1913. He supported industrialisation, opposed antisemitism as economically counterproductive, resisted breaking up the large estates and opposed extending the vote to soldiers on active duty; before 1918 only 10 per cent of the citizens of the Kingdom of Hungary could vote.

Tisza was seen by many as the representative of the war policy of the Monarchy, and he survived three attempts on his life, the first in the Hungarian parliament in 1912. On 31 October 1918 soldiers broke into his home, the Róheim Villa in Budapest, in front of his wife and grandniece and killed him. Some sources suggest that they were deserters who blamed him for starting the war. His son István died of Spanish flu five days later. A trial that ended on 6 October 1921 found six men guilty, among them József Pogány and Pál Kéri.
istvan-werboczy: Werbőczy began his political career as the deputy of Ugocsa County at the Hungarian diet of 1498, where his eloquence and learning helped to extend the privileges of the gentry and to exclude all foreign candidates from future elections to the Hungarian throne. At the diets of 1500, 1501 and 1505 he was the spokesman and leader of the gentry against the magnates and prelates. At the last of these he petitioned the king that the law should bind all the gentry alike, and he promoted the principle of a national monarchy.

His standing was such that the diet voted him two denarii per hearth for his services in 1505, something without example in Hungarian history. In 1517 he was made guardian of the infant Louis II and sent abroad to seek the aid of Christendom against the Turks. On his return he found the strife of the parties fiercer than ever and the country in a state of anarchy.

At the diet of Hatvan on 25 June 1525 a conciliatory speech by Werbőczy so moved the assembly that it elected him palatine. In that office he tried to humble the magnates, whom he held chiefly responsible for the decay of the realm, but the following diet deposed him. He withdrew from public life until the election of János Szapolyai, whose kingship realised his idea of a national king and under whom he accepted the chancellorship.

Werbőczy's interests centred on Roman law, canon law and the Hungarian legal system, and he was also known as a theologian. He was appointed to accompany Emperor Charles V to Worms to oppose Martin Luther, and Pope Clement VII commended his learning in canon law and theology during his dispute with Luther at the Imperial Diet of Nuremberg.

His Opus tripartitum juris consuetudinarii inclyti regni hungariae, known simply as the Tripartitum, was printed by Singrenius in 1517 and remained the de facto lawbook of Hungary until 1848; as late as 1945 some laws of inheritance still followed it. The full Latin text with an English translation, edited by János M. Bak, Péter Banyó and Martyn Rady, appeared in 2005.
isurium-brigantum: The Roman road through the town formed part both of Dere Street, which ran from Eboracum (York) to the Antonine Wall, and of the Roman equivalent of Watling Street, which here linked Eboracum with Luguvalium (Carlisle). The name is thought to come from the Latin name of the river, Iseur, now the River Ure. The modern village keeps part of the Roman street plan, and its church stands on the site of the forum.

Isurium was one of the northernmost urban centres of the Roman Empire. Excavations in 1993 found two forts at Roecliffe near Boroughbridge, and the town probably began as a civilian settlement between the Roecliffe fort and the River Ure in the last part of the first century. There is no archaeological evidence of an earlier Brigantian settlement on the site; the likeliest Iron Age centre is Stanwick, near Richmond, where Cartimandua had her base. The civitas capital, with the same status as Exeter, Leicester, Chichester and Canterbury, was probably established in about 160.

The town had substantial buildings probably by the early 2nd century. Bank and ditch defences came later, and stone walls with four gates were added in the mid-3rd century. Over the following hundred years elaborate private houses with decorative mosaic floors were built. In the middle of the 4th century bastions were added to the defences, and unrest across the Empire seems to have affected the town's prosperity. There is little evidence of occupation after the end of Roman rule, and by the 7th century the Anglo-Saxons held the area.

The Aldborough Roman Site, in the care of English Heritage, consists of a stretch of the town wall with its towers and two mosaic pavements still in place from a Roman townhouse, with finds shown in its museum. The town is a scheduled monument. Geomagnetic scanning in 2011 revealed an amphitheatre, and the Aldborough Roman Town Project, led by Rose Ferraby and Martin Millett, has studied the site since 2016.
itagaki-taisuke: Itagaki was born on 21 May 1837 into a middle-ranking samurai family in Tosa Domain, in present-day Kōchi Prefecture, and became a Councillor of State (sangi) in 1869. In 1873 the first major schism of the Meiji oligarchy came over the Seikanron, the proposed military expedition to Korea. Itagaki and Saigō Takamori argued that it would give an outlet to the disaffected samurai. Leaders just back from the Iwakura Mission, among them Ōkubo Toshimichi, held that internal reform came first, and the proposal was rejected in October 1873. Itagaki resigned. Unlike Saigō, who later led an armed rebellion, he chose political means: "Saigō fights the government with arms, but we will fight it with people's rights."

On 12 January 1874 he formed the Aikoku Kōtō, Japan's first political association, and on 17 January he and eight associates submitted a memorial calling for an elected assembly. Ōkubo dismissed it, but its publication in the press set off a nationwide debate. In April 1874 Itagaki founded the Risshisha in Tosa. He rejoined the government after the Osaka Conference of 1875, persuaded by Itō Hirobumi and Inoue Kaoru, but resigned in October 1875.

After the Imperial Rescript of 1881 promised a national assembly by 1890, the Liberal Party (Jiyūtō) was founded on 29 October 1881 with Itagaki as president. Its prospectus, written mainly by Nakae Chōmin, declared liberty the natural state of man, and its support came chiefly from rural landowners resentful of the land tax. On 6 April 1882 an elementary school teacher stabbed Itagaki at Gifu; he is reported to have cried, "Itagaki may die, but liberty will not!"

From November 1882 to June 1883 he toured Europe with Gotō Shōjirō and met Herbert Spencer in London. The tour, funded by the Mitsui company, brought accusations that he had been bought off. Peasant uprisings such as the Chichibu incident of 1884 divided the party, which dissolved on 29 October 1884. His own early view of the franchise was elitist, for the 1874 memorial would have limited it to samurai and wealthier farmers and merchants.

The party was refounded in 1890. In June 1898 it merged with Ōkuma Shigenobu's Progressive Party, and on 30 June 1898 the Ōkuma–Itagaki cabinet, Japan's first party-based government, was formed, with Itagaki as Minister of Home Affairs. It fell within four months, and Itagaki resigned on 27 October 1898. He retired in 1900 and died on 16 July 1919. Some contemporaries called him an opportunist, but his choice of agitation over armed revolt set a precedent for non-violent opposition in modern Japan.
itaipu-dam: The plan for a power plant on the Paraná grew out of negotiations between Brazil and Paraguay in the 1960s. The Iguaçu Act, signed on 22 July 1966 by the foreign ministers Juracy Magalhães and Raúl Sapena Pastor, declared a shared interest in studying the use of the river's water from the Salto de Sete Quedas to the Iguaçu River watershed. The Itaipu Treaty followed on 26 April 1973, and the body Itaipu Binacional was created on 17 May 1974 to manage construction, which began in January of the following year. The name comes from an island near the site, called in Guarani after the idea of a sounding stone.

Argentina first contested the project. The dispute ended with the Tripartite Agreement of 19 October 1979, which set the permitted river levels and became the basis of later Argentine–Brazilian integration. The river was diverted on 14 October 1978 to dry the section of bed where the dam was built.

The dam is 7,235 metres long and 196 metres high, and is really four dams joined: an earth fill dam, a rock fill dam, a concrete buttress main dam and a concrete wing dam. The reservoir began to fill on 13 October 1982, and the first generating unit started on 5 May 1984. The last two of the twenty units, each of 700 MW, began work in September 2006 and March 2007, bringing the capacity to 14 GW.

Ten units generate at 50 Hz for Paraguay and ten at 60 Hz for Brazil. Paraguay's output exceeds its own demand, so most of it goes directly to the Brazilian side, and two 600 kV direct-current lines about 800 kilometres long carry the bulk of the power to south-eastern Brazil. Around forty thousand people worked on the construction, which shifted 50 million tonnes of earth and rock.

The project displaced about 10,000 families and flooded the Guaíra Falls, the waterfall largest by volume in the world; some 80 people died when a crowded bridge over the falls collapsed shortly before the reservoir was filled. The falls had separated two freshwater ecoregions, and after they vanished more than 30 fish species from below them spread above. In 1994 the American Society of Civil Engineers named Itaipu one of the seven modern wonders of the world. The composer Philip Glass wrote a symphonic cantata called Itaipu.
itakh: Itakh's nisba, al-Khazari, marks him as a Khazar by origin. He is said to have worked as a slave in the kitchen of Sallam al-Abrash al-Khadim, which earned him the nickname al-Tabbakh, the cook, before he was bought as a ghulam by al-Mu'tasim, who reigned as caliph from 833 to 842. He rose to become one of the senior commanders of al-Mu'tasim's Turkic guard and took part in several expeditions.

Under al-Mu'tasim he served as sahib al-shurta at Samarra and commanded the caliph's personal guard. By the accession of al-Wathiq in 842 he and the Turk Ashinas were the mainstay of the caliphate. Al-Wathiq made him governor of the Yemen in 843/4, and after the death of Ashinas in 844/5 named him governor of Egypt, though Itakh appointed Harthamah ibn al-Nadr al-Jabali to govern there in his place. Ya'qubi reports that he also received the governorships of Khurasan, al-Sind and the districts of the Tigris.

When al-Wathiq died unexpectedly in August 847, Itakh met with the vizier Muhammad ibn al-Zayyat, the chief qadi Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad and the Turkish general Wasif al-Turki to choose a successor. Ibn al-Zayyat proposed al-Wathiq's son Muhammad, the future al-Muhtadi, but he was passed over for his youth in favour of another son of al-Mu'tasim, the 26-year-old Ja'far, who became al-Mutawakkil. The new caliph was resolved to destroy the circle of his father's officials, and his first target was Ibn al-Zayyat, who had once treated him with disrespect.

On 22 September 847 al-Mutawakkil sent Itakh to summon the vizier as if to an audience; instead Ibn al-Zayyat was taken to Itakh's residence and held there. This was the height of Itakh's career, when he combined the posts of chamberlain, head of the personal guard, intendant of the palace and head of the barid, the public post that also served as the government's intelligence network.

In 848 he was persuaded to go on the pilgrimage and laid down his powers, only to be arrested on his return. His possessions were confiscated, and in his house alone the caliph's agents reportedly found one million gold dinars. He died of thirst in prison the following year.
italian-campaign-of-1796-1797: By the spring of 1794 the Army of Italy had been at war for two years with the Kingdom of Sardinia of Victor Amadeus III. Bonaparte, made a brigadier general after the victory at Toulon in 1793, served it as inspector of artillery, and in 1795 he urged the reconquest of Vado Ligure and Ceva. On 27 March 1796 he took command, with Sérurier, Augereau and Masséna as his senior generals of division. The Austrians under Johann Peter Beaulieu and their Sardinian allies had about 54,500 men, and Paris treated Italy as a secondary front to the Rhine.

The campaign opened with the Montenotte campaign on 10 April 1796, and after the victory at Mondovì Sardinia was forced out of the war. Bonaparte chased the Austrians across Lombardy to Lodi on 10 May, put down revolts in Pavia and Milan, and in June began the long siege of Mantua, defeating four Austrian relief efforts between August 1796 and January 1797. Meanwhile his forces invaded Modena and Reggio, Genoa and the Papal States, and Pope Pius VI bought the armistice of Bologna with territory, money and works of art.

After the destruction of the last relief army at Rivoli in January 1797, Mantua surrendered on 2 February, and the Treaty of Tolentino with the Papal States followed on 19 February. Bonaparte then crossed the Alps, reaching Klagenfurt by the end of March, and drove on into Austria until the Peace of Leoben of 18 April 1797. Its terms gave Venice to Austria, and Bonaparte dissolved the Republic of Venice on 12 May.

The Directory was shocked by the terms of Leoben but accepted them. When elections gave the conservatives a supermajority, Bonaparte sent troops under Augereau to Paris and supplied evidence against Jean-Charles Pichegru, helping the Directory purge the legislature in the Coup of 18 Fructidor on 4 September 1797. Ignoring the Directory's order not to give up Venice, he signed the Treaty of Campo Formio on 17 October 1797, ending the War of the First Coalition.

The campaign was his first in command of a whole army and made him well known throughout Europe. The Directory's representative Henri Jacques Guillaume Clarke wrote that there was nobody there who did not look upon him as a man of genius.
italian-east-africa: Italy colonized Eritrea in 1890 and Italian Somaliland in 1905, and its invasion of Ethiopia in the First Italo-Ethiopian War of 1895–1896 failed. After the First World War, nationalist feeling grew from the belief that Italy had been denied its due, a sentiment called the Mutilated Victory, and it contributed to the rise of Benito Mussolini in 1922. A border clash at Ual-Ual in 1934 gave Mussolini a pretext for war. The Second Italo-Ethiopian War began without a declaration in October 1935. Italian troops used mustard gas in aerial bombardments against combatants and civilians, and Emperor Haile Selassie fled to England. Italian forces entered Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, and Mussolini proclaimed the Italian Empire on 9 May.

A decree of 1 June 1936 united Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia as Italian East Africa. It was ruled by a Governo Generale from Addis Ababa under a viceroy appointed by the Italian king, who took the title Emperor of Ethiopia, and it was divided into six governorates. The League of Nations ended its sanctions in July 1936, and by November 1938 47 countries had recognized the king's new title. The administration divided inhabitants into citizens, meaning Italians and other Europeans, and subjects, and racial legislation of 1939 prohibited mixed marriages. It marginalized the Amhara elite and often treated the Oromo and Muslim communities more favourably.

Roads were the main public works, linking Addis Ababa with Massawa, Mogadishu and Assab. By 1939 about 165,270 Italian colonists lived there, though by 1940 only 3,200 farmers had reached Ethiopia, less than ten percent of the regime's goal. The population in 1939 was estimated at 12.1 million. Ethiopian resistance never ceased. After an attempt on Rodolfo Graziani's life on 19 February 1937, Italian troops and Blackshirts massacred thousands of civilians in Addis Ababa, with estimates from 1,400 to 19,000 deaths.

British forces attacked Italian East Africa in the East African campaign of the Second World War, and after the Battle of Gondar in November 1941 all its territories came under British military administration. Haile Selassie was restored, and Ethiopia's full sovereignty returned in 1944. British-occupied Somalia became a Trust Territory under Italian administration in 1950 until independence in 1960, and Eritrea became an autonomous part of Ethiopia in 1952. Italian archaeologists began studying the obelisks of Axum and the churches of Lalibela in 1938.
italian-empire: Italy, unified as a nation-state in the late 19th century, wished to compete with the other European powers and saw its interests in the Mediterranean and the Horn of Africa. It arrived late and depended on the acquiescence of Britain, France and Germany. When France imposed a protectorate over Tunisia in May 1881, what the Italian press called the Slap of Tunis left Italy isolated and led it to sign the Triple Alliance in 1882 with Germany and Austria-Hungary.

The genesis of the empire was the purchase in 1869 of Assab Bay on the Red Sea by an Italian navigation company wanting a coaling station as the Suez Canal opened. The government took it over in 1882, making it modern Italy's first overseas territory.

Italy joined the Allies in 1915 after being promised territorial spoils, mainly from Austria and Turkey. Albania and Dalmatia saw Italian occupations during the First World War. In 1923 the Treaty of Lausanne formalised Italian administration of Libya and the Dodecanese. Mussolini, in power from 1922, sought to enlarge the empire, and in 1939 drew up a document, The March to the Oceans, arguing that countries without free access to the high seas were not independent. By 1939 Italian settlers numbered 120,000 to 150,000 in Libya and 165,000 in Italian East Africa, where the government encouraged systematic demographic colonisation.

At its peak, between 1936 and 1941, the colonial possessions in Africa covered present-day Libya, Eritrea, Somalia and Ethiopia, the last three grouped as Africa Orientale Italiana. Outside Africa Italy held the Dodecanese Islands and Albania and had a concession at Tianjin in China. In the World War II it allied with Germany in 1940 and occupied British Somaliland, western Egypt, much of Yugoslavia and most of Greece.

The Italian Army was expelled from East Africa by British and Commonwealth forces in 1941, and by the autumn of 1943 the empire had effectively ended. Mussolini was deposed on 25 July 1943, and an armistice with the Allies was made public on 8 September, after which German forces ended Italian rule in Albania, Croatia and the Dodecanese. In 1947 Italy relinquished its claims on its former colonies. In 1950 the former Italian Somaliland became a UN trust territory under Italian administration, which lasted until its independence in 1960.
italian-riviera: The Italian Riviera, or Ligurian Riviera, is the narrow coastal strip between the Ligurian Sea and the mountain chain formed by the Maritime Alps and the Apennines. It runs from the French border near Ventimiglia, a former customs post, eastwards to Capo Corvo, also called Punta Bianca, at the eastern end of the Gulf of La Spezia. It includes nearly all the coastline of Liguria, about 350 km long, and crosses all four Ligurian provinces: Genoa, Savona, Imperia and La Spezia.

The point of division between the Riviera di Ponente, 'the coast of the setting sun', and the Riviera di Levante, 'the coast of the rising sun', is the apex of the Ligurian arc at Voltri. The Ponente's part centred on Savona is called the Riviera delle Palme, and the part centred on Sanremo the Riviera dei Fiori, after its long-established flower growing.

The history of the Italian Riviera is chiefly that of the Liguria region. Historically the name Riviera extended further west, through what is now French territory as far as Marseille. The coast has been a destination for travellers since the time of Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Ezra Pound and Ernest Hemingway were among the writers inspired by it. The musician Niccolò Paganini (1782-1840) and the poet Eugenio Montale (1896-1981) are among the figures linked with the region.

About 1.6 million people live on the Riviera, most of them in the coastal area. Its mild climate supports a tourist trade in resorts such as Alassio, Bordighera, Camogli, Portofino, Sanremo and Santa Margherita Ligure, and in the Cinque Terre. Industry is concentrated around Genoa, Savona and the Gulf of La Spezia: Genoa and La Spezia are leading Italian shipyards, La Spezia is Italy's major naval base, and Savona is a major centre of the iron industry.

Two World Heritage Sites lie on the coast: the Strade Nuove and the system of the Palazzi dei Rolli in Genoa, and Portovenere, the Cinque Terre and the islands of Palmaria, Tino and Tinetto. Local foods include pesto, focaccia and farinata, and the Sanremo Music Festival and the Milan-Sanremo cycling race are held on the coast.
italian-somaliland: Italian interest began with exploring societies founded from 1876. In 1889 two Somali rulers sought protection from Italy by treaty: Sultan Yusuf Ali Kenadid of Hobyo, who signed on 8 February, and Boqor Osman Mahamuud of the Majeerteen Sultanate, who signed on 7 April. Each hoped for Italian support against rivals. The treaties promised that Italy would not interfere in their administration, in return for arms and an annual subsidy.

In the south the consul at Zanzibar, Vincenzo Filonardi, was charged with creating outposts on the Banaadir coast. The port of Adale was occupied in February 1891 and renamed Itala. In 1893 Filonardi and the Italian navy occupied Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa and Warsheekh, and Giumbo followed in 1895.

Somali resistance marked the whole period. In November 1896 Antonio Cecchi, administrator for the Benadir Company, and thirteen others were killed in an ambush at Lafoole by Biimaal and Wa'daan fighters. A punitive expedition under Giorgio Sorrentino in 1897 destroyed villages and seized livestock. Further wars against the Biimaal and their allies in 1905 to 1908 extended Italian control over the whole Lower Shabelle region. The Dervish movement of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan defeated an Italian advance at Hiraan in 1913.

After the First World War Britain ceded Jubaland to Italy in 1925, and by the end of 1927 the sultanates of Hobyo and the Majeerteen had been annexed after a two-year campaign under Governor Cesare Maria De Vecchi. The colony saw railways, dams, farms and villages, among them an agricultural settlement at Jowhar. By 1935 more than 50,000 Italians lived there, about 5 per cent of the population. In October 1935 the southern front of the invasion of Ethiopia was launched from the colony, and in June 1936 it became the Somalia Governorate of Italian East Africa.

British forces defeated the Italians in 1941 and administered the territory until 1950. The Somali Youth Club, the first modern Somali political party, was founded in Mogadishu in 1943 and became the Somali Youth League. In November 1949 the United Nations granted Italy trusteeship on condition that Somalia become independent within ten years, and Italian administration began on 1 April 1950. The Somali Youth League won 75.58 per cent of the vote in the parliamentary election of 1959. On 1 July 1960 the Trust Territory united with former British Somaliland to form the Somali Republic, with Mogadishu as its capital.
italian-war-of-1499-1504: The war followed the Italian War of 1494–1498, which began when Ludovico Sforza, regent of Milan, invited Charles VIII of France into Italy. Charles took Naples with ease, but after he went home Ferdinand II of Naples won it back with the support of Ferdinand II of Aragon. Charles died on 7 April 1498 and was succeeded by Louis XII, who inherited the Angevin claim to Naples and claimed Milan through his grandmother Valentina Visconti. By the Treaty of Blois of 9 February 1499 he allied with the Republic of Venice, which was promised Cremona and lands east of the Adda, while Pope Alexander VI approved the invasion in return for French backing of Cesare Borgia in Romagna.

French troops under Gian Giacomo Trivulzio overran the duchy, Ludovico fled to Emperor Maximilian, and the French entered Milan on 6 October 1499. With 20,000 mercenaries Ludovico retook the city on 5 February 1500, but he could not pay them, his army was destroyed at the Battle of Novara in April, and his own men betrayed him to the French, who held him until his death in 1508. By the Treaty of Granada of 11 November 1500 Louis and Ferdinand agreed to divide Naples, and Frederick of Naples abdicated on 25 July 1501.

Disputes over the shared lands brought war between the partners in the second half of 1502. Gonzalo de Cordoba at first avoided battle, and the fighting became a matter of skirmishes, among them the Challenge of Barletta on 13 February 1503. Helped by supplies brought by the Spanish navy and by quarrels between the French and Italian knights, the Spanish won at Cerignola on 28 April 1503. On 29 December they surprised the French army at the Garigliano while it rested after Christmas and destroyed it, killing about 4,000 of just over 15,000 soldiers.

Louis withdrew to Lombardy on 2 January 1504, and the Treaty of Lyon, signed on 31 January, gave France northern Italy from Milan and Spain Sicily and the south; Milan stayed in French hands for thirteen years. A second treaty of Blois, of 22 September 1504, proposed to marry Louis's daughter Claude to the future Charles V with Milan and Burgundy in her dowry, but the union never took place. The next phase of the Italian Wars, the War of the League of Cambrai, broke out in 1508.
italian-war-of-1521-1526: After Maximilian I died on 12 January 1519, Charles I of Spain and Francis I of France competed for the imperial crown. Charles bought the votes of the electors with money borrowed from the Fugger banking family, and he was crowned King of the Romans on 23 October 1520. Pope Leo X needed his support against Martin Luther, and Charles issued the Edict of Worms in May 1521. Leo promised to help expel the French from Lombardy, which left Francis with only the Republic of Venice as an ally. Francis tried to divert Charles by attacking Luxembourg and Navarre in 1521, but both offensives failed.

Imperial troops invaded northeastern France in August 1521, and Charles and Henry VIII signed the secret Treaty of Bruges in November. On 27 April 1522 the Imperial and Papal army defeated the French at the Battle of Bicocca, and Lombardy was abandoned. England declared war on France on 29 May 1522. Charles de Bourbon, angered by Francis's attempt to seize his inheritance, entered the Emperor's service, and Venice changed sides by the Treaty of Worms of 29 July 1523. A French attack in 1524 failed at the Battle of the Sesia, where Bayard was killed, and Bourbon invaded Provence. Francis then crossed the Alps and besieged Pavia.

On the night of 23 February 1525 the Imperial army moved against his camp, and in the four-hour battle that followed arquebusiers cut down the French cavalry. Francis was captured by Charles de Lannoy.

Francis was held at Pizzighettone and then in Madrid. His mother, Louise of Savoy, sent a mission to Suleiman, which brought an Ottoman ultimatum to Charles and laid the foundation of the Franco-Ottoman alliance, a scandal in the Christian world. Suleiman defeated Charles's allies at the Battle of Mohács in 1526. Francis signed the Treaty of Madrid, giving up his claims to Italy, Artois, Flanders and Burgundy, but repudiated it a few weeks after his release, which began the War of the League of Cognac. The Italian Wars went on for three more decades.
italian-war-of-1551-1559: The war grew out of a dispute over Parma. After Pier Luigi Farnese, Duke of Parma, was assassinated on 10 September 1547, troops of Emperor Charles V occupied the duchy. Pope Julius III, elected on 7 February 1550, confirmed Pier Luigi's son Ottavio Farnese as duke, and on 27 May 1551 Ottavio placed Parma under the protection of Henry II of France. Henry had already renewed the Franco-Ottoman alliance after Andrea Doria captured Mahdia for Charles V in 1550.

At sea the Ottoman fleet, joined by French galleys, raided Calabria, captured Reggio and defeated Doria at the Battle of Ponza in 1552, and in 1553 the allies invaded Corsica. On land the War of Parma ended in a truce on 29 April 1552, but by the Treaty of Chambord Henry had allied with the German Protestant princes, and he took the Three Bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and held Metz against an imperial siege. In Tuscany Siena, which had expelled its Spanish garrison and taken a French one, was besieged from January 1554 and fell to Spanish forces in April 1555, after the French defeat at the Battle of Marciano.

The Truce of Vaucelles of 5 February 1556 did not last. After Charles V abdicated, Philip II invaded the Papal States with 12,000 men under the Duke of Alba, and Pope Paul IV made peace in September 1557. Mary I of England declared war on France in June 1557. Both crowns were straining their finances: the Spanish Empire, followed quickly by France, defaulted on its debts in 1557, and Henry II also faced a growing Protestant movement at home.

The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis consisted of two treaties, signed on 2 and 3 April 1559, and ended the Habsburg-Valois conflict as a whole. Henry II renounced his claims to the Duchy of Milan and recognised Spanish rule in Naples, Sicily and Sardinia. France returned Corsica to Genoa, gave Savoy–Piedmont back to Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, and accepted Florence's conquest of Siena, but kept the Three Bishoprics and five fortresses in Piedmont. England left the Pale of Calais to France for an initial eight years; it remained French thereafter.

Emmanuel Philibert married Henry's sister Margaret of France, and Henry's daughter Elisabeth of Valois became Philip's third wife. During a tournament held to celebrate the peace, Henry was wounded by a splinter from the lance of Gabriel Montgomery and died on 10 July 1559. The instability that followed, together with the demobilisation of thousands of largely unpaid troops, led to the outbreak of the French Wars of Religion in 1562.
italian-wars: The Treaty of Lodi of 1454 ended the long Wars in Lombardy, and a non-aggression pact, the Italic League, followed shortly afterwards. It brought forty years of stability and economic expansion. The League's main supporter was the Florentine ruler Lorenzo de' Medici, who tried to keep France and the Holy Roman Empire out of the peninsula. His death in April 1492 weakened it just as France was seeking to expand in Italy. Louis XI of France had inherited the County of Provence in 1481 together with the Angevin claim to the Kingdom of Naples, and his son Charles VIII became king of France.

The first war began when Ludovico Sforza, regent of Milan, encouraged Charles VIII to invade Italy on the strength of the Angevin claim. Charles crossed into the peninsula in September 1494, saying he meant to use Naples as a base for a crusade against the Ottoman Turks. The French marched through Italy almost unopposed, entering Florence on 17 November and Rome on 31 December, and Charles withdrew in 1495. After 1503 most of the fighting began with French invasions of Lombardy and Piedmont.

The League of Cambrai, signed on 10 December 1508, turned against Venice, and the French largely destroyed a Venetian army at Agnadello on 14 May 1509. Charles I of Spain was elected Emperor Charles V on 28 June 1519, which left France surrounded by what was called the Habsburg ring, and his rivalry with Francis I of France became one of the fundamental conflicts of the sixteenth century. A Franco-Ottoman alliance followed in 1536, and a Franco-Ottoman fleet captured Nice on 22 August 1543, an attack on a Christian town that was regarded as shocking.

The growth of Protestantism meant that by 1557 the main belligerents faced internal conflict over religion and had to turn to domestic affairs. Under the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, France was largely expelled from Italy but gained Calais from England and the Three Bishoprics from Lorraine. Spain acquired sovereignty over the Kingdoms of Naples and Sicily and the Duchy of Milan.

The wars were fought with considerable brutality. Some historians see them as the dividing point between medieval and modern warfare. Charles VIII brought in 1494 the first truly mobile siege train, with guns on wheeled carriages drawn by horses and iron cannonballs, and Francesco Guicciardini wrote that a city could be taken in days and hours rather than months. A skirmish in 1503 first showed the use of the arquebus.
italic-league: In the first half of the 15th century the larger Italian powers had been consolidating their territories. Savoy expanded towards the Ligurian coast, and Venice concentrated on its mainland Terraferma while Turkish expansion threatened its Stato da Màr. Milan expanded southwards and kept the bulk of Lombardy even after the empire of Gian Galeazzo Visconti broke up at his death. Florence had gained most of Tuscany, the Papal States had begun an expansion in central Italy, and King Alfonso V of Aragon had extended his rule from Sicily into the Kingdom of Naples.

The league, also called the Most Holy League, was concluded in Venice on 30 August 1454, a few months after the Treaty of Lodi. It was solemnly proclaimed on 2 March 1455, when Pope Nicholas V, King Alfonso and other small states acceded to it; Malatestine Rimini was excluded at Alfonso's insistence. The members forbade separate alliances and treaties and committed themselves to maintaining the established boundaries.

The other Italian states acknowledged the condottiero Francesco Sforza, who had married the only daughter of Filippo Maria Visconti, as successor to the last of the Visconti of Milan, and the peace allowed him to consolidate his rule there. Ending the traditional rivalry between Florence and Sforza's Milan was Cosimo de' Medici's most important foreign policy decision.

The league underpinned the balance of power later pursued by Lorenzo de' Medici; its only cracks were the Pazzi conspiracy, the Barons' conspiracy and the Salt War. Its stability let the economy of the peninsula recover from the losses of the Black Death, in an expansion that lasted into the 17th century. To watch over the ban on supporting exiled dissidents, the states created the first permanent embassies among themselves, and in 1490 Ermolao Barbaro wrote De Officio Legati, apparently the first treatise on ambassadorship.

The death of Lorenzo in 1492 marked the decline of the league. It failed to prevent the French invasion of 1494 that began the Italian Wars, though as the League of Venice it raised the army that fought Charles VIII at Fornovo after his sack of Naples. The Venetian alliance with France and Spain against Milan and Naples in the Italian Wars of 1499–1504 ended it. Francesco Guicciardini and Niccolò Machiavelli later debated why Italy had not united into a single monarchy.
italica: Italica was an ancient Roman city in Hispania, close to the town of Santiponce in the province of Seville. It stood near the Guadalquivir, close enough to control the area, and near the larger native and Roman city of Hispalis, modern Seville, which would remain the greater of the two. The original old city, the vetus urbs, lies under present-day Santiponce, while the archaeological site covers mainly the new city that Hadrian added to the north.

Italica was the first Roman settlement in Spain. It was founded in 206 BCE by Publius Cornelius Scipio during the Second Punic War, close to a native Iberian town of the Turdetani, as a settlement for his Italic veterans, a mixture of allies and Roman citizens, and was named after them. It grew by drawing migrants from the Italian peninsula and the children of Roman soldiers and native women. Among the settlers were a branch of the gens Ulpia from Tuder in Umbria and a branch of the gens Aelia from Hadria, the families of the emperors Trajan and Hadrian. According to some authors it was also the birthplace of Theodosius I.

The old city was laid out on a Hippodamian street plan with a forum at the centre, linked to a busy river port. Italica thrived under the patronage of Hadrian, who expanded it northwards as the new city and, at its request, raised it to the status of colonia, although it already held the rights of municipium. He added temples, including the enormous Traianeum, which honoured his predecessor and adoptive father, and rebuilt public buildings. The city began to dwindle as early as the 3rd century, when a shift in the bed of the Guadalquivir left its port high and dry. In late antiquity it had a bishop and, in the Visigothic age, a garrison, and its walls were restored by Leovigild in 583.

Because no modern city covers much of the new city, Italica is an unusually well preserved Roman site, with cobbled streets and mosaic floors still in place. Its amphitheatre, the third largest in the Roman Empire at the time, seated 25,000 spectators in a city whose population is estimated at only 8,000. The Traianeum measured 108 by 80 metres and was decorated with over a hundred columns of Cipollino marble, and an aqueduct of 37 kilometres fed a huge cistern that remains intact. Houses of the elite quarter keep splendid mosaics, among them the House of the Birds and the House of the Neptune Mosaic.

The ruins were long used as a quarry: in 1740 Seville ordered the amphitheatre's walls demolished to build a dam. A first law of protection took effect in 1810, and Italica was declared a National Monument by Royal Order of 1912.
italo-balbo: Italo Balbo was born on 6 June 1896 in Quartesana, part of Ferrara. He supported Italy's entry into the First World War, served with the Alpini, and by the end of the war had earned one bronze and two silver medals for valour and the rank of captain. He then took a law degree and a degree in Social Sciences, with a thesis on the thought of Giuseppe Mazzini, and worked as a bank clerk in Ferrara. In 1921 he joined the National Fascist Party and soon became secretary of the Ferrara Fascist organization.

Balbo formed his own group, nicknamed Celibano, which broke strikes for landowners and attacked communists and socialists. At twenty-six he was the youngest of the four Quadrumvirs who planned the March on Rome in 1922, and in 1923 he became a founding member of the Grand Council of Fascism. In 1926 he became Secretary of State for Air and began building the Italian Royal Air Force. He organized air cruises over the Mediterranean in 1928 and 1929, and led twelve flying boats from Orbetello to Rio de Janeiro between 17 December 1930 and 15 January 1931, in which some aircraft were lost.

From 1 July to 12 August 1933 twenty-four seaplanes flew from Rome to the Century of Progress exposition in Chicago and back. Chicago renamed a street Balbo Drive, and President Franklin Roosevelt presented him with the Distinguished Flying Cross. Back in Italy he was made Marshal of the Air Force.

Balbo governed the new colony of Libya, formed on 1 January 1934, and was in effect removed from Roman politics, where Mussolini saw him as a threat. He built the Via Balbia and the Marble Arch, unveiled on 16 March 1937, and tried to attract Italian immigrants. He was the only leading Fascist to oppose strongly the Racial Laws of 1938 and to criticize publicly the alliance with Nazi Germany.

On 28 June 1940, shortly after British aircraft had attacked Tobruk, Italian anti-aircraft batteries misidentified his Savoia-Marchetti SM.79 and shot it down, killing everyone aboard. Rumours that Mussolini ordered his assassination have been debunked. The RAF dropped a wreath with a note of condolence. He was buried outside Tripoli on 4 July 1940, and in 1970 his remains were brought to Orbetello and reburied by his family.
italo-turkish-war: Italian claims to Libya date back to the Ottoman defeat by Russia in the war of 1877–1878. At the Congress of Berlin in 1878 France and the United Kingdom agreed to a French occupation of Tunisia and British control over Cyprus, and the French told Italian diplomats that Tripoli would be a counterpart for Italy. Italy made a secret agreement with Britain in February 1887, and in 1902 signed a secret treaty with France giving freedom of intervention in Tripolitania and Morocco. In the 1909 Racconigi Bargain Russia acknowledged Italy's interest in Tripoli and Cyrenaica.

Italy published a declaration of its direct interest in Libya on 29 September 1911, and military operations began with the bombardment of Tripoli on 3 October. The Ottomans had sent their Libyan battalions to Yemen and had no full army in Tripolitania; their officers travelled there secretly through Egypt, and local Libyans were organised for the defence. Italian forces captured Tripoli, Tobruk, Derna, Bengasi and Homs between 3 and 21 October, but suffered a defeat at Shar al-Shatt. The corps was then enlarged to 100,000 men, and the war became one of position, with the Italians unable to advance far inland.

The war saw early uses of new technology. On 23 October 1911 Capitano Carlo Piazza flew the first aerial reconnaissance mission, and on 1 November Sottotenente Giulio Gavotti dropped the first aerial bomb on Ottoman troops. At sea the Italian Navy, with seven times the tonnage of the Ottoman, sank Ottoman gunboats at Kunfuda Bay in January 1912 and ships at Beirut on 24 February. On land the Ottomans turned to guerrilla tactics, and the Italians answered with repressive measures including public hangings; in October 1911 Italian troops killed thousands of civilians in the Tripoli massacre.

The Treaty of Ouchy, signed on 18 October 1912, gave Italy possession of Libya, and Italy agreed to return the Dodecanese. The vagueness of its text, the Balkan Wars and the First World War kept the islands under Italian administration, and in 1923 Turkey recognised the Italian annexation at the Treaty of Lausanne. The islands became part of Greece by treaty in 1947.

The war cost Italy 1.3 billion lire, nearly a billion more than Giovanni Giolitti had estimated. Resistance by the Senussi continued, and Italian control of the interior was ineffective until the late 1920s, when Pietro Badoglio and Rodolfo Graziani waged pacification campaigns. Resistance ended after the execution of Omar Mukhtar on 15 September 1931. The war is considered a precursor of the First World War: the Balkan League attacked the Ottoman Empire in October 1912, starting the First Balkan War days before the treaty.
italy: Italy consists of the Italian Peninsula, which extends into the Mediterranean Sea, together with Sicily, Sardinia and nearly 800 islands. It covers 301,340 square kilometres, with the Alps along most of its northern boundary and the Apennine Mountains forming the backbone of the peninsula. Over 35% of its territory is mountainous, and the highest point is the summit of Mont Blanc at 4,810 metres. Many parts are of volcanic origin, and active volcanoes include Mount Etna in Sicily, the largest in Europe, as well as Vulcano, Stromboli and Vesuvius. The sovereign states of San Marino and Vatican City are enclaves within Italy.

Lower Paleolithic artefacts dating back 850,000 years have been recovered from Monte Poggiolo. Pre-Roman Italy was inhabited mostly by Italic peoples, along with the Etruscans, the Elymians and Sicani of Sicily, and the prehistoric Sardinians who gave rise to the Nuragic civilisation. Phoenicians established emporiums on the coasts of Sicily and Sardinia, and during the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Greek colonies were founded, an area later known as Magna Graecia. Rome, a settlement on the River Tiber traditionally founded in 753 BCE, was ruled by monarchs for 244 years, and in 509 BCE the Romans expelled the monarchy and established a republic.

Roman expansion consolidated the peninsula, named Italia, and Rome grew into an empire stretching from Britain to the borders of Persia. Augustus, the first emperor, began an age of peace and prosperity. Barbarian invasions led to the decline and fall of the Western Roman Empire, after which the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy was created.

By the 11th century Italian city-states and maritime republics expanded, and the Italian Renaissance flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries. After centuries of political division the Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861, following wars of independence and the Expedition of the Thousand. The fascist dictatorship was established in 1922, and in 1946 a republic replaced the monarchy.

Italy has 58,915,561 inhabitants, and Rome is the capital. It has been a unitary parliamentary republic since 1946, with a president elected for a single seven-year term and a perfectly bicameral Parliament made up of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate of the Republic.
From the late 19th century to the 1960s Italy was a country of mass emigration, and the diaspora included more than 25 million Italians. Italy has 62 World Heritage Sites.
itchan-kala: Khiva is divided in the traditional way into two parts: the Inner City, Itchan Kala, enclosed by an inner defensive wall, and the outer city, Dishan-Qal'a, enclosed by an outer wall. Both walls are of mud brick. The walls of Itchan Kala are 8 to 10 metres high and 5 to 6 metres thick, with a perimeter of 6,250 metres. Watchtowers project outward every 30 metres, and the top of the wall is crenellated for defenders to shoot from.

Water-filled moats were part of the defence, and remnants can still be seen in the south, while in the north and west old clay pipes cover them. Four gates remain: Bogcha Gate in the north, Polvon Gate in the east, Tosh Gate in the south and Ota Gate in the west. They have towers on both sides of the passage and galleries above, and a long passage may have several domes.

The building of the monuments falls into four periods. The first runs from ancient Khorezm to the Mongol invasion, and from it come the western wall of the Konya Ark, an ancient tower in the north-eastern corner of the castle wall and remains of the castle wall. The second is the restoration after the Mongol invasion of 1220, when the Said Alovuddin Mausoleum was built.

In the third period, in the 16th and 17th centuries under Abulgazi Khan and Asfandiyar Khan, Anusha Khan's bathhouse (1657), the Ak Mosque (1675) and the madrasa of Khojamberdibi (1688) were raised, and the khan's reception hall was built in 1686-1688. In the first half of the 18th century the war between Bukhara and Iran for the Khanate of Khiva badly damaged the town.

The fourth period runs from the 18th to the 20th century. The Juma Mosque, established in the 10th century, was rebuilt in 1788-1789 and kept a hypostyle hall with 112 columns taken from ancient structures. A main road was laid between two gates and the ruined walls were restored. Building quickened under Muhammad Rahim Khan I (1806-1825), Alla-Kulli-Khan (1825-1842) and Muhammad Amin Bahadur Khan (1845-1855): the palace in the Konya Ark was finished, the Toshhovli Palace was built, and a caravanserai, madrasa and tim went up near the Polvan Gate. The Pahlavon Mahmud Mausoleum was also built in this period.

The old town keeps more than 50 historic monuments and 250 old houses, mostly of the 18th or 19th century. Among the notable buildings are the Konya Ark, the Juma Mosque, the Ak Mosque, the Hasanmurod Qushbegi Mosque, the madrasas of Alla-Kulli-Khan, Muhammad Aminkhon and Muhammad Rakhimkhon, the mausoleums of Pahlavon Mahmoud and Sayid Allavuddin, and caravanserais and markets. Local legend holds that the water channel of Khiva was dug by Shem, the son of Noah.
itjtawy: The exact site of Itjtawy is still unknown. Circumstantial evidence places it beneath cultivated fields east of the pyramids of Amenemhat I and Senusret I at Lisht. It lay hundreds of miles down the Nile from Thebes, and it may have been chosen to be close to the route of Asiatic incursions into Egypt, in order to guard against further attacks.

There is evidence that Amenemhat I, founder of the 12th Dynasty, established the city in the twentieth year of his reign, replacing Thebes as the capital. The earliest known mention of Itjtawy, however, comes ten years later, on a double-dated stela of his thirtieth year, now in the Cairo Museum as CG 20516.

The hieroglyph used to write the name is not the usual sign for a city but that of a fortified enclosure. From this the Egyptologist Steven Snape suggested that Itjtawy was a disembedded capital: a small centre of administrative buildings and a royal residence, lived in only by the staff who ran them, while the great economic and cultural centres remained older cities such as Memphis and Thebes.

Itjtawy remained the capital through the 12th and 13th dynasties at least until the reign of Merneferre Ay, the last king of the period attested by objects from outside Upper Egypt. It is believed that around this time people from Canaan invaded Lower Egypt, bringing the Middle Kingdom to an end and opening the Second Intermediate Period. The kings of the 13th Dynasty then abandoned Itjtawy and withdrew south to Thebes.
ito-hirobumi: Itō Hirobumi was born Hayashi Risuke on 16 October 1841 in Tsukari village in Suō Province, within the Chōshū Domain, the son of a farmer of humble origins. His father entered the service of a low-ranking samurai, Itō Naoemon, and was adopted with his household into the Itō family, which gave them samurai status at the lowest rank. His name became Itō Shunsuke in 1858 and Hirobumi around 1869. In 1863 he was one of the Chōshū Five who secretly travelled to Britain, against the shogunate's ban on overseas travel, and studied at University College London.

After the Meiji Restoration of 1868 his knowledge of the West advanced him. He became the first governor of Hyōgo Prefecture, and in 1870 and 1871 he toured the United States to study finance, which influenced the New Currency Regulation of 1871 that put Japan on the gold standard. From late 1871 to 1873 he was one of four deputy ambassadors of the Iwakura Mission to the United States and Europe, where his ability to speak English made him useful. On his return he sided with those who opposed a military expedition to Korea, and was appointed councilor and minister of public works.

In the Political Crisis of 1881 he used Ōkuma Shigenobu's proposal for a British-style parliament to force Ōkuma's resignation and secured agreement on a gradual, Prussian-influenced course, emerging as first among equals in the Meiji oligarchy. He then travelled in Europe and from 1884 headed the bureau drafting the constitution. In 1885 he replaced the Daijō-kan with a cabinet and became the first prime minister. He led the Privy Council that reviewed the constitution before its promulgation in 1889.

His pragmatism earned him the nickname Round Itō. He accepted reluctantly that a government party was needed, an idea Yamagata and the other elder statesmen vetoed in 1892, and he founded the Rikken Seiyūkai in 1900.

Itō oversaw the First Sino-Japanese War and negotiated the Qing dynasty's surrender on terms that included the annexation of Taiwan. After the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905 he became the first Resident-General of Korea. He first supported a protectorate rather than annexation, but pressure from the army leadership and the failure of his gradualist approach contributed to his support for annexation. He resigned in June 1909 and four months later was assassinated at Harbin in Manchuria by the independence activist An Jung-geun.
its-a-long-way-to-tipperary: Jack Judge met Harry Williams at the Malt Shovel public house in Oldbury, Worcestershire. Their partnership produced 32 music hall songs published by Bert Feldman. Judge could not read or write music, so Williams taught the songs to him by ear. In January 1912 Judge was performing at the Grand Theatre in Stalybridge and accepted a bet of 5 shillings that he could compose and sing a new song by the next night. On 31 January he performed the song for the first time, and it was an immediate success. Feldman published it in October 1912 and promoted it as a march.

After Williams's death in 1924 Judge claimed sole credit, saying he had agreed to share the credit with Williams as recompense for a debt. Williams's family showed that the tune and most of the lyrics already existed in a 1909 manuscript, "It's A Long Way to Connemara", co-written by Williams and Judge, with Tipperary replacing Connemara. In 1917 Alice Smyth Burton Jay sued the publishers Chappell & Co., alleging that she had written the tune in 1908; the court dismissed the suit in 1920.

The song was written as a sentimental ballad for Irish expatriates in London and tells of an Irish worker in London who misses his homeland. Unlike songs of earlier wars, such as the Second Boer War, it did not call soldiers to glorious deeds but dwelt on longing for home. In the verses an Irishman comes to London, where the streets are said to be paved with gold, and writes to his sweetheart Molly, who replies that Mike Maloney wants to marry her. The chorus says goodbye to Piccadilly and Leicester Square and declares that it is a long way to Tipperary but that his heart is already there.

Feldman persuaded Florrie Forde to sing the song in 1913, but she disliked it and dropped it; it nevertheless became the hit of 1913. British soldiers marching to Mons sang it, and the Daily Mail correspondent George Curnock saw the Connaught Rangers singing it as they marched through Boulogne on 13 August 1914. As soldiers lost hope of a quick end to the war they came to abhor the song, and the veteran F. T. Nettleingham called it "never Tommy's song". John McCormack recorded it in November 1914, which helped its worldwide popularity.
itsukushima: Itsukushima, popularly known as Miyajima, which means Shrine Island, lies in the western part of the Inland Sea of Japan, in the north-west of Hiroshima Bay. It is one of Hayashi Gahō's Three Views of Japan, specified in 1643, and belongs to the city of Hatsukaichi in Hiroshima Prefecture; before a merger in 2005 it was the town of Miyajima. The island and the waters around it lie within Setonaikai National Park. Strong tides expose the sea bottom beyond the shrine's torii at low tide, and at high tide the sea fills the areas under the shrine boardwalk.

The island is mountainous and sparsely settled, with an area of only 30.39 square kilometres and a population of about 2,000. Its highest point is the peak of Mount Misen, at 535 metres. Because the island is seen as sacred, trees may not be cut for lumber, and sika deer roam freely; in Shinto they are thought of as messengers of the gods. Its maple trees are known throughout Japan, and momiji manjū, pastries with maple-leaf emblems, are a popular souvenir.

The site was considered sacred for a long time, and locals may have built a simple shrine there before the complex was built in 593. In 1168 Taira no Kiyomori, a warrior-courtier, contributed greatly to giving the shrine its present form. The existence of the shrine is confirmed by early 9th century texts, and the Nihon Shoki confirms the sacredness of these structures during the Heian period. Daiganji Temple was reconstructed around 1200, in the Kamakura period. The Five-storied Pagoda was built in 1407.

In the 16th century Toyotomi Hideyoshi began the Senjōkaku, a pavilion of a thousand mats and the largest structure on the island, as a Buddhist library where sutras could be chanted for fallen soldiers. He died in 1598 and it was never fully completed. Until the Meiji Restoration forbade the mixing of Shinto and Buddhism in 1868, Daishō-in temple administered the Itsukushima Shrine. The Senjōkaku was then converted into a Shinto shrine dedicated to Hideyoshi.

The Itsukushima Shrine, a Shinto shrine known for its floating torii gate, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the National Treasures of Japan. Next to it stands Daiganji Temple, dedicated to the goddess Benzaiten, one of the three best-known Benzaiten temples in Japan, which opens its Benzaiten to the public only on 17 June. Daishō-in on Mount Misen is the headquarters of the Omuro branch of Shingon Buddhism and the 14th temple of the Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage. A ferry of about ten minutes crosses to the mainland at Miyajimaguchi.
itza-language: Itzaʼ was a language of administration across much of the Yucatán Peninsula when Chichen Itza was supreme, and it was later the language of the last independent Maya nation in Mesoamerica, which held out in the Petén Basin until 1697. When the Spanish subjugated the Itza capital, its people fled or lived among the Spaniards, as at San José, where the language is still spoken on the north shore of Lake Petén Itzá. It belongs to the Yucatecan branch with Yucatec, Lacandon and Mopan, though Itzaʼ and Yucatec speakers have difficulty understanding each other.

Itzaʼ has no tone, and vowel length is contrastive; the sounds d, g, f, v, r and ɲ occur only in loanwords from Spanish. It is an ergative-absolutive language with split ergativity. Possession uses the same ergative marker as verbs, and body parts, kin and personal property are possessed differently from parts of a whole. Nouns have gender, the masculine and feminine marked by a prefix, typically on proper nouns and professions. The future is formed with the irrealis mood and the past with the perfect, each with a temporal adjective. The basic word order is VOS, though VSO is also common.

The government of Guatemala banned the speaking of Itzaʼ in the 1930s, and two generations grew up learning only Spanish. Interest in preserving Maya heritage rose in the late 1980s, and the Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala works to preserve the language. Its vocabulary for crops and animals distinguishes varieties by size, colour and taste, and its farming words have barely changed since they were first recorded. Speech relies on repetition, parallelism and framing particles that set each phrase within the wider discourse.
itza-people: The Itza descended from the Ah Itzá lineage of the Yucatecan Maya, and accounts of their beginnings differ. One holds that they came from the Chanes of the Chontal region of Tabasco and moved to Bacalar and northern Yucatán in the 10th century; another that they may have come from the Classic Period city of Motul de San José near Lake Petén Itzá and moved north during the Maya collapse. From their capital at Chichén Itzá, whose name means at the mouth of the well of the Itza, they built a trade empire reaching south to Naco in Honduras.

The books of Chilam Balam tell how Hunac Ceel, founder of the Cocom dynasty of Mayapan, survived being thrown into the cenote of Chichén Itzá and later destroyed the city. The story is partly mythical, but the Itza are generally held to have lost a power struggle among the Cocom, Xiu and Itzá lineages. Around 1331 Chichén Itzá and other Itza sites such as Isla Cerritos were abandoned, as Mexicanized Putún Maya moved in from Tabasco and central Mexico. The Itza went south to the Petén Basin and built their capital Nojpetén, great island, which early Spanish accounts called Tayasal.

After the fall of the Aztecs, Hernán Cortés passed through Itza territory on his expedition to Honduras, executed the last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtémoc, there, and visited Nojpetén, where he held mass with the Kan Ek' of the Itza. Spanish priests still preached to the last Itza king in 1696, and on 13 March 1697 the kingdom submitted to a force led by Martín de Ursua, governor of Yucatán.

Spanish colonial rule and later Guatemalan governments pursued policies that hastened the loss of Itza culture and language. In the 1930s the government of President Jorge Ubico Castañeda banned the use and teaching of the Itza language and traditional dress in Petén. The census of 2002 counted 1,983 ethnic Itza. The few descendants live in the town of San José, north of Lake Petén Itzá, and only 36 elderly native speakers remain. Itza agro-forestry, including the use of dietary and medicinal plants, may still show how the pre-colonial Itza managed the Maya lowlands.
itzamna: Itzamná is an upper god and creator deity of Maya mythology, thought to reside in the sky. Little is known about him beyond scattered references in early colonial Spanish reports and dictionaries. J. Eric S. Thompson read his name as "lizard house", from itzam, iguana, and na, house, but that reading has gradually been abandoned. There is no consensus on its meaning; the root itz denotes secretions such as dew, sap and semen and also sorcery, so itzam could mean "asperser" or "sorcerer". The early colonial sources variously connect Itzamná with, and sometimes identify him as, Hunab Ku, the sun deity Kinich Ahau, and the omen bird Yaxcocahmut.

The most reliable source, Diego de Landa, mentions him in his account of the ritual year. In the month of Uo the books were ritually sprinkled under the invocation of Kinich Ahau Itzamná, "the first priest". In Zip he was invoked as one of the gods of medicine, and in Mac the very old venerated him alongside the Chaacs, the rain deities. One year of the four-year cycle was under his patronage.

Diego López de Cogolludo states that Itzamná invented the priestly art of writing and describes Zamna as a priest who divided the land of Yucatán and named its features. Itzamná was also the creator of humankind and the father of Bacab, a fourfold deity of the interior of the Earth. In another tradition he fathered thirteen sons with Ixchel, two of whom created the Earth and humankind.

Before the names of the Maya deities were deciphered, he was known as God D, and archaeologists still sometimes use that name. The Dresden Codex gives him a role like that described by Landa. Classic images show him as an upper god on a celestial throne, governing agriculture and the hunt, sometimes dressed as a high priest and identified in hieroglyphs as the god of rulership. From the Paris Codex back to the San Bartolo murals he takes the form of the Principal Bird Deity, whose wings carry the signs for daylight and night. Kings of Yaxchilan, Dos Pilas and Naranjo bore Itzamnaaj in their names or titles.
itzcoatl: Itzcoatl, whose name in Classical Nahuatl, Itzcōhuātl, means "Obsidian Serpent", was born around 1380. He was the natural son of the tlatoani Acamapichtli and an unknown Tepanec woman from Azcapotzalco. His half-brother was Huitzilihuitl, and he was an uncle of Chimalpopoca and of Moctezuma I. He married the princess Huacaltzintli, and they had a son, Tezozomoc.

Itzcoatl was elected king of Tenochtitlan, the fourth to hold the office, after his nephew and predecessor Chimalpopoca was killed by Maxtla of the neighbouring Tepanec city-state of Azcapotzalco. Allied with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco, he defeated Maxtla and ended Tepanec domination of central Mexico. Itzcoatl, Nezahualcoyotl and Totoquilhuaztli, king of Tlacopan, then formed the Triple Alliance, the basis of the later Aztec Empire.

Itzcoatl next turned to the chinampas districts on the south shores of Lakes Xochimilco and Chalco, where fresh water springs had allowed extensive raised gardens to be built on the shallow lake floors. Campaigns against Xochimilco in 1430, Mixquic in 1432, Cuitlahuac in 1433 and Tezompa secured agricultural resources for Tenochtitlan. With the conquest of Culhuacan and Coyoacán, they cemented the Triple Alliance's control over the southern half of the Valley of Mexico. In 1439 he led a campaign outside the valley, against Cuauhnahuac, now Cuernavaca.

According to the Florentine Codex, Itzcoatl ordered the burning of all historical codices because it was "not wise that all the people should know the paintings". Among other purposes, this allowed the Aztec state to develop an official history and mythology that honoured Huitzilopochtli. During his reign temples, roads and a causeway were built at Tenochtitlan.
Itzcoatl also set up the religious and governmental hierarchy that his nephew Moctezuma I took over when Itzcoatl died in 1440. He is regarded as the founder of the Aztec Empire.
iuput-ii: Iuput II, also spelled Auput II, ruled Leontopolis in the late Third Intermediate Period, a time of disorder when several kings shared Lower Egypt, among them Osorkon IV at Bubastis and the prince Tefnakht at Sais. His throne name, known from monuments of the Delta that name a king Usermaatre Setepenamun, Iuput Si-Bast, was Usermaatre-setepen-amun/re.

He allied himself with Tefnakht in resisting the Kushite king Piye's invasion of Lower Egypt. After Piye defeated Tefnakht's coalition and conquered the north, around the 20th year of his reign, he allowed Iuput II to stay on as local governor of Leontopolis, as Piye's Victory Stela from Jebel Barkal records.

The 21st year of Iuput's reign is attested on a stela from Mendes, fully published in 1982, which shows the great chief of the Ma Smendes, son of Harnakht and ruler of Mendes. The British Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen notes that it gives Iuput's name but not his throne name. Other objects of his reign include a statue base from Tell el Yahudieh, a bronze door hinge from Tell Moqdam, the site of Leontopolis, which also names his chief queen, Tent-kat, and a glazed plaque now in the Brooklyn Museum.

The Brooklyn plaque stands out from the art of its period. Instead of the long-legged, slender figure usual in the Third Intermediate Period, it shows Iuput shorter and more muscular, in proportions that recall Old Kingdom art. For this reason it has been taken as evidence that the archaising style once thought to have come from Nubia and spread through Egypt under the 25th Dynasty began earlier, in the Delta, and that Kushite and later Saite artists took up a trend that already existed.
ivan-alexander-of-bulgaria: Ivan Alexander was the son of Despot Sratsimir of Kran and of Petrica, a sister of Michael Asen III of Bulgaria, and so a nephew of Michael Asen III and a descendant of the Asen dynasty. The date of his birth is unknown. By 1330 he was a despot governing the city of Lovech. That year he fought the Serbs at the Battle of Velbazhd alongside his father and his father-in-law Basarab of Wallachia, and Bulgaria was defeated. The defeat and worsening relations with the Byzantine Empire brought an internal crisis, and in 1331 a coup drove Ivan Stefan out of Tarnovo and the conspirators placed Ivan Alexander on the throne.

In 1331 he reconquered north-eastern Thrace from the Byzantines. Relations with Serbia eased under Stefan Uroš IV Dušan, who allied with him and married his sister Helena of Bulgaria in 1332. In the summer of 1332 the Byzantine emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos advanced while a rebellion by Belaur broke out at Vidin. Ivan Alexander defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Rusokastro and made peace on the status quo. In 1344 the regency of John V Palaiologos ceded him Philippopolis and nine fortresses in the Rhodope Mountains for his support in the Byzantine civil war, his last major foreign success.

Afterwards the empire suffered Turkish raids on Thrace, the Black Death and the loss of his sons Ivan Asen IV in 1349 and Michael Asen IV by 1355. Louis I of Hungary conquered Vidin in 1365 and took Ivan Sratsimir captive, but Ivan Alexander, with money paid by John V after Count Amadeus VI of Savoy had seized Bulgarian coastal cities, induced Dobrotica of Dobruja and Vladislav I of Wallachia to reconquer it in 1369. He also crowned sons of his second marriage, Ivan Shishman and Ivan Asen V, as co-emperors, while Ivan Sratsimir became effectively independent around 1356.

Ivan Alexander died on 17 February 1371 and was succeeded by Ivan Sratsimir at Vidin and Ivan Shishman at Tarnovo. His reign saw a cultural flowering, sometimes called the Second Golden Age of Bulgarian culture. He ordered many monasteries and churches built or renovated, and portraits of him as a donor survive at the Bachkovo Monastery and the Rock-hewn Churches of Ivanovo.

Works of the period include the Middle Bulgarian translation of the Manasses Chronicle of 1344 to 1345, the Tetraevangelia of Ivan Alexander of 1355 to 1356, now in the British Library, and the Tomić Psalter of 1360. He convened councils in 1350 and 1359 to 1360 that condemned heresies such as the Bogomils, and the writer Ivan Vazov made him the hero of a novelette and a drama.
ivan-asen-i: Ivan Asen came from the Byzantine theme of Paristrion; his exact place and date of birth are unknown. Chronicles of the late 12th and early 13th centuries describe him and his brothers Theodor, later called Peter, and Kaloyan as Vlachs, but they were most likely of mixed Bulgarian, Cuman and Vlach ancestry, a question that remains controversial. Ivan was his baptismal name; Asen and Belgun are Turkic, meaning sound, safe, healthy and wise. Robert of Clari wrote that Asen had charge of one of the emperor's horse farms, which may show that he was a pastoralist rather than a landowner.

In autumn 1185 Asen and Theodor met the Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos at Kypsela in Thrace to ask for a grant. The emperor refused, and on the order of his uncle John Doukas Asen was struck across the face for impudence. A special tax for the emperor's marriage to Margaret of Hungary had already brought the Bulgarian and Vlach population to the edge of revolt. The brothers had shamans declare that Saint Demetrius of Thessalonica would come over to their side, and Theodor was crowned as Peter. After Isaac II defeated them in early 1186 they fled across the Danube, and returned in the autumn with Cuman reinforcements, seizing Paristrion.
